## Document Metadata
- Type: SBIR Phase I Final Report
- Client/Agency: NASA
- Program/Solicitation: 2016 NASA SBIR
- Date: September 10, 2016
- BST Products/Systems Referenced: SuperSwift XT, DragonEye (reference platform), Vector Wing 100 & 500 (reference platforms)
- Key Personnel: Jack Elston (PI), Dr. Dixon, Dr. Stachura, Prof. Argrow (CU), Dr. David Pieri (JPL), Dr. Lois Wardell (Arapahoe SciTech), Dr. Jorge Diaz (volcano sampling expert)

## Executive Summary
This Phase I SBIR report documents Black Swift Technologies' development of the SuperSwift XT UAS system for scientific monitoring of volcanic plumes and ash emissions. The Phase I effort focused on establishing mission requirements, sensor selection, and airframe specifications for high-altitude volcano sampling operations, with planned Phase II implementation of payload integration and flight testing in Colorado and eventual deployment to active volcanoes like Popocateptl (Mexico) and Turrialba (Costa Rica).

## Technical Approach

### Mission Development
BST established a Concept of Operations (CONOPS) based on five primary volcanic sampling mission types:
1. **Volumetric plume profiling** - Grid sampling at multiple altitudes over 30 km radius
2. **Cylindrical profiling** - Continuous vertical profile via helical climb pattern
3. **Long-distance gradient sampling** - 30 km out-and-back transects downwind
4. **Vent contouring** - Terrain-following flight at 50 ft AGL around vents
5. **Terrain mapping** - High-resolution photogrammetry (8 km² per flight at 3.7 cm/pixel)

The CONOPS was driven by past missions to Turrialba volcano (Costa Rica) using DragonEye and Vector Wing platforms, with recommendations from expert volcanologists including Dr. Pieri (JPL) and Dr. Diaz.

### Airframe Requirements Development
SuperSwift XT functional requirements derived from mission profiles:
- Hand-launchable with 1 lb payload to 12,000 ft MSL
- Rail/bungee launchable with 5 lb payload to 12,000 ft MSL
- Ceiling: ≥20,000 ft MSL with 200 ft/min climb capability
- Maximum climb angle: >31° at 18,000 ft with 3 lb payload
- Flight range: >50 nm (80 km) at 20,000 ft
- Endurance: >100 minutes at cruise altitude 8-20,000 ft
- Enhanced roll/pitch authority vs. original SuperSwift
- Operational wind limit: 30 kts (with 40 kts gust capability via airframe upgrade)

### Atmospheric Operational Envelope
- Ambient temperatures: Standard conditions at altitude (icing possible at high altitude)
- Particulate concentrations: Design baseline 500 μg/m³ (maximum 2,000 μg/m³); potential testing up to 4,000 μg/m³
- Maximum wind: 30 kts operational (15.4 m/s), 40 kts gust capability
- Launch altitude: Up to 11,800 ft (Popocateptl worst-case scenario)
- Target altitudes: Up to 19,800 ft MSL

## Products & Capabilities Described

### SuperSwift XT
- **Description**: Ruggedized fixed-wing UAS for harsh environment operations, evolved from original SuperSwift platform
- **Proposed Use**: High-altitude volcano monitoring platform carrying multiple scientific payloads
- **Specifications**:
  - Maximum payload capacity: 5 lbs (rail launch) to 1 lb (hand launch)
  - Flight ceiling: ≥20 kft MSL
  - Endurance: >100 minutes
  - Range: >50 nm
  - Launch methods: Hand launch, rail launch, bungee launch, belly landing on unimproved terrain
  - Payload interfaces: Mechanical and electrical integration planned for Phase II

### Sensor Payload Suite (Selected for Phase II Integration)

**Meteorological:**
- iMet-XF: PTH (pressure, temperature, humidity) measurements
  - Weight: 52g
  - Accuracy: ±2.5 hPa, ±0.7°C, ±5% RH
  - Power: 0.1 W
  
- BST 5-hole probe: 3D wind velocity measurement
  - Weight: 50g
  - Accuracy: ±0.5 m/s, ±0.5° direction
  - Power: 0.5 W

**Trace Gas:**
- iMet-MiniGAS: Multi-gas sensor package
  - Weight: 1,200g (with battery)
  - Measures: CO₂, SO₂, H₂S (PTH integrated)
  - Performance:
    - CO₂: 0-2000 ppm, 20 ppm resolution, <10s response
    - SO₂: 0-200 ppm, 0.5 ppm accuracy, <20s response
    - H₂S: 0-200 ppm, 0.25 ppm accuracy, <35s response
  - Power: ~3.0 W
  - Note: Long response time requires 2-4 minute loitering periods for accurate sampling

**Particulates:**
- MSE Inc. Mini PCS Nephelometer
  - Weight: 250g
  - Forward-looking inlet for particle size-frequency distribution
  - Resolvable sizes: 1-100 μm
  - Power: 20 W

**Imaging:**
- MapIR Survey2 (EO/multispectral): 47g, 1.0 W
- Forward FPV camera (COTS): 200g, 0.9 W
- FLIR VUE thermal imager: 113g, 2.2 W

**Total Payload Mass**: ~2.4 kg (~5.3 lbs) with all sensors

### Reference Platforms Analyzed

## Use Cases & Applications

### Primary Mission: Volcanic Plume Monitoring
**Volcanoes Targeted for Phase II Testing & Deployment:**
- Turrialba Volcano, Costa Rica (10,958 ft elevation)
- Popocateptl, Mexico (17,802 ft elevation) - primary worst-case planning reference

**Mission Scenarios:**
1. **Volumetric Profiling** (example: Popocateptl)
   - 4 parallel 6 km sampling lines spaced 1 km apart
   - 3 altitude levels, 500 ft spacing
   - Total flight distance: 27 km per altitude level
   - Maximum altitude: 19,300 ft MSL
   - Time of flight: 75 minutes
   - Maximum range from launch: 10.4 km

2. **Cylindrical Profiling (Plume Column)**
   - Helical climb pattern directly above volcano
   - Climb/descent rate: 200 ft/min (1 m/s)
   - Maximum height: 2,000 ft above volcano summit
   - Helix diameter: 1 km (adjustable)
   - Time of flight: 34 minutes
   - Maximum altitude: 19,800 ft MSL

3. **Long-Distance Gradient**
   - Downwind transect at ~1,500 ft above summit
   - 30 km out-and-back sampling pattern
   - Maximum altitude: 19,300 ft MSL
   - Time of flight: 74 minutes
   - Maximum range: 37.3 km

4. **Vent Contouring**
   - Terrain-following flight 50 ft AGL over vents
   - Climb slope: up to 31° (steepest portions of Popocateptl)
   - Requires laser altimeter for AGL measurement
   - Time of flight: 14 minutes

5. **Terrain Mapping**
   - High-resolution photogrammetry capability
   - Area coverage: up to 8 km² per flight
   - Ground resolution: 3.7 cm/pixel
   - Flight time: ~90 minutes
   - Total path length: ~62 km

### Secondary Applications
- Validation of volcanic ash transport and dispersion (VATD) models
- Validation of satellite data (OMI, TOMS volcanic SO₂ measurements)
- Aviation hazard characterization (ash concentrations for aircraft safety)
- Atmospheric input data for volcanic hazard forecasting
- Support for remote sensing validation (DOAS, FTIR measurements)

### Operational Timeline (Example Two-Flight Campaign)
- T-24 hrs: Mission planning and flight pattern development
- T-2 hrs: Transport equipment to launch site (man-portable)
- T-45 min: Site identification and preparation
- T-30 min: Aircraft assembly and payload calibration
- T-0: Launch
- T+85-90 min: Mission execution
- T+100 min: Landing, post-flight inspection, data download
- T+2 hrs: Second payload installation
- T+4 hrs: Second flight completion and data download
- T+4.5 hrs: Equipment pack-out and team egress

## Key Results (Phase I Findings)

### Mission Requirements Finalized
- Five sampling scenarios defined and validated with expert volcanologists (Pieri, Wardell)
- Mission profiles confirmed as covering all current and planned volcano monitoring missions
- Sensor compatibility verified with mission profiles (loitering strategies developed to accommodate sensor response times)
- Airframe requirements updated to accommodate refined mission and sensor specifications

### Sensor Selection Completed
Two candidate payload configurations developed and refined based on:
- Weight/size constraints (optimized for SuperSwift XT)
- Scientific capability (measurements of CO₂, SO₂, H₂S, particulates, PTH, wind)
- COTS availability (avoiding prototypes not yet commercialized)
- Integration feasibility (no extensive hand-held device modifications)

**Final Payload Selected:**
- iMet-miniGAS (trace gas + PTH)
- BST 5-hole probe (3D winds)
- MSE Mini PCS Nephelometer (particulates)
- MapIR Survey2 + FLIR VUE (imaging)
- Total mass: 2.4 kg (well within SuperSwift capacity)

### Airframe Capability Gaps Identified
Compared to reference platforms (DragonEye, Vector Wing 100/500), SuperSwift XT must achieve:
- Higher altitude ceiling (20 kft vs. 12-15 kft of predecessors)
- Greater endurance (>100 min vs. 30-60 min)
- Better climb performance (31° slope capability)
- Multi-launch method flexibility (hand, rail, bungee)
- Enhanced control authority for turbulent volcanic environments

### Atmospheric Operational Envelope Defined

## Executive Summary
This is a Pix4D photogrammetry quality report documenting the processing results from a Black Swift UAS aerial survey conducted on November 9, 2016. The survey captured 450 images over a 0.1633 km² area with 1.53 cm ground sampling distance using an ILCE-5100 RGB camera, achieving high-quality orthomosaic and digital surface model (DSM) outputs with strong calibration and geolocation accuracy.

## Technical Approach
The workflow involved:
1. **Image Acquisition**: 450 RGB images captured with Sony ILCE-5100 camera (16mm lens, 6000x4000 resolution)
2. **Photogrammetric Processing**: Pix4D Discovery v3.0.13 software
3. **Calibration**: Bundle block adjustment with automatic tie point extraction and camera parameter optimization
4. **Georeferencing**: Ground control points (GCPs) used for absolute positioning
5. **Product Generation**: Orthomosaic and DSM creation at 1 cm/pixel resolution

## Products & Capabilities Described

### Orthomosaic and Digital Surface Model (DSM)
- **Output Resolution**: 1.53 cm/pixel GSD
- **Coverage Area**: 0.1633 km² (16.33 hectares, 40.36 acres)
- **Processing**: Full 100% image calibration with densification; includes noise filtering and sharp surface smoothing

### Camera System
- **Camera**: Sony ILCE-5100 with 16mm F2.8 lens
- **Resolution**: 6000 x 4000 pixels
- **Sensor Dimensions**: 23.333 mm x 15.556 mm
- **Optimized Focal Length**: 3964.042 pixels (15.416 mm)

## Key Results

### Image Processing Quality
- **Keypoint Detection**: Median 92,045 keypoints per image
- **Keypoint Matching**: Median 52,434 matches per calibrated image
- **Total 3D Points**: 6,181,308 points generated from bundle block adjustment
- **Reprojection Error**: 0.256 pixels (excellent)
- **Image Calibration**: 450/450 images (100%) successfully calibrated and geolocated

### Positional Accuracy

**Absolute Camera Position/Orientation Uncertainties (Mean ± Sigma)**:
- X: 0.119 ± 0.020 m
- Y: 0.121 ± 0.021 m
- Z: 0.148 ± 0.033 m
- Omega: 0.071 ± 0.007 degrees
- Phi: 0.060 ± 0.014 degrees
- Kappa: 0.035 ± 0.002 degrees

**Relative Camera Position/Orientation Uncertainties (Mean ± Sigma)**:
- X: 0.028 ± 0.005 m
- Y: 0.035 ± 0.007 m
- Z: 0.050 ± 0.029 m
- Omega: 0.043 ± 0.013 degrees
- Phi: 0.049 ± 0.023 degrees
- Kappa: 0.012 ± 0.004 degrees

### Ground Control Point Performance
- **GCPs Evaluated**: 11 check points
- **Marked Inaccurate**: 1 (90.9% acceptance rate)
- **Mean Error**: 2.23 m (X), -2.08 m (Y), -1.46 m (Z)
- **RMS Error**: 2.37 m (X), 2.16 m (Y), 1.61 m (Z)
- **Relative Geolocation Accuracy**: 
  - 97.33% of images within ±2.0 m in X
  - 100% of images within ±2.0 m in Y
  - 94.67% of images within ±2.0 m in Z

### Image Overlap
- Strong multi-image overlap achieved across survey area
- Green areas indicate 5+ image overlap per pixel (good quality zones)
- Red/yellow areas with low overlap minimal

## Notable Details

### Technical Specifications
- **Survey Area**: Small-scale (0.1633 km²) demonstration survey
- **Ground Sampling Distance**: 1.53 cm/pixel—excellent resolution for detailed mapping
- **Processing Hardware**: Intel i7-4710HQ, 16GB RAM, Windows 10
- **Coordinate System**: WGS84 / UTM zone 13N

### Processing Performance
- Camera parameter optimization showed only 3.65% relative difference between initial and optimized values, indicating stable calibration
- 23,426,064 total 2D keypoint observations processed
- Majority of 3D points (3.12 million) observed in 2 images; significant points (up to 28 images) for dense coverage verification

- High-quality orthomosaic generation confirmed by:
  - Low reprojection error (0.256 pixels)

  - Strong absolute and relative position uncertainties within acceptable ranges

## Executive Summary

This proposal aims to advance methane detection and quantification technologies from TRL-5 to TRL-6 for monitoring emissions from orphaned and abandoned oil and gas wells across the U.S. (estimated 310,000-800,000 wells). The project integrates Black Swift Technologies' S2 fixed-wing drone with Quanta3 methane sensors, LI-COR eddy covariance tower systems, novel FluxMapper™ software for geospatial emission tracking, and remote connectivity systems (HOO-nah device from Hyde Park West Telecommunications) to enable continuous, real-time monitoring of methane emissions from orphaned wells, with a focus on detecting emissions as low as 0.2-0.4 kg/hour over a 3-year study period.

---

## Technical Approach

### Overall Strategy
The proposal employs a multi-method, comparative approach to methane detection:

1. **Drone-Based Aerial Surveys** (Aim 1): Black Swift S2 UAS with Quanta3 methane sensor performing eddy covariance analysis during ~50 flights over 3 years at identified orphaned well sites in Colorado
2. **Tower-Based Continuous Monitoring** (Aim 2): LI-COR eddy covariance system deployed for 6-month periods at 3 sites (2 months per site) in Year 2
3. **Software Enhancement** (Aim 3): FluxMapper™ geospatial flux analysis software to convert eddy covariance measurements into spatially-georeferenced emission maps with 0.2 kg/hour sensitivity
4. **Remote Connectivity** (Aim 4): HOO-nah device and Hyde Park West Telecommunications systems for real-time data transmission from remote well sites

### Key Technical Details

**Eddy Covariance Methodology:**
- Combines high-frequency methane concentration data (2 Hz or 10 Hz) with simultaneous wind speed/direction measurements
- Calculates methane flux by tracking atmospheric eddies and covariance of CH₄ concentration with vertical wind velocity
- Enables both plume inversion analysis (near-field, <100 m) and far-field Gaussian plume integration over hours

**Black Swift S2 System Specifications:**
- Flight endurance: up to 90 minutes
- Wingspan: 3 meters
- Payload capacity: 2 kg
- Operational capability: extreme environments, high winds, low temperatures
- Quanta3 sensor sensitivity: 2 ppb (parts per billion)
- Quanta3 sampling frequency: 2 Hz
- Quantification range: detects leaks down to 0.4 kg/hour with eddy covariance analysis

**LI-COR Methane System Specifications:**
- Instrument: LI-7700 open-path laser analyzer
- Operating principle: Wavelength Modulation Spectroscopy (WMS) at near-infrared frequencies
- Precision: 5-10 ppb at 1 Hz sampling for ambient ~2 ppm
- Linearity: ±1% for 0-25 ppm range
- Power draw: <30 W (operates on solar/battery systems)
- Detection without FluxMapper™: 2 kg/hour
- Detection with FluxMapper™: 0.2 kg/hour
- Data storage: 4 GB internal (22-44 days depending on sampling frequency; ~40 MB/day at 0.5 Hz)
- Tower height: 3-5 m for initial deployment; 7 m with 7900-300 tripod mast for FluxMapper™ studies

**FluxMapper™ Software (TRL-5, advancing to TRL-6):**
- Operating principle: Traces 10 Hz eddy covariance measurements backward along wind trajectory to geographic source
- Technology: Time-frequency decomposition + adaptive source detection + knowledge-guided AI + geospatial layers
- Output: Geospatified flux maps at decameter resolution, sub-hourly intervals, in units of kg/hour
- Spatial coverage: 4 km² per deployment
- Sensitivity enhancement: Reduces detection threshold from 2 kg/hour to 0.2 kg/hour
- Emission capture improvement: 95% vs. 60-80% with classical eddy covariance
- Key benefit: Disaggregates flux tower data into individual pixel time-series, enabling multi-well simultaneous monitoring

**Validation/Supplementary Instruments:**
- **Xplorobot**: Ground-based TDLAS laser device for episodic methane quantification
  - Sensitivity: 0.5 ppm
  - Detection range: 50 meters
  - Includes integrated anemometer
  - Used for independent validation at each drone and tower site
  
**Remote Connectivity System (HOO-nah Device):**
- Portable, proprietary system from Hyde Park West Telecommunications
- Connectivity modes: Dynamic switching between cellular, satellite (Starlink, Hughes 9502), optical fiber
- Features: Encrypted transmission, proprietary low-bandwidth video teleconferencing
- Power: Low-power design with solar/battery options
- Data handling: Ethernet and USB interfaces; compatible with LI-COR equipment
- Patents: 7 patents (2 US, 1 pending; 1 EPO covering Germany, Ireland, UK, Switzerland, Liechtenstein; 4 Australia)

## Products & Capabilities Described

### Black Swift S2 UAS
**What it is:** Fixed-wing unmanned aircraft system designed for long-range environmental monitoring in extreme conditions

**Proposed use in this project:**
- Platform for carrying Quanta3 methane sensor
- Performing ~50 episodic flights over 3 years across orphaned well sites in Colorado
- Each flight complemented by ground-based Xplorobot measurements for validation
- Initial screening of methane-emitting orphaned wells to identify sites for intensive tower-based monitoring

**Performance specifications:**
- Flight endurance: 90 minutes
- Wingspan: 3 meters
- Payload: 2 kg
- Operational range: Capable of flying in extreme weather (high winds, low temperatures)
- Quanta3 sensitivity: 2 ppb
- Methane quantification with eddy covariance: 0.4 kg/hour
- TRL advancement goal: TRL-5 → TRL-6

**Key advantages noted:**
- Covers larger areas than tower systems
- Provides spatial distribution of emissions
- Eliminates human exposure risk
- Automated data collection with high data density
- Reduced operational costs compared to continuous tower monitoring
- Adapts well to high wind speeds (including hurricane-force conditions)

**Limitations identified:**
- Requires access for takeoff/landing within 1 km of source
- Sensitive to cloud cover
- Wind speed dependency: optimal 2-6 m/s; unreliable <2 m/s due to plume variability
- May require re-visiting sites if emissions not detected or are episodic
- Deployment affected by meteorological conditions (insolation, wind direction steadiness)

### Quanta3 Methane Sensor
**What it is:** Custom-built, integrated methane detector for the S2 UAS platform

**Specifications:**
- Sensitivity: 2 ppb (parts per billion)
- Sampling frequency: 2 Hz
- Operating range: Stable across wide range of temperatures
- Integration: Designed for eddy covariance analysis (wind sensing + CH₄ concentration)

**Design features:**
- Provides high-resolution, real-time methane concentration data
- Maintains precision across varying environmental conditions

### FluxMapper™ Software
**What it is:** Advanced data analysis software for converting eddy covariance measurements into geospatially-referenced emission maps

**Proposed use:**
- Post-processing of both drone-based and tower-based eddy covariance data
- Converting flux tower measurements from flux density (kg/hour/m²) to discrete source emissions (kg/hour)
- Creating time-series emission maps at decameter resolution
- Monitoring multiple wells simultaneously across 4 km² areas
- Enhancing detection sensitivity for low-emitting orphaned wells

**Performance claims:**
- TRL-5 → TRL-6 advancement through this project
- Detection sensitivity: 0.2 kg/hour (vs. 2 kg/hour for classical eddy covariance)
- Emission capture: 95% (vs. 60-80% for classical methods)
- Geospatial resolution: Decameter-scale pinpointing
- Temporal resolution: Sub-hourly intervals
- Statistical power increase: 10-fold through pixel disaggregation

**Validation basis:**
- Cross-validation with controlled methane release experiments
- Comparison with independent eddy covariance measurements
- Large eddy simulation confirmation of landscape-level accuracy

### LI-COR Methane System Components
**LI-7700 Open-Path Methane Analyzer:**
- Laser technology: Single-mode tunable near-infrared
- Detection method: Wavelength Modulation Spectroscopy (WMS)
- Compensation: Temperature and pressure algorithms maintain stability
- Precision: 5-10 ppb (1 Hz sampling)
- Range: 0-25 ppm linear response (±1%)
- Temperature stability: Self-cleaning mirrors, regulated optics

**Tower Configuration:**
- Sonic anemometer: Gill WindMaster (10 Hz wind vector measurement)
- Supporting analyzers: LI-7500DS (CO₂, H₂O open-path)
- Data system: SmartFlux acquisition
- Connectivity: Sierra Wireless AirLink RV50X (cellular) or Hughes 9502 (satellite)
- Time synchronization: GPS clocks with Precision Time Protocol (sub-microsecond accuracy)

**Use in project:**
- Deployed for 6-month periods at 3 sites in Year 2 (2 months per site)
- Additional 3-month deployments in Years 2-3 at sites selected based on positive drone results
- Bi-weekly orientation adjustments based on wind patterns and real-time data
- Complementary episodic Xplorobot measurements every two weeks

**Advantages:**

## Executive Summary
Black Swift Technologies proposed to mature SuperSwift sUAS and L-band radiometer technologies for soil moisture mapping through improved manufacturability, new radiometer design, payload integration, and 10 validation flight campaigns. The work aims to transition mature SBIR technology (TRL 6→9) to NASA programs, government agencies, and the commercial precision agriculture market.

## Technical Approach
- Build three SuperSwift aircraft using new manufacturing methods (assessed one-at-a-time for process validation)
- Redesign L-band radiometer for scalable, lower-cost production (current design requires custom calibration and integration)
- Integrate new payloads with modular SuperSwift nose cone design
- Conduct 10 flight campaigns to validate and test all improvements
- Perform manufacturing optimization focused on ease of production and rapid deployment

## Products & Capabilities Described

### SuperSwift sUAS
- Mature, robust small UAS platform
- Multi-payload capable (ability to swap payloads in field)
- Design focused on reliability and cost savings
- Modular nose cone for integrated payloads
- Proposed as mission-enabling technology for NASA with secondary market in commercial UAS

### L-Band Radiometer (Soil Moisture)
- New revision with significant performance improvements
- More stable operation enabling wider adoption
- Current version: custom setup, calibration, and integration required
- Proposed new design: focused on rapid, lower-cost production
- New circuit board design and electronics integration planned

### MALIBU Payload
- Compatible with SuperSwift airframe
- Used for NASA satellite calibration/validation missions
- Can be swapped with soil moisture radiometer in field using same aircraft

## Use Cases & Applications

### NASA Applications
- Product validation for satellite missions: JPSS-1, GOES-R, Sentinel 2a/b, 3a/b, Landsat-8, MSG-3
- Reference measurements for CEOS (Committee on Earth Observation Satellites) calibration and validation framework
- Land validation support as NASA leads CEOS validation activities

### Non-NASA Applications
- **Precision Agriculture**: Soil moisture mapping for irrigation optimization
  - Colorado test site demonstrated >15% water savings with accurate soil moisture data
- **NOAA Mission**: Wildland fire sampling (ongoing collaboration noted)

## Key Technical Objectives
1. Improve airframe manufacturability
2. Design radiometer version optimized for manufacturing
3. Integrate new payloads with modular architecture
4. Validate through 10 flight campaigns

## Notable Details
- Technology maturation path: TRL 6 (beginning) to TRL 9 (end) - near commercialization
- Multi-market strategy: NASA, government agencies (NOAA), commercial precision agriculture
- Emphasizes scalability and rapid adoption pathway
- Quantified benefit: 15%+ water savings demonstrated in precision ag application
- Field swappable payload design enables single aircraft to support multiple mission types
- One-time build methodology ensures manufacturing process validation before scale-up# Certificate of Training Completion

## Document Metadata
- Type: USDA SBIR Proposal - Equipment Documentation (Field 11)
- Client/Agency: USDA

## Executive Summary
This document describes Black Swift Technologies' S2 unmanned aircraft system customized for high-resolution soil moisture mapping using an L-band radiometer payload. The S2 has been specially designed with electromagnetic interference mitigation and optimized payload integration to enable soil moisture measurements at higher spatial and temporal resolution than satellite-based remote sensing, providing agricultural and hydrological insights at root-depth scale.

## Technical Approach
**System Architecture:**
- S2 airframe extensively modified to house L-band antenna and radiometer payload with exact volume matching
- Critical design changes implemented to mitigate electromagnetic interference (essential for measurement accuracy and repeatability)
- Integration of SwiftCore™ flight management system for autonomous and remote operations
- Payload power budget: 50W available, 1.3W used by soil moisture payload

**Flight Management System (SwiftCore™):**
- Comprises SwiftPilot™ (autopilot), SwiftStation™ (ground station), and SwiftTab™ (mobile UI)
- SwiftPilot™: dual 168 MHz Cortex-M4 processors with FPU for autonomous operation; optional 1 GHz Cortex-A8 payload processor
- Modular CAN-bus architecture for flexible payload integration
- SwiftStation™: portable tripod-mounted ground station (<1.5 kg), standard 3dBi 900 MHz dipole and GPS antenna
- SwiftTab™: Android-based interface with gesture controls for field operations
- 10 Hz telemetry update rate via 900 MHz real-time radio link
- Capabilities: autonomous flight planning, pre-defined banking/spirals, real-time data analysis, intervention capability

## Products & Capabilities Described

**S2 UAS (Soil Moisture Mapping Configuration)**
- **Design Purpose:** Customized to house L-band radiometer payload with optimized volume matching
- **Specifications:**
  - MTOW: 7.3 kg / MGTOW: 9.0 kg
  - Wingspan: 3.0 m
  - Fuselage length: 187 cm (excluding air intake nozzle)
  - Propulsion: Electric, propeller-driven
  - IP42 ingress protection rating
  - Launch: Pneumatic or car launch
  
- **Performance:**
  - Flight ceiling: 6,000 m AMSL
  - Cruise speed: 19.0 m/s
  - Stall speed: 12.0 m/s
  - Max stable wind: 15 m/s
  - Endurance: 120 min max / 90 min nominal
  - Max range: 110 km (60 nm) max / 92 km (50 nm) nominal
  - Area coverage: <1,100 acres per mission
  - Take-off/landing corridor: 200 m × 15 m
  - Attitude capability: ±45° roll, ±20° pitch

- **Payload Capacity:**
  - Nominal payload mass: 5.0 kg
  - Available payload power: 50 W
  - Payload mass capacity: 3.5 kg
  - Nose cone: 20.3 cm diameter, 63.2 cm length
  - Geotagging accuracy: <4 m (all directions)
  - Downlink data rate: 9,600 bps (serial)
  - Data storage: SD card

**SwiftCore™ Flight Management System**
- NASA-approved system used on major scientific missions
- NOAA deployments documented
- Designed for complex aerial network operations
- Features real-time telemetry, autonomous-to-landing capability, and field-based decision support

**L-band Radiometer Payload**
- Revision 2 build mentioned with flight testing
- Designed specifically for soil moisture measurement
- Payload power consumption: 1.3 W (well within 50 W budget)
- L-band antenna sized to match S2 payload volume

## Use Cases & Applications
- **Agricultural Soil Monitoring:** Root-depth soil drainage and moisture retention diagnostics
- **End Users:** Government agencies, agronomists, crop consultants, farmers
- **Capability Advantage:** Provides spatial and temporal resolution previously unobtainable through satellite-based remote sensing

## Key Technical Achievements
- Electromagnetic interference mitigation design validated through flight testing with new launcher
- Successful integration of L-band radiometer into S2 platform
- 3D CAD models and Revision 2 prototype documented with flight test data

- Emphasis on American-made equipment compliance for SBIR funding

## Document Metadata
- Type: Statement of Work (SOW) for subcontract
- Client/Agency: DARPA (Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency)
- Program/Solicitation: Albatross Program
- Date: 12/9/2024 (Rev 1; Original Release 11/25/2024)
- BST Products/Systems Referenced: Small uncrewed aircraft systems (s-UAS) fleet
- Key Personnel: 
  - **BST Technical**: Maciej Statchura
  - **BST Program Management**: Beck Cotter
  - **BST Subcontracts**: Parker Vollmer
  - **Prime Contractor (BAE Systems)**: Marco Pravia (Technical), Caroline Richard (PM), Emily Haan (Subcontracts)

## Executive Summary
Black Swift Technologies will serve as a subcontractor to BAE Systems (Information and Electronic Systems Integration Inc.) on the DARPA Albatross program, a 24-month effort to develop and demonstrate autonomous aircraft soaring capabilities. BST will provide a fleet of small uncrewed aircraft systems (s-UAS) and support integration of weather-informed mission planning tools, real-time wind sensing, and autonomous soaring control systems to harness wind energy and extend aircraft range and endurance.

## Technical Approach

**Program Philosophy**: Albatross is NOT an airframe design effort. Instead, it integrates planning tools, sensors, and control solutions on existing or quickly-assembled small uncrewed aircraft to autonomously identify and respond to soaring conditions.

**Core Technical Components**:

1. **Pre-flight Planning Perk (PF2P)**
   - Integrate terrain, land cover, weather, solar, and oceanic forecast data
   - Develop models to predict harvestable energy by geologic feature type and UAV performance
   - Design user interface (ground station + Android map-based UI)
   - Export functionality for in-flight plan use

2. **Sensing and Harnessing Control System (SHCS)**
   - Real-time flow condition detection sensors and processing
   - Integration with PF2P for balancing energy harvesting with mission objectives
   - Soaring location detection algorithms
   - Obstacle avoidance subsystem
   - Real-time flight safety implementation

3. **Soaring Platform (BST Primary Responsibility)**
   - Select appropriate s-UAS platforms for test events and practice test events
   - Procure/build/modify s-UAS to meet program goals and government specifications
   - Provide both baseline and Albatross-enabled s-UAS for metrics comparison
   - Ensure MAV Link compatibility and government range certification
   - Maintain adequate quantities to account for hardware failures and flight incidents

4. **Integration, Test, and Evaluation**
   - System component integration
   - Simulation-based integration testing
   - Test event readiness reviews
   - Multi-location flight test execution and logistics
   - System performance evaluation against program metrics

## Products & Capabilities Described

**Small Uncrewed Aircraft Systems (s-UAS) Fleet**
- What it is: A fleet of small UAS platforms selected and adapted to demonstrate autonomous soaring
- Use in program: Baseline platforms to integrate soaring planning and control systems; demonstration of autonomous soaring in multiple operational domains
- Specifications/Requirements:
  - Must meet government specifications per solicitation
  - Must comply with MAV Link interface requirements
  - Must obtain US government range flight certification
  - Must support both baseline avionics payload and Albatross-enhanced payloads
  - Redundant quantities needed to account for flight incidents and hardware failures

## Use Cases & Applications

**Operational Domains & Test Locations** (across 24-month period):
- **CONUS Test Events (12 MAC)**: Fort Irwin, California; Yuma Proving Ground, Arizona
- **OCONUS Test Events (18 MAC)**: Pacific Missile Range Facility (Hawaii); San Clemente Island (California); Roosevelt Roads (Puerto Rico)
- **Extended Test Events (24 MAC)**: Vandenberg Space Force Base (California); Kodiak (Alaska); South of Agadir (Morocco)

**Mission Capability**: Autonomous soaring to "actively harvest energy from the natural environment's atmospheric flow field to reduce onboard power demand and enable increased range and/or endurance"

## Program Schedule & Milestones

**24-Month Period of Performance**: April 2025 – March 2027

**Key Milestones**:
- **Month 1 (MAC)**: Kickoff (Burlington, MA; 2 people, 2 days)
- **Month 6 (MAC)**: System Checkout at Black Swift Flight Range (Boulder, CO; 2 people, 3 days) — Go/No-Go gate
- **Months 8, 10, 14, 16, 20, 22 (MAC)**: Pre-Test Events (7-day engagements at Fort Irwin, Yuma Proving Ground, San Clemente Island, Vandenberg)
- **Months 12, 18, 24 (MAC)**: Test Events (7-day CONUS engagements; 12-day OCONUS engagements at Hawaii, Puerto Rico, California, Alaska, Morocco)
- **Recurring**: Monthly technical and financial status reports (5th of each month)

**Two-Month Test Cycle Pattern**: System checkout at 6 months, then alternating pre-test events and full test events every 2 months thereafter.

## Deliverables

| Item | Deliverable | Due Date(s) |
|------|-------------|------------|
| A001 | Presentation Materials | 24 hours prior to each presentation |
| A002 | Technical and Financial Status Reports | Monthly (5th of month) |
| A003 | Test Plan and Review Inputs | Months 6, 12, 18, 24 MAC |
| A004 | Test Reports | Months 12, 18, 24 MAC |
| A005 | Software Data Package | Months 12, 18, 24 MAC |
| A006 | Final Report | Month 24 MAC |

**Rights**: Minimum Government Purpose Rights (GPR) for all deliverables

## Milestone Payment Schedule

12 payment milestones tied to deliverables and participation:
1. Month 1: Presentation Material
2. Month 3: Engineering Software, Integration Test Results, Interim Progress Report
3. Month 6: System Checkout participation, Hardware/Software Test Plan, Test Reports, Software Package
4. Months 8, 10, 14, 16, 20, 22: Pre-Test Event participation, Engineering Software, Integration Test Results
5. Months 12, 18, 24: Test Event participation, Test Plans, Test Reports, Software Packages

## Notable Details

- **Prime Contractor Relationship**: BAE Systems (Information and Electronic Systems Integration Inc.) is the prime contractor; Black Swift is a subcontractor
- **Document Ownership**: BAE Systems proprietary; further dissemination prohibited without written permission
- **Contract Award Window**: Period of performance estimated April 2025 – March 2027
- **Geographic Diversity**: Flight testing spans continental US, Hawaii, Puerto Rico, Alaska, and international location (Morocco) — indicating development across diverse climate and wind regimes
- **Safety Emphasis**: Multiple references to safety requirements, readiness reviews, obstacle avoidance, and government range certification
- **Travel Budget Considerations**: Estimated for "most expensive" location options; bidding should account for OCONUS travel (Hawaii, Puerto Rico, Alaska, Morocco) with 12-day durations
- **Dual-Baseline Approach**: Program requires both "baseline s-UAS" (unmodified) and "Albatross-enabled s-UAS" for comparative metrics evaluation# D2P2 Technical Volume Template (Topic X236-ODCSO2)

## Document Metadata
- Type: SBIR/STTR proposal template (Direct-to-Phase II)
- Client/Agency: U.S. Department of Defense / Department of the Air Force (DAF)
- Program/Solicitation: Topic X236-ODCSO2 - Direct-to-Phase II Call for Innovative Defense-Related Dual-Purpose Technologies/Solutions with a Clear Air Force Stakeholder Need
- Date: March 28, 2023
- BST Products/Systems Referenced: None (this is a template document)
- Key Personnel: Not applicable (template only)

## Executive Summary
This is a template document for Black Swift Technologies (or any SBIR contractor) to use when submitting a Direct-to-Phase II (D2P2) proposal to the U.S. Air Force. It provides the required structure, section headings, compliance questions, and evaluation criteria for proposals adapting non-Defense commercial solutions to meet Air Force end-user needs, with funding up to $1.25M and 21 months period of performance.

## Technical Approach
The template guides contractors to:
- Describe adaptation of an existing non-Defense commercial solution to meet DAF needs
- Demonstrate Phase I-type feasibility work conducted independently (since D2P2 skips Phase I)
- Propose 3-5 clear technical objectives with measurable key results
- Develop prototype hardware/software and conduct testing
- Define work plan with specific milestones, deliverables, and acceptance criteria
- Demonstrate end-user and customer commitment through signed Customer Memoranda

## Products & Capabilities Described
Not applicable—this is a blank template. However, the example milestone schedule embedded in the template references a medical device project (EVAC and ARS wireless integration for physiologic testing), which appears to be illustrative only and not a BST project.

## Use Cases & Applications
The template accommodates multiple use case categories:
- Air Force Technology Strategic Capabilities: Air Superiority, ISR, Rapid Global Strike, Command and Control, etc.
- Space Force Technology Strategic Capabilities: Space Superiority, Combat Power Projection, Space Mobility and Logistics, etc.
- Dual-purpose (defense + commercial) technologies

## Compliance & Regulatory Requirements
The template includes mandatory compliance checklist covering:
- Flight testing (indoor/outdoor, manned/unmanned)
- Hardware/software delivery and Mil-Std-882E hazard analysis
- Government personnel, facilities, and equipment use
- Weapons, munitions, explosives testing
- Directed energy devices and RF radiation
- Hazardous materials
- Animal testing
- Human subject research (32 CFR 219)
- Toxins and recombinant DNA
- Human interaction and data use

## Key Deliverables (Required for all Phase II awards)
- Final Report (draft within 30 days of technical completion; includes single-page non-proprietary summary)
- Status Reports (quarterly minimum)
- Technical Interchange Meetings (quarterly minimum with end-user)
- Phase II Summary Report (≤700 words)
- Software documentation, engineering drawings, operation/maintenance docs
- Preliminary Hazard Analysis (if hardware delivered)
- Hazardous Material Reports (if applicable)

## Proposal Structure
1. **Technical Summary** – Problem/opportunity, Air Force/Space Force strategic fit, non-Defense commercial baseline, proposed adaptation, answers to 7 specific commercialization questions
2. **Phase I-Type Feasibility Results** – Technical research, customer exploration methods, empowered/committed end-users and customers (with mandatory signed Customer Memoranda)
3. **Compliance & Regulatory Activities** – 13-point checklist
4. **Phase II Technical Objectives & Key Results** – 3-5 objectives tied to trials, 3-5 measurable key results per objective
5. **Phase II Work Plan** – Scope, task outline, milestone schedule with deliverables and acceptance criteria, payment amounts
6. **Commercialization Strategy** – Company info, customer/competition analysis, market sizing, IP strategy, financing, mentoring plans, answers to 10 specific questions

## Notable Details

**Mandatory Requirements:**
- Signed Customer Memorandum from DAF end-user and customer (mandatory; proposals without it will not be considered)
- Proposals must follow the prescribed template format
- At least one DAF/Joint end-user and customer required (non-DAF government end-users permitted as secondary)
- Clear distinction between SBIR-funded and private investment-funded tasks in work plan

**Funding & Duration:**
- Not-To-Exceed (NTE): $1.25M
- 21-month period of performance (18 months technical + 3 months reporting)
- Milestone payments tied to deliverables with defined acceptance criteria

**Commercial Baseline Requirements:**
- Proposed solution must be based on a non-Defense commercial solution with evidence of commercial sales/adoption
- Must answer questions about commercial similarity, supplier modifications for non-government customers, essential use changes, and COTS/modification details
- Must include 12-month revenue from non-Defense commercial sales

**Foreign National Restrictions:**
- All foreign nationals/dual citizens must be identified with country of origin, visa/permit type, and task assignment
- When subject to export control, foreign citizens limited to public domain work
- Foreign citizens cannot be in key positions (PI, Senior Engineer, etc.)
- Tasks assigned must not reveal project's overall objectives

**Key Personnel Requirements:**
- Technical resume for PI required, including publications
- Education, experience, citizenship information for all key personnel
- Emphasis on both RDT&E and commercialization qualifications

**Non-Defense Commercial Customer Evidence:**
- Past revenue from commercial customers (mandatory documentation)
- Potential revenue-generating projects (ongoing/completed preferred over potential)
- Active users, subscriptions, pre-sales, or other commercial traction indicators

This template represents Black Swift Technologies' understanding of the D2P2 proposal structure as of March 2023 and would be used to guide any future BST submissions to this Air Force solicitation.# USDA NIFA Phase I SBIR Application - Other Attachments Instructions

## Document Type & Purpose
This is a guidance document outlining requirements for Field 12 (Other Attachments) of a USDA NIFA SBIR Phase I application. It specifies what documentation BST needed to include with their soil moisture mapping UAS proposal.

## Key Requirements for Application Attachments

### 1. Facility/Equipment Use Letters
- Required if using university, private, or government lab facilities
- Must include letter from authorized representative confirming exclusive use and control

### 2. Outside Services Documentation
- Consultants, subcontractors, or CRADA partnerships permitted
- Maximum 1/3 of grant funds can be used for outside services
- Requires letters of commitment from all proposed outside parties

### 3. Letters of Support (Strongly Encouraged)
- Should demonstrate market validation and technical support
- Must show evidence of stakeholder dialogue (potential customers, partners, investors)
- Should include affiliation and contact information for signatories
- Recommended limit: 2 pages per letter
- If not included, applicant must provide 2-page justification addressing technical and commercial considerations
- Must be submitted in PDF format

### 4. Project Duration Justification
- Phase I projects normally limited to 8 months
- If exceeding 8 months, requires written justification
- Maximum allowable duration: 20 months

### 5. Subsidiary Documentation (if applicable)
- Parent company small business status must be demonstrated
- Parent company must reside in U.S. and cannot be nonprofit
- Subsidiary must document independent viable financial status

### 6. Federal Debt Delinquency Statement
- Required if applicant is delinquent on federal debts
- Must include detailed explanatory information in PDF format

### 7. Non-Domestic Performance Explanation
- Budget justification required for foreign travel
- Must specify: purpose, destination, method of travel, number of persons, duration, estimated cost
- All foreign travel requires prior written USDA NIFA approval

- This is a template/guidance document rather than a substantive proposal

## Document Metadata
- Type: NASA Form 1679 - Disclosure of Invention and New Technology
- Client/Agency: NASA
- Program/Solicitation: NASA SBIR Phase I (Contract NNX13CG33P)
- Date: 2013-11-23
- BST Products/Systems Referenced: NDVI/Thermal sensor board; Soil Moisture Mapping sUAS
- Key Personnel: Maciej Stachura (CTO), Jack Elston, Raymond Oung (BST); Albin Gasiewski (University of Colorado Boulder, collaborator)

## Executive Summary
Black Swift Technologies developed a compact NDVI/Thermal sensor board during NASA SBIR Phase I for measuring vegetation indices and ground temperature to correct soil moisture measurements from L-band radiometers. The six-sensor board combines red and near-infrared optical sensing (nadir and zenith directions) with thermal temperature sensing, designed to integrate into small unmanned aircraft systems.

## Technical Approach
The NDVI/Thermal board uses the following components:
- **Optical Sensing**: Si-J146 photodiodes with amplifiers (Electro Optical Components), spectral range 400-1100 nm, with filters to sample red (550-700 nm) and near-infrared (700-1300 nm) wavelengths from both nadir and zenith directions
- **Thermal Sensing**: MLX90615 sensor for surface and cloud-bottom infrared (10 µm) temperature measurement
- **Data Processing**: STM32F103 Cortex-M3 microcontroller samples all sensors and outputs digital data packets

**Development Timeline**:
- 05/28/2013: Initial discussion and conceptual design
- 08/16/2013: Photodiode and filter selection for red/NIR
- 08/20/2013: Thermal sensor selection
- 10/28/2013: Sensor board design complete
- 11/08/2013: Circuit boards printed
- 11/18/2013: Boards populated and initial tests conducted

## Products & Capabilities Described

**NDVI/Thermal Sensor Board**
- **What it is**: A multi-sensor payload for small unmanned aircraft systems capable of measuring sky-corrected Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) and surface/cloud-bottom temperature
- **Proposed use**: Provide auxiliary measurements to correct L-band radiometer soil moisture data; support precision agriculture applications
- **Key specifications**:
  - Dual-direction sensing (nadir and zenith) for improved NDVI accuracy
  - Red band: 550-700 nm
  - Near-infrared band: 700-1300 nm
  - Thermal band: 10 µm wavelength
  - Small size, low weight, low power consumption for sUAS integration

## Use Cases & Applications

- **Soil Moisture Mapping**: Primary application is providing ground truth corrections for L-band radiometer soil moisture measurements via small unmanned aircraft
- **Precision Agriculture**: Identified as largest potential market for sUAS in US with 2.2+ million farms; NDVI measurements support crop health monitoring and field management decisions

## Notable Details

- **Novel features**: Combination of nadir and zenith-facing sensors with integrated thermal measurement; previously unavailable in compact, low-cost form factor
- **Competitive advantages**: Superior to low-cost EO cameras with filters (lacks scientific precision) and TetraCam sensors (higher cost, no thermal); small size and low power enable sUAS integration without significant payload penalty
- **Technology significance**: Classified as "Modification to Existing Technology" rather than breakthrough
- **State of development**: Prototype stage (11/2013), with planned Phase II flight testing using Soil Moisture Mapping sUAS to validate performance
- **Partnership**: Collaboration with University of Colorado Boulder's Electrical Engineering department (Albin Gasiewski involvement)
- **Market context**: References AUVSI research identifying precision agriculture as single largest sUAS market opportunity# High Data Rate Compact Logger

## Document Metadata
- Type: NASA Technology Disclosure Form (Form 1679)
- Client/Agency: NASA
- Program/Solicitation: NASA SBIR Grant NNX13CG33P
- Date: 2013-11-23
- BST Products/Systems Referenced: High Data Rate Compact Logger (microSD card array-based)
- Key Personnel: Maciej Stachura (CTO), Jack Elston, Eric McIntyre (University of Colorado Boulder)

## Executive Summary
Black Swift Technologies developed a compact, lightweight high-rate data logger capable of sampling at 180 mega-samples per second (MS/s) using a microSD card array, designed to fit within the size, weight, and power constraints of small unmanned aircraft systems (sUAS). This represents a substantial advancement over comparable systems, which typically max out at 0.2 MS/s.

## Technical Approach
The innovation employs an array of 36 microSD cards sequentially written to by an FPGA operating at 720 MHz clock speed (4x the desired sampling rate). Key technical specifications:
- **Sampling Rate**: 180 MS/s
- **Data Rate**: 810 MB/s
- **ADC**: AD9643-210 ADC (210 MS/s sampling capability)
- **Resolution**: 16-bit analog-digital converter channels
- **Processing**: FPGA-based sequential writing with post-processing data reconstruction
- **Prototype Status**: Lower-rate prototype built and tested at ~1 kS/s using single microSD card; software written to extract binary data

## Products & Capabilities Described

**High Data Rate Compact Logger**
- What it is: A miniaturized data acquisition system using microSD card arrays for high-speed logging
- Proposed use: Logging microwave radiometer system data on sUAS platforms
- Unique advantage: Achieves 180 MS/s sampling in a form factor suitable for sUAS (addressing severe size/weight/power constraints where comparable systems only manage 0.2 MS/s)
- Key innovation: Uses low-cost microSD cards in parallel array configuration rather than single high-speed storage device

## Use Cases & Applications
- **Primary**: Microwave radiometer data collection on small unmanned aircraft
- **Market context**: General sUAS sensor advancement; part of broader civil UAS market projected at $2.4 billion annual sales by 2020 (AUVSI estimate)
- **Follow-on possibilities**: Advanced sensing systems in sUAS beyond initial radiometer application

## Development Timeline
- 04/03/2013: Initial discussion and conceptual design
- 04/15/2013: Detailed design, data rate/bus speed analysis, component selection
- 07/01/2013: Design and build of lower-rate prototype
- 11/05/2013: Lower-rate prototype build complete
- 11/12/2013: Software testing and verification

## Notable Details
- **State of Development**: Prototype (lower-rate version complete and tested; full 180 MS/s version still in design phase requiring "considerable design and testing")
- **Technology Significance**: Marked as "Substantial Advancement in the Art"
- **Collaborative Development**: Joint effort between Black Swift Technologies and University of Colorado Boulder
- **Component Roles**: Stachura (overall design), Elston (PCB assembly/firmware), McIntyre (PCB design)
- **Prior Art Gap**: Innovators unable to locate comparable alternative systems meeting both the sampling rate and sUAS size/weight/power requirements
- **Leverage Point**: Utilizes low-cost, readily available microSD card components in innovative array configuration rather than custom high-speed logging hardware# Apollo Modular Airframe - Disclosure of Invention and New Technology

## Document Metadata
- Type: NASA Form 1679 (Disclosure of Invention and New Technology)
- Client/Agency: NASA
- Program/Solicitation: SBIR (Grant/Cooperative Agreement No. NNX14CP21P)
- Date: 2014-12-30
- BST Products/Systems Referenced: Apollo airframe (CAPS project - Cooperative Airborne Platform System)
- Key Personnel: Jack Elston (President and CEO, Black Swift Technologies); Coby Leuschke (President, Rocketship Systems Inc.)

## Executive Summary
This invention disclosure documents modifications to the Apollo small unmanned aircraft system (sUAS) airframe developed during Phase I of a NASA SBIR project. The work resulted in a highly modular, field-swappable airframe design that enables tool-less replacement of payloads and aircraft components, significantly improving operational flexibility and usability in harsh field conditions.

## Technical Approach
- Based on Rocketship Systems Inc.'s Apollo reference design as foundation
- Modified to support forward-mounted, modular payload bay (nose cone) with standardized mechanical and electrical connections to main fuselage
- Designed two payload bay configurations in 3D CAD to accommodate various sensor sizes and types
- Incorporated forward-swept wing design for improved spanwise efficiency and favorable center of gravity positioning for larger forward-mounted payloads
- Tool-less assembly/disassembly methodology enabling rapid field swaps
- Iterative test and rapid prototyping approach

## Products & Capabilities Described

### Apollo Airframe (CAPS Configuration)
**What it is:** Lightweight, hand-launchable sUAS with modular architecture based on Apollo reference design

**Key specifications/features:**
- Compact and rugged for hand launch and landing in unimproved terrain
- Forward-swept wing configuration
- Modular nose cone design (field-swappable without tools)
- Swappable major airframe components (also tool-less)
- Standardized payload bay mechanical and electrical interfaces
- Robust flight management system enabling low-altitude operations in hazardous conditions

**Proposed use:** Multi-platform cooperative missions with interchangeable sensor payloads

## Use Cases & Applications
- Plume monitoring
- Atmospheric remote sensing
- Radiation and particulate monitoring
- Radio frequency monitoring and localization
- Operations in rough terrain, inclement weather, and cold temperature environments
- Field campaigns requiring rapid sensor swapping between cooperative platforms

## Development Timeline
- **06/23/2014:** Initial discussion and conceptual design
- **07/2014:** First sketch/drawing created at Rocketship Systems Inc.
- **12/2014:** 3D CAD design completed
- **12/19/2014:** Construction of battery, nose cone, and autopilot module prototypes completed

## Notable Details

**Innovator Contributions:**
- Coby Leuschke: CAD creation and initial prototype construction
- Jack Elston: Electrical interface design and project management

**Unique/Novel Features:**
- Tool-less, field-swappable nose cone without requiring tools—particularly valuable in cold/inclement weather
- Tool-less swappable components throughout airframe for rapid field replacement of damaged parts
- Modular design enables deployment with multiple sensors that can be cycled during operations
- Streamlined operations for field scientists with focus on data gathering

**Technology Significance:** Classified as "Substantial Advancement in the Art"

**State of Development:** Prototype stage (initial prototypes of battery, nose cone, and autopilot modules completed)

**Competitive Advantage:** Modularity and tool-less operational design not typically considered in most sUAS designs; enables successful deployments in areas previously problematic due to logistics and component damage.

**Partner Organization:** Collaboration between Black Swift Technologies LLC and Rocketship Systems Inc.

**NASA COTR:** Robert Jones# CAPS Multi-hole and PTH Probe - NASA Invention Disclosure

## Document Metadata
- Type: NASA Form 1679 - Disclosure of Invention and New Technology
- Client/Agency: NASA
- Program/Solicitation: NASA SBIR Phase I (Grant/Cooperative Agreement No. NNX14CP21P)
- Date: 2014-12-30
- BST Products/Systems Referenced: CAPS Multi-hole Probe
- Key Personnel: Jack Elston (President and CEO), Maciej Stachura (CTO)

## Executive Summary
Black Swift Technologies developed the CAPS Multi-hole Probe during Phase I of a NASA SBIR program to measure 3D winds, pressure, temperature, and humidity from small unmanned aircraft systems (sUAS). The innovation combines a compact multi-hole pressure probe with integrated thermodynamic sensors in a lightweight, robust package specifically designed for hand-launched sUAS operations.

## Technical Approach
The CAPS Multi-hole Probe employs the following technical design:

- **Probe Head**: 1-inch radius hemispherical design with 5 pressure ports
- **Wind Measurement**: Center hole measures total pressure; comparison with static pressure determines airspeed; four offset ports (45-degree spacing) measure angle of attack and sideslip angle
- **Pressure Sensors**: 
  - SM9541 sensors in 20cm H₂O version for airspeed measurement
  - SM9541 sensors in 10cm H₂O version for increased resolution on angle of attack/sideslip
- **Additional Measurements**: MS5607 sensor provides high-resolution static pressure, temperature, and humidity
- **Manufacturing**: Laser-cut scaffolding guides drilling for accurate port placement
- **Electronics**: Custom sensor board with integrated electronics; outputs on CAN bus for autopilot/data logger integration

## Products & Capabilities Described

### CAPS Multi-hole Probe
- **What it is**: A compact atmospheric sensor package measuring 2" × 4" and weighing 1.5 oz
- **Measurements**: 3D wind vectors (airspeed, angle of attack, sideslip), static pressure, temperature, humidity
- **Integration**: Modular nose cone design for field swapping in sub-5-lb sUAS
- **Design advantage**: Blunt, integrated design doesn't protrude from airframe, improving robustness and reducing ground-handling damage risk
- **Key components**: SM9541 dynamic pressure sensors, MS5607 thermodynamic sensor, custom PCB

## Use Cases & Applications
- Local and global weather model validation
- Dynamic small-scale atmospheric phenomenon measurement
- Severe weather prediction (6-24 hour forecasts for convection-driven events)
- High-risk missions where sUAS loss is probable (low-cost replacement important)
- Arctic and other unimproved field operations

**Target customers identified**: NASA, NOAA, NSF, UCAR/NCAR (specifically Mesoscale Predictability Experiment - MPEX)

## Key Results
- **Initial Design**: January 2014
- **Circuit Board Design**: October 4, 2014
- **3D CAD Design (scaffolding)**: November 10, 2014
- **Construction and Testing**: November 25, 2014
- **Circuit Board Prototype Build**: December 1, 2014
- **Complete 3D CAD Design**: December 4, 2014
- **State of Development**: Prototype stage completed

## Notable Details
- **Innovation Classification**: Substantial Advancement in the Art (not merely a modification)
- **Design Philosophy**: Simplicity and low cost enable use in high-risk/probable-loss missions
- **Competitive Advantage**: Lighter and more compact than existing commercial multi-hole probe systems; unique integration of all measurements (3D wind + pressure + temperature + humidity) in this form factor
- **Modularity**: Field-swappable payload bay design for rapid reconfiguration
- **Robustness**: Blunt nose design eliminates protrusion risk during ground handling and storage
- **Weight Efficiency**: Enables integration into sub-5-lb sUAS platforms# SuperSwift Aircraft – NASA New Technology Disclosure

## Document Metadata
- Type: NASA Form 1679 – Disclosure of Invention and New Technology
- Client/Agency: NASA (Grant/Cooperative Agreement)
- Program/Solicitation: Soil Moisture Mapping SBIR Phase II (Contract NNX14CG09C)
- Date: 2016-04-07
- BST Products/Systems Referenced: SuperSwift aircraft airframe
- Key Personnel: 
  - Jack Elston (President and CEO, BST)
  - Cory Dixon (Director of Engineering, BST)
  - Maciej Stachura (CTO, BST)
  - Geoffrey Bland (NASA/Aerospace Flight Systems, COTR)

## Executive Summary
The SuperSwift is a modular electric-powered small unmanned aircraft system (sUAS) with a 10-foot wingspan specifically designed to house an L-band radiometer payload in a removable nose cone for soil moisture mapping missions. The airframe combines hand-launchability with 1.5+ hour flight endurance and a modular design enabling rapid sensor integration and field-swappable payloads for multiple scientific applications.

## Technical Approach

### Aircraft Configuration
- **Airframe Type**: Pusher configuration with V-tail design
- **Wingspan**: 120 inches (10 feet)
- **Empty Weight**: 7.5 lbs
- **Gross Takeoff Weight**: 10.5 lbs
- **Payload Capacity**: 3 lbs nominal, 5 lbs maximum
- **Propulsion**: Electric motor with pusher propeller
- **Flight Endurance**: ≥1.5 hours
- **Operational Requirement**: Hand-launchable from unimproved areas

### Aerodynamic Design
- **Wing Airfoil**: MH 70 (11.08% thickness-to-chord ratio)
  - Maximum sectional lift coefficient: ~1.5
  - Pitching moment coefficient: ~-0.05
  - Provides low stall speed and smooth stall transition
- **Wing Planform**:
  - Area: 1,100 in² (7.64 ft²)
  - Root chord: 10 in
  - Tip chord: 7.5 in
  - Mean aerodynamic chord: 9.24 in
  - Taper ratio: 0.84
  - Aspect ratio: 13.09
  - No dihedral angle; forward sweep of 0.6°
- **Wing Loading**: 22 oz/ft²
- **Stall Speed**: 33.5 ft/s at 6,000 ft altitude
- **V-Tail Configuration**:
  - NACA 0012 airfoils
  - Root chord: 7.0 in; tip chord: 5.75 in
  - Located 40 in from wing leading edge
  - Horizontal tail volume: 0.48; vertical tail volume: 0.015
  - 1° positive incidence angle for near-zero lift operation
  - Predicted downwash angle: 1.3°

### Stability & Control
- **Neutral Point**: 4.25 in aft of wing leading edge
- **Center of Gravity**: 2.0 in from wing leading edge
- **Static Margin**: 21% (0.5 in forward of wing root quarter-chord)
- Forward CG placement balances moments in powered flight and maintains V-tail zero-lift condition

### Design Rationale

**Pusher Configuration**: 
- Keeps nose cone clear and easily removable for payload integration
- Separates motor/propeller from scientific payload area
- Enables safe hand launch

**V-Tail Design**:
- Reduces structural weight vs. conventional tail
- Simplifies mechanical/structural design
- Enables faster field setup and teardown
- Requires low-pitching-moment airfoil for efficiency

**Hand-Launchability**:
- Wing loading ~20 oz/ft² (rule of thumb for hand-launched aircraft)
- Low stall speed (33.5 ft/s) for safe operations
- Structural placement protects operator from propeller

## Products & Capabilities Described

### SuperSwift Aircraft
**What It Is**: A modular electric unmanned aircraft system designed as a scientific platform for soil moisture mapping and other remote sensing missions.

**Primary Innovation – Removable Nose Cone**:
- Houses all soil moisture payload subsystems
- Field-swappable for different sensor packages
- Eliminates conducting materials that would interfere with L-band radiometer antenna
- Fiberglass construction of minimum thickness to avoid signal degradation

**Key Capability Features**:

## Executive Summary
Black Swift Technologies developed a high-rate compact data logger capable of sampling at 60 megasamples per second (MS/s) for integration into small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (sUAS). The system combines highly accurate differential analog input with solid-state storage and optional integration with the Black Swift SwiftPilot autopilot for soil moisture mapping applications.

## Technical Approach

**System Architecture:**
- **Analog/RF Board**: Interfaces with instruments and auxiliary sensors; conditions analog signals
- **A/D Board**: Utilizes Linear Technology LTC2143-14 (14-Bit, 80MS/s, Low Power Dual ADC)
- **FPGA Module**: Spartan-6 based EFM-02 FPGA module outputs data over USB 3.0
- **Host Computer**: VIA EPIA-P910-10Q Pico ITX board with on-board SSD for data storage
- **Microcontroller**: Collects auxiliary data from internal thermistors and CAN data packets from autopilot, interleaves all data for logging

**Key Specifications:**
- Sample rate: 60 MS/s
- ADC resolution: 14-bit
- Interface: USB 3.0 for data transfer
- Storage: Solid-state drive (SSD) with timestamp capability
- Power/Size: Meets sUAS constraints for weight and power consumption

## Products & Capabilities Described

**High Data Rate Compact Data Logger**
- High-speed data acquisition system designed for sUAS integration
- Captures data from multiple sources simultaneously (L-band antenna outputs, thermistors, autopilot state data)
- Includes onboard FPGA for digital signal processing (DSP) algorithm implementation
- CAN bus interface for integration with SwiftPilot autopilot system
- Enables future signal processing capabilities (e.g., FFT analysis)

**SwiftPilot Autopilot Integration**
- Optional CAN data packet integration providing auxiliary state data (position, altitude, attitude)
- Data used for geo-location of sensor measurements
- Enables precision flight control for low-altitude missions

## Use Cases & Applications

**Primary Application: Soil Moisture Mapping**
- Small UAS-based passive L-band microwave radiometer system
- Maps volumetric soil moisture content over agricultural plots
- Achieves 15-meter spatial resolution with 5-20 cm depth sensitivity
- Low-cost, simple-to-operate platform

**Supporting Measurements:**
- L-band antenna outputs (2 channels at high rate)
- Temperature monitoring via 8 thermistors (2 on antenna, 6 in LDCR)
- Radio frequency interference (RFI) mitigation algorithm testing

**Broader UAS Market Applications:**
- Emerging civil UAS market projected at $2.4 billion annual sales by 2020 (per AUVSI)
- System enables advanced sensing systems in sUAS through compact high-rate data logging
- Potential for follow-on sensing applications beyond radiometry

## Notable Details

**Unique Capabilities:**
- No comparable alternative system found with this sampling rate while meeting sUAS size, weight, and power requirements
- Compact form factor differentiates from existing high-speed data loggers
- FPGA architecture allows for future algorithm implementation without hardware redesign

## Document Metadata
- Type: NASA Form 1679 - Disclosure of Invention and New Technology
- Client/Agency: NASA

- BST Products/Systems Referenced: Soil moisture mapping sUAS, LDCR (Lobe Differencing Correlating Radiometer)
- Key Personnel: Jack Elston (BST New Technology Representative, elstonj@blackswifttech.com); Albin Gasiewski, Dai Eryan, Eric McIntyre (University of Colorado innovators)

## Executive Summary
This disclosure describes a novel Microstrip Colinear (MiCo) antenna array designed specifically for integration into a small unmanned aircraft system (sUAS) for soil moisture sensing. The lightweight L-band antenna operates at 1.4135 GHz and connects to the LDCR radiometer, enabling high-resolution soil moisture measurements at 15-meter resolution compared to satellite-based systems at 40 km resolution.

## Technical Approach

**Antenna Design Specifications:**
- L-band frequency: 1400-1427 MHz (SMAP frequency band), operating frequency 1.4135 GHz
- Configuration: 2x2 rectangular microstrip antenna array (prototype 2x1 validated, full 2x2 investigated)
- Element type: 5-segment microstrip colinear patch antenna per element
- Element pattern: Omnidirectional radiation pattern
- Array arrangement: Half-wave horizontal separation, quarter-wave vertical separation
- Quarter-wave vertical separation provides 90° phase shift for quadrature-phased LDCR receiver channels
- Radiation pattern: Horizontal radiation at horizon is canceled; broad end-fire beams realized in nadir and zenith directions
- Construction: PCB-based design (low-cost, scalable manufacturing)
- Mechanical stability: Styrofoam blocks used for mechanical support and resonant frequency tuning

**Design Development Process:**
- 11/03/2013: Initial concept design and simulation
- 05/04/2014: Refined design including aircraft fuselage in simulations
- 07/01/2014: Initial build and lab test of antenna array
- 10/04/2014: Integration with fuselage, testing, and tuning
- 04/01/2015: Outdoor testing fully integrated into airframe
- 09/08/2015: First flight test over instrumented field (Canton, OK)

**Key Technical Studies:**
- Impedance matching and input impedance validated through HFSS simulation vs. prototype measurement
- Mutual coupling analysis for 2x2 array configuration
- Optimal vertical separation distance identified to minimize mutual coupling and maximize main-to-back lobe ratio
- Resonant frequency tuning methodology developed

## Products & Capabilities Described

**MiCo Antenna Array:**
- **What it is:** A 2x2 L-band microstrip colinear antenna array optimized for sUAS integration
- **Use in this context:** Primary antenna for the soil moisture mapping sUAS, interfacing with the LDCR radiometer receiver
- **Key specifications:** 1.4135 GHz operating frequency, downward-pointing beam pattern suitable for nadir/zenith observations, lightweight design to fit within sUAS constraints, PCB-based construction

**LDCR (Lobe Differencing Correlating Radiometer):**
- **What it is:** A lightweight L-band microwave radiometer with lobes viewing both nadir and zenith
- **Integration:** The MiCo antenna was specifically designed to connect with and support LDCR operations
- **Capability:** Passive microwave soil moisture sensing

## Use Cases & Applications

1. **SMAP Mission Validation & Augmentation:**
   - SMAP satellite provides ~40 km resolution soil moisture data
   - sUAS with MiCo antenna provides 15-meter resolution validation data
   - Supports calibration and validation plan for SMAP spacecraft operations

2. **High-Resolution Local Soil Moisture Mapping:**
   - Watershed monitoring
   - Drought area assessment
   - Local soil moisture characterization in support of broader SMAP science

3. **Flood Risk Assessment and Warning:**
   - Support for FEMA in understanding flash flood vulnerability
   - Historical precedent: 2007 NASA-funded effort by Prof. Gasiewski mapped soil moisture in North Texas and Oklahoma flood region, providing alert/warning data for flash flood-susceptible areas
   - Cost-effective alternative to manned aircraft operations for vulnerable watersheds nationwide

## Notable Details

**Unique Features:**
- Specifically dimensioned to fit sUAS constraints (minimal weight/volume priority)
- PCB-based manufacturing enables rapid large-scale production if needed
- Novel quarter-wave vertical separation approach provides required 90° phase shift for quadrature receiver channels
- Substantial advancement in the art (per technology significance assessment)

**Performance Advantage:**
- Delivers 26.7x finer resolution than SMAP satellite (15 m vs. 40 km)

**Publications & Public Disclosure:**
- Conference presentation: "High Resolution sUAS-based Passive Microwave L-band Imaging of Soil Moisture" (2014-12-09)
- Oral presentation: "L-band Soil Moisture Mapping Using a Small Unmanned Aerial System" (2016-01-08)

  - Eric McIntyre (University of Colorado)

## Executive Summary
This disclosure documents modifications made to the Lobe Differencing Correlating Radiometer (LDCR) during Phase II development to prepare it for flight testing on an unmanned aircraft system. The work addressed three critical integration issues: electromagnetic noise contamination, insufficient output voltage range for analog-to-digital conversion, and temperature-dependent measurement drift. Solutions included power filtering, amplification stages, and thermistor-based temperature monitoring.

## Technical Approach

### Primary Problems Addressed
1. **Noise contamination** - Output noise was 6x higher than expected, traced to the analog correlator board
2. **Voltage range limitation** - Analog correlator output voltage was insufficient for data logger A/D converter resolution
3. **Temperature drift** - Radiometer gain varies with temperature, requiring compensation for accurate measurements

### Solutions Implemented

**Noise Mitigation:**
- Added LC filter to input power voltage
- Inserted IF gain amplifiers between LDCR output and analog correlator
- Built low-pass filter at analog correlator output (1.5ms time constant)
- Enhanced power supply isolation from RF interference:
  - Two parallel decoupling capacitors (0.1 µF and 22 µF) with 1 µH series inductor at DC feed-through
  - Shielded twisted triple wires for DC power supply lines
  - 0.1 µF capacitor pairs in parallel on TEC (thermoelectric cooler) heating/cooling pins

**Voltage Scaling:**
- Added video amplifier between low-pass filter output and A/D input of data logger

**Temperature Compensation:**
- Installed 5 thermistors on LDCR receiving board to monitor:
  - TEC on channel 1
  - TEC on channel 2
  - Isolator
  - Local oscillator
  - IF signal filter

## Products & Capabilities Described

### Lobe Differencing Correlating Radiometer (LDCR)
- **What it is:** L-band passive microwave radiometer instrument designed for soil moisture measurement
- **Original development:** NASA NESSF Award NNX12AO08H
- **Use case in this project:** Integrated into small UAS platform for soil moisture mapping; paired with MiCo antenna
- **Performance capability:** Enables soil moisture measurements at 15-meter resolution (vs. ~40 km from SMAP satellite)
- **Key specifications:** L-band receiver with analog correlator architecture; temperature-sensitive gain requiring monitoring and correction

### Soil Moisture Mapping sUAS
- **What it is:** Small unmanned aircraft system equipped with LDCR and MiCo antenna for measuring soil moisture
- **Flight test:** Conducted September 8, 2015, in Canton, Oklahoma
- **Ground testing:** Outdoor ground tests completed October 6, 2014

## Use Cases & Applications

1. **SMAP Satellite Validation and Enhancement**
   - Provides ground-truth validation data for NASA's Soil Moisture Active Passive (SMAP) satellite mission
   - Augments SMAP science data products with finer (15m vs. 40km) resolution in specific areas

2. **Watershed and Drought Monitoring**
   - High-resolution soil moisture data near watersheds
   - Local soil moisture information in drought-affected areas
   - Supports FEMA in understanding flash flood vulnerability

3. **Flood Prediction and Early Warning**
   - Historical application: 2007 NASA-funded research mapping soil moisture in North Texas/Oklahoma flood-affected regions
   - Data used to provide flood alerts and warnings to vulnerable areas
   - Cost-effective alternative to manned aircraft operations

## Key Development Timeline
- **May 4, 2014:** Local oscillator leakage identified; initial power circuit filter design work began
- **July 15, 2014:** Power filtering circuits completed; amplifier added to output
- **October 6, 2014:** Outdoor ground testing of updated LDCR
- **April 10, 2015:** Thermistor installation and testing completed
- **September 8, 2015:** First successful flight test (Canton, Oklahoma)

## Executive Summary
The SuperSwift XT is a ruggedized modification of the SuperSwift airframe designed to operate in harsh volcanic environments. Key innovations include sealed airframe design for ash protection, a redundant airspeed measurement system, and enlarged control surfaces for high-altitude turbulence. The aircraft carries 5 lbs of payload with 1.5+ hour flight time capability and can operate at elevations up to 20,000 ft.

## Technical Approach

### Airframe Modifications
- **Ash Protection**: Motor encased in protective cowling that maintains cooling while preventing ash ingress
- **Hatching/Sealing**: Permanent gasket solution on control rod access hatches positioned away from airflow direction (replacing field tape solutions)
- **Control Surfaces**: Increased length and span of ailerons and flaps based on aerodynamic analysis for volcanic turbulence

### Airspeed Measurement Redundancy
- **Primary**: New large-opening (1/4 inch) pitot tube designed to prevent water droplet bridging in rain/wet conditions
- **Backup 1**: Multi-hole probe (also subject to clogging)
- **Backup 2**: Nephelometer - laser-based particle measurement sensor providing independent airspeed confirmation

### Propulsion & Configuration
- Electric-powered pusher configuration with V-tail design
- Motor cooling design critical to harsh environment operation

## Products & Capabilities Described

### SuperSwift XT Aircraft
- **What it is**: Ruggedized modification of the original SuperSwift airframe (originally developed for soil moisture mapping)
- **Specifications**:
  - Payload capacity: 5 lbs
  - Flight endurance: 1.5+ hours
  - Operating altitude: Up to 20,000 ft
  - Configuration: Electric pusher with V-tail
- **Novel Features**:
  - Modular, field-swappable nose cone for scientific payloads
  - Sealed airframe design minimizing mass penalty
  - Multiple redundant airspeed sensors
  - Ruggedization for ash, moisture, and high-altitude turbulence

## Use Cases & Applications

### Primary Mission
- Volcanic sampling and ash collection in harsh volcanic environments
- Operations in mountainous terrain with difficult landing sites

### Proposed Secondary Applications
- Arctic science and research
- Climate monitoring
- Atmospheric sampling (coherent structures: smog, volcano plumes, wildfire smoke, chemical fires)
- Wildlife research
- Wildfire detection and monitoring
- Weather monitoring
- Forest humidity measurement

- **01/10/2015**: Engine and propeller selection completed

- **02/03/2016**: Mechanical design of fuselage completed
- **04/04/2016**: Delivery of first production fuselage
- **11/20/2016**: Completion of new payload interface

## Executive Summary
Black Swift Technologies developed an improved, compact multi-hole probe for measuring 3D winds and static pressure from small unmanned aircraft systems (sUAS). The innovation leverages 3D printing technology to create a lightweight (62g), robust sensor package that is significantly smaller and more durable than commercial alternatives, enabling deployment on high-risk missions and atmospheric research.

## Technical Approach

**Core Design:**
- Small hemispherical sensor head with 5 pressure ports
- Center hole measures total pressure (airspeed)
- Four outer ports offset by 45° and equally spaced around hemisphere to measure angle of attack and sideslip

**Sensor Suite:**
- **SM9541 sensors:** 20cm H₂O version for airspeed measurement; 10cm H₂O versions for angle of attack/sideslip resolution
- **MS5607 sensor:** High-resolution static pressure, temperature, and humidity measurements
- **Custom sensor board:** Integrates all 5 dynamic pressure sensors with MS5607
- **Electronics:** Custom design with CAN bus output for autopilot or data logger integration

**Manufacturing & Materials:**
- Entire mechanical assembly 3D printed to high accuracy
- Custom designed electronics and firmware for data collection

**Development Timeline:**
- 01/2014 - Initial design discussion
- 10/2014 - Circuit board design
- 11/2014 - 3D CAD design of scaffold
- 11/25/2014 - Initial prototype construction & testing
- 12/2014 - Circuit board prototype complete
- 09/2015 - New 3D CAD design for 3D printing
- 10/2016 - Laser-cut parts ordered & assembled
- 10/20/2016 - Firmware/code completion
- 12/02/2016 - Wind tunnel testing & comparison to commercial system

## Products & Capabilities Described

**Multi-hole Probe (MHP):**
- **Purpose:** Measure 3D wind vectors and static pressure from sUAS
- **Key Specifications:**
  - Dimensions: 2" × 4"
  - Weight: 62g
  - Compact hemispherical design (does not protrude from airframe)
  - Measures: airspeed, angle of attack, sideslip angle, static pressure, temperature, humidity
  - Output: CAN bus interface
- **Advantages Over Prior Art:**
  - Lighter and more compact than commercial multi-hole probes
  - Robust blunt design eliminates fragility of protruding sensors
  - Low cost enables deployment on high-loss-probability missions
  - Rapid construction and design modification capability via 3D printing
  - Integrable into most existing sUAS platforms

## Use Cases & Applications

**Primary Applications:**
- Volcanic plume sampling and characterization
- Atmospheric validation of weather models (local and global scale)
- Mesoscale weather prediction improvement (6-24 hour convection forecasts)
- Coherent atmospheric structure measurement: smog, wildfire smoke, chemical fires, forest humidity

**Target Organizations:**
- NASA
- NOAA (National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration)
- NSF (National Science Foundation)
- UCAR/NCAR (National Center for Atmospheric Research)
- NCAR Mesoscale Predictability Experiment (MPEX)
- Commercial partners: iMET (existing commercial interest noted)

**Mission Context:**
- Harsh environment operations requiring robustness
- High-risk missions where sUAS loss is probable
- Field operations in unimproved areas
