- Context: Found in NOAA 2019 SBIR Phase II proposal references folder; last edited by Maciej Stachura (BST)

## Executive Summary
This is a comprehensive academic review of deep learning approaches to optical flow estimation, documenting the transition from classical energy-based methods to CNN-based regression architectures. The paper surveys the evolution of techniques from FlowNet through state-of-the-art methods like PWC-Net and VCN, covering supervised, unsupervised, and semi-supervised learning paradigms, as well as multi-frame approaches.

## Technical Approach
The document traces the evolution of optical flow estimation methods through three main paradigms:

1. **Classical Energy-Based Methods**: Horn and Schunck formulation minimizing brightness constancy and spatial smoothness
2. **CNNs as Feature Extractors**: Using trained feature descriptors within classical MRF/energy minimization frameworks (PatchBatch, CNN-based matching with Siamese architectures)
3. **End-to-End CNN Regression**: Direct prediction from image pairs using fully trainable networks

Key architectural innovations documented:
- **Coarse-to-fine estimation**: Multi-scale pyramid processing (SPyNet, PWC-Net)
- **Cost volume construction**: 3D and 4D volumetric representations of feature correspondences
- **Iterative refinement**: Stacking multiple networks or weight-shared refinement (FlowNet2, IRR scheme)
- **Backward warping**: Using estimated flow to warp feature maps for progressive refinement

## Products & Capabilities Described

### FlowNet Family
- First end-to-end CNN architecture (FlowNet, FlowNetS, FlowNetC)
- Hourglass encoder-decoder architecture
- Initial model size: 38-39M parameters
- Demonstrated feasibility but initially underperformed classical methods
- Established standard practices: synthetic dataset pre-training (FlyingChairs), learning rate schedules, data augmentation

**FlowNet2**: Stacking multiple networks improved accuracy >50% over FlowNet
- Required FlyingThings3D dataset for adequate pre-training
- 162.49M parameters

### SPyNet
- 5-level image pyramid with residual flow updates
- 96% parameter reduction vs. FlowNet (1.20M parameters)
- Comparable accuracy to FlowNet while more efficient

### PWC-Net
- Three design principles: pyramid, warping, cost volume
- 6-level feature pyramid with 3D cost volume
- 8.75M parameters
- 17x smaller than FlowNet2, 2x faster, superior accuracy
- Set state-of-the-art with practical efficiency

### LiteFlowNet
- 6-level feature pyramid, residual flow updates
- 5.37M parameters
- Per-pixel local flow regularization module
- 13% error reduction vs. base architecture

### IRR (Iterative Residual Refinement)
- Weight-shared iterative refinement applicable to multiple backbones
- Improved accuracy without adding parameters
- Improved generalization to unseen datasets
- IRR-PWC: 26.4% parameter reduction while improving accuracy
- Extended to occlusion and bi-directional flow (17.7% improvement)

### HD³
- Probabilistic framework estimating match density rather than direct flow
- Provides uncertainty quantification
- State-of-the-art accuracy with uncertainty measures

### VCN (Volumetric Correspondence Networks)
- True 4D volumetric processing with 4D convolutions
- Separable 4D convolutions reduce complexity by N²
- 6.20M parameters
- Fastest training convergence (7x fewer iterations than competitors)
- Best accuracy on benchmarks (EPE: 2.808 on Sintel Clean)

## Use Cases & Applications

Not explicitly specified for BST applications. The document is purely academic reference material on optical flow technology. However, implicit applications include:
- Motion estimation for video analysis
- Autonomous vehicle perception
- Video interpolation and frame synthesis
- Scene flow and 3D reconstruction

## Key Results (Academic Benchmarks)

**MPI Sintel Dataset (End Point Error - lower is better):**
| Method | Clean | Final |
|--------|-------|-------|
| FlowNetS | 6.158 | 7.218 |
| SPyNet | 6.640 | 8.360 |
| FlowNet2 | 3.959 | 6.016 |
| PWC-Net | 4.386 | 5.042 |
| LiteFlowNet | 3.449 | 5.381 |
| IRR-PWC | 3.844 | 4.579 |
| HD³ | 4.788 | 4.666 |
| **VCN** | **2.808** | **4.404** |

**KITTI Dataset (Outlier percentage - lower is better):**
| Method | 2012 | 2015 |
|--------|------|------|
| FlowNet2 | 4.82% | 10.41% |
| PWC-Net | 4.22% | 9.60% |
| LiteFlowNet | 3.27% | 9.38% |
| IRR-PWC | 3.21% | 7.65% |
| **HD³** | **2.26%** | 6.55% |
| VCN | – | **6.30%** |

## Learning Paradigms

### Supervised Learning
- Requires dense ground-truth optical flow annotations
- Challenges: Limited real-world labeled data, domain overfitting
- Standard approach: Pre-train on synthetic datasets (FlyingChairs, FlyingThings3D), fine-tune on target domain
- Per-pixel L2 loss with multi-scale intermediate supervision

### Unsupervised/Self-Supervised Learning
- Minimizes proxy loss based on photometric consistency (brightness constancy)
- **Key methods:**
  - Ahmadi & Patras: Classical optical flow constraint as loss
  - Yu et al., Ren et al.: MRF-inspired proxy loss (data + smoothness terms)
  - Meister et al.: Advanced proxy with occlusion handling and higher-order smoothness
  - Wang et al.: Bi-directional flow with disocclusion-based occlusion detection
  - DDFlow/SelFlow: Data distillation with teacher-student networks and pseudo-labels
  - Multi-frame extensions: Temporal coherence constraints

### Semi-Supervised Learning
- **GAN-based approach** (Lai et al.): Discriminator distinguishes between generated and ground-truth flow warp error patterns
- **Conditional prior networks** (Yang et al.): Learning regularizer from one domain, training on another for better generalization

## Multi-Frame Optical Flow
- Exploits temporal coherence/constant velocity assumption across 3+ consecutive frames
- **Ren et al.**: Fusion of adjacent two-frame flows
- **Maurer et al.**: Learning to predict forward from backward flow in online manner; 27% improvement in occluded regions
- **Neoral et al.**: Recursive joint estimation of flow and occlusion; 25% flow improvement, 12% from temporal feedback
- All multi-frame methods show particular benefits in occlusions and motion boundaries

## Notable Details

### Training Datasets
- **FlyingChairs**: Synthetic dataset with rendered chairs on natural images; good for initial pre-training
- **FlyingThings3D**: More complex synthetic data with 3D motion and photometric effects; essential for achieving competitive results
- **MPI Sintel, KITTI**: Public benchmark datasets driving research

### Architectural Design Principles (Table 1 analysis)
1. Pyramid structures (coarse-to-fine) reduce parameters and improve accuracy
2. Network stacking improves accuracy linearly with parameters (FlowNet2)
3. Cost volume construction standard practice for feature matching
4. Iterative refinement achieves gains without parameter increase
5. Output representation innovations (match density, 4D cost volumes) provide significant gains
6. Subtle design differences (regularization modules, skip connections) accumulate improvements

### Domain Generalization Challenge
- Models trained on synthetic data significantly underperform on real data
- Pre-training/fine-tuning schedule critical (20% accuracy difference in FlowNet2)
- Unsupervised and semi-supervised approaches address domain gap without target-domain labels
- IRR and conditional prior approaches show improved cross-domain generalization

### Performance Trade-offs
- Early methods (FlowNet): High accuracy but large (38M params), slow
- Efficient methods (SPyNet): Much smaller but lower accuracy
- PWC-Net/LiteFlowNet: Balance of accuracy and efficiency (5-9M params)
- VCN: State-of-the-art accuracy with efficiency and fast training

### Why This Document in BST's NOAA SBIR Phase II Folder
This reference appears to support deep learning approaches potentially applicable to:
- Motion/flow estimation from aerial drone imagery (S2, S3 applications)
- Atmospheric or oceanographic video analysis
- Possibly temporal coherence in LIDAR or imaging time-series data
- General computer vision methodology for next-generation sensors

## Executive Summary
The DOE Office of Science and partner offices (CMEI, EM, NE, OE, HGEO) are soliciting interdisciplinary team applications to address the Genesis Mission National Science and Technology Challenges. Teams will accelerate scientific discovery and R&D workflows using novel AI models and frameworks across 9+ topic areas (advanced manufacturing, biotechnology, critical materials, nuclear fission, nuclear fusion, quantum information science, semiconductors, discovery science, and energy). Total funding available: $293.76 million for FY26 Phase I ($500K-$750K per award, 9 months) and Phase II ($1.5-3.75M, 3 years).

## Program Structure

### Phased Approach
**Phase I (9 months, $500K-$750K):** Teams design and demonstrate clear research workflows incorporating AI with concrete evaluation of AI advantage. Success metrics may include increased predictive power, improved scientific insight from curated data, tighter data-experiment coupling, new model development, scaling metrics, accelerated experimental workflows, or other quantitative metrics showing trajectory toward transformative capability.

**Phase II (3 years, $1.5-3.75M):** Meritorious Phase I teams and new Phase II teams pursue promising directions. Level of effort envisioned at 3-5x Phase I. Receipt of Phase I award not prerequisite for Phase II; teams believing they've achieved Phase I goals may apply directly for Phase II.

### Team Requirements
- **Phase I:** Multi-institutional teams required with partners from at least 2 of 3 categories: (1) DOE/NNSA National Laboratory or Scientific User Facility, (2) Industry, (3) Institute of Higher Education/Non-profit/Other
- **Phase II:** Large teams with at least one partner from categories (1) and (2); category (3) strongly encouraged but not required
- Industrial partners may receive up to 20% of total requested budget
- Partners must provide intellectual contributions but don't require DOE funding

## Eligibility Requirements

### Eligible Applicants
- All types of domestic applicants except 501(c)(4) nonprofit organizations engaged in lobbying after December 31, 1995
- DOE/NNSA National Laboratories eligible as lead or team member (not as subrecipients)
- Non-DOE FFRDCs eligible in collaborative applications (not as subrecipients)
- Other Federal Agencies eligible in collaborative applications (not as subrecipients)

### Cost Sharing Requirements
- **Non-profit entities and academic institutions:** Cost sharing not required for basic and applied research
- **For-profit entities (prime or sub):** Minimum 20% cost share for R&D activities; 50% for demonstration/commercial tasks
- Cost share based on each for-profit entity's budget portion, minimum 20% of allowable R&D costs
- Cost share must originate from non-federal sources
- Institutional commitments (space, facilities, equipment, faculty release time, student scholarships, waived F&A) strongly encouraged but separate from cost share requirement
- Cost share not required from DOE/NNSA National Labs, other Federal agencies, or FFRDCs

### PI Requirements
- Must be in permanent or indefinitely extensible position (tenured, tenure-track, or staff appointment)
- Not eligible if in term-limited appointments (adjunct, visiting, fellow)
- Part-time permanent positions eligible
- Joint appointment eligible if work performed at applicant institution and PI on applicant's payroll
- Individuals receiving >50% salary from DOE/NNSA National Lab cannot be PI at other institutions
- Can be senior/key personnel on unlimited applications but lead PI on only one application
- Non-U.S. citizens and non-permanent residents eligible

## Key Challenge Areas/Topics

**Topic 1: Reenvisioning Advanced Manufacturing and Industrial Productivity**
- Participating Offices: SC-BES, CMEI-ITO, CMEI-AMMTO, SC-FES, SC-ASCR
- Challenge: Bridge "valley of death" between scientific discovery and commercial viability
- AI Solution: Agentic/generative AI to navigate multi-scale systems, integrate data into digital twins, enable automated decision support
- Focus Areas:
  - A. Agentic AI-Driven Chemical Manufacturing (BES)
  - B. AI-Driven Materials Processing (BES)
  - C. AI-Enabled Manufacturing for Extreme Energy Systems (FES)
  - D. Digitalization of Industrial Processes (ITO)
  - E. AI-Enabled Smart Manufacturing (AMMTO)
  - F. Energy Material Manufacturing (AFFO) - primarily National Lab led

**Topic 2: Scaling the Biotechnology Revolution**
- Participating Offices: SC-BER, CMEI-AFFO, SC-ASCR
- Challenge: Design biology on demand; overcome nonlinear complexity and long development cycles
- AI Solution: AI to integrate genomics, multi-omics, imaging, phenomics data; establish genotype-phenotype relationships; guide autonomous experimentation
- Focus Areas:
  - A. Biomolecular Science (BER)
  - B. Genotype to Phenotype (BER)
  - C. Predictive Engineering of Microbial Communities (BER)
  - D. Bio Design (BER)
  - E. AI-Enabled Biological Reaction Engineering, Bioreactor Design, Scale-up (AFFO)

**Topic 3: Securing America's Critical Minerals Supply**
- Participating Offices: CMEI-ASO, CMEI-AMMTO, CMEI-AMMPTO, SC-BES, SC-BER, SC-ASCR
- Challenge: Dependency on foreign supply chains for critical minerals threatens security and competitiveness
- AI Solution: Integrate geophysical data, science data, process optimization into connected system; physics-based AI for predictive capabilities
- Focus Areas:
  - A. Resource Mapping and Development (AMMPTO)
  - B. AI-Enabled Materials Discovery and Engineering (AMMTO)
  - C. Economic Modeling and Market Analysis (ASO)
  - D. Extraction and Processing Technologies (AMMPTO/AMMTO)
  - E. Geological Finders/Keepers (BES/BER)
  - F. Connections for Isolation (BES)
  - G. Biological Pathways to CMM (BER)

**Topic 4: Delivering Nuclear Energy that is Faster, Safer, Cheaper**
- Participating Offices: NE, SC-ASCR
- Challenge: Long development timelines and escalating costs limit affordable nuclear energy deployment
- AI Solution: Accelerate deployment with explainable AI solutions including surrogate models, agentic workflows, autonomous labs, digital twins. Goal: 2x schedule acceleration and >50% operational cost reductions
- Focus: Proof-of-concept demonstrations leveraging AI to accelerate nuclear engineering/licensing pipelines with quantifiable cost/schedule/regulatory uncertainty reductions

## Genesis Mission Integration Framework

All funded teams become part of the Genesis Mission and must contribute to relevant components in coordinated fashion. Core components include:

1. **American Science Cloud (AmSC):** Collaborative cloud ecosystem for scientific research, data sharing, and analysis
2. **Transformational AI Models Consortium (ModCon):** Curating data and building foundational, self-improving AI models for science
3. **American Science and Security Platform:** Collaborative effort between AmSC/ModCon and NNSA-funded teams

### Expected Contributions
- Host data, models, and artifacts on Genesis Mission platform with discoverable metadata
- Participate in coordination activities across Genesis Mission for data, models, infrastructure
- Provide information on project requirements, needs, and best practices as requested
- Leverage platform capabilities provided by DOE/NNSA National Laboratories and Genesis Mission Consortium members

## Document Metadata
- Type: Design presentation/concept document
- Client/Agency: Not explicitly named (referenced as "they/their")
- Program/Solicitation: Unknown
- Date: Created June 19, 2020; Modified June 25, 2020
- BST Products/Systems Referenced: Appears to be for an airborne platform (nose cone, pressure sensing system)
- Key Personnel: Jack Elston (last editor)

## Executive Summary
This document presents design concept iterations for a flush air ballast cover system with integrated static pressure ports and water intrusion prevention mechanisms. The design addresses pressure measurement and environmental protection for what appears to be an airborne platform, with focus on resolving water ingestion and electromagnetic interference (EMI) issues.

## Technical Approach

### Flush Air Ballast Cover Assembly
- Inner radius configured in 'x'-pattern at 15° from centerline
- Outer radius in standard '+'-pattern at 25° from centerline
- Enclosed removable lid design
- Optional metal-mesh insert for improved EMI shielding
- Manifold required to distribute pressure to differential sensors
- Static pressure lines routed into system

### Static Ports
- Four (4) holes drilled in nose cone perimeter
- Ports glued directly into nose cone
- Simple design with no integrated water prevention at port level

### Water Intrusion Prevention Mechanisms
- **Surface ridges**: 0.5mm ridges prevent water from running along surface and covering holes
- **Hole sizing**: 2mm diameter holes reduce likelihood of total blockage by small water droplets; can be enlarged if needed
- **Direct impact requirement**: Design relies on water requiring direct droplet impact rather than surface flow

### Moisture Trap Design
- Printed as separate component, installed into cap pocket
- Provides outer lip on cap
- Includes weep hole on back side to allow airflow and water clearing
- Weep hole created by melting with heated metal rod/needle near nipple junction
- Wicking mechanism within trap clears main air channel once droplet reaches trap
- Cannot print 0.5mm wall on cover surface; moisture trap tube provides this wall function

### Enclosure & Integration
- Box with removable lid
- Support rails for PCBA slide-in/out installation
- Cable passthrough via drilled/cut holes in back lid
- Tight fit design for internal tubing

## Use Cases & Applications
Airborne environmental sensing platform requiring:
- Pressure measurement (differential sensors)
- Static pressure sampling
- Operation in wet/humid conditions with water ingestion risk

## Interference Issues Noted
- **Front clearance area**: Client may not update requested clearance; design can still be delivered but with severely restricted feature additions and port blockage solutions
- **Pressure line routing**: If clearance not updated, pressure lines must be routed within 3D-printed components (feasible but constrained)
- **EMI concerns**: Addressed through optional metal-mesh insert in box

## Notable Details
- Design relies on active airflow to clear moisture trap (passive system limitation)
- Extensive use of 3D printing with manufacturing constraints (0.5mm wall features not feasible)
- Iterative design process showing unresolved interference issues and client coordination challenges
- Unconventional weep hole creation method (heated needle melt-through) suggests tight spatial constraints
- Design prioritizes simplicity over sophistication due to physical space limitations# Detailed Mishap Report

## Document Metadata
- Type: Incident report / mishap investigation
- Client/Agency: NASA / JPL (Jet Propulsion Laboratory)
- Program/Solicitation: SoOp (Signals of Opportunity) - Fraser Experimental Forest snow water equivalent characterization
- Date: 2018-05-22
- BST Products/Systems Referenced: BST aircraft (two variants), p-band radiometer payload system
- Key Personnel: Jack Elston (author), Simon Yueh (JPL PI), Xiaolan, Maciej

## Executive Summary
During a third scheduled flight operation at Fraser Experimental Forest (elevation ~10,000 MSL) to characterize snow water equivalent using a p-band radiometer, a BST aircraft suffered a mishap when trim adjustments during flight resulted in an unrecoverable dive, causing the aircraft to contact multiple trees. The aircraft sustained moderate damage (fractured right wing spar, damaged nose and scaffolding) while payload equipment (SDR, LNA) remained largely intact. All procedures were followed and the incident was properly reported.

## Technical Approach

### Mission Context
- Location: Fraser Experimental Forest, mountainous forested terrain at ~10,000 MSL
- Payload: p-band radiometer for signals of opportunity snow water equivalent measurement
- Aircraft: Two variants of BST aircraft available; second aircraft selected for its lighter weight and improved construction, enabling steeper climb-out angles
- Launch/Recovery: Conducted from forest service road with tall trees on both sides and potential mountain wind shear
- Planned Operations: Three flights scheduled at 6:00, 9:00, and 12:00

### Flight Profile and Incident Sequence

**First Flight (6:30, successful):**
- Initial payload issues caused slight delay
- Successful launch and recovery using first aircraft
- Determined that second, lighter aircraft would be safer for subsequent flights

**Second Flight (9:00, incident flight):**
- Successful launch in autonomous mode
- During mapping mission: nose-down behavior observed during turns, within safe margins but indicative of trim/CG issue
- Suspected cause: elevator trim state (CG had been measured pre-flight; components secured and checked)
- Decision: Adjust trim settings during straight-level flight near end of mission at ~120m AGL
  - Rationale: Better handling needed for tight landing with little margin for error; altitude provided safety margin for manual intervention if needed
- Trim command execution: Aircraft began to dive and gain speed
- Pilot intervention attempt: Unable to slow descent despite manual control input
- Autopilot mode reinstatement: Aircraft could only slightly slow descent before contacting trees

### Root Cause Analysis (from flight logs)

1. Aircraft had been using nearly full up elevator deflection to maintain level flight before trim adjustment
2. Resetting trim condition zeroed the control loop integrators, causing the dive
3. Aircraft was slowly recovering but recovery time uncertain
4. Manual pilot throws available were slightly less than autopilot maximum deflection—insufficient to arrest descent
5. Direct line of sight being lost periodically through trees, making continued manual control problematic
6. Decision to return to autonomous mode was optimal given circumstances

## Products & Capabilities Described

### BST Aircraft (two variants)
- **General Characteristics:**
  - 10' wing span
  - Equipped with detachable nose section
  - Autonomous and manual control modes
  - Capable of operations from constrained locations (forest service roads)
  
- **First Variant (Flight 1):**
  - Standard construction
  - Heavier than second variant
  - Shallower climb-out angle
  
- **Second Variant (Flight 2 incident aircraft):**
  - Lighter weight due to improved construction techniques
  - Steeper climb-out angle capability
  - Better suited for confined launching areas
  - Design improvements under development post-incident

### Payload System (p-band radiometer)
- Mounted in internal scaffolding structure
- Components: SDR (Software Defined Radio), LNA (Low Noise Amplifier), antenna
- Detachable nose design houses payload scaffolding
- Designed for signals of opportunity snow water equivalent characterization

## Use Cases & Applications

**Snow Water Equivalent Characterization:**
- Partnership with Simon Yueh (JPL)
- Fraser Experimental Forest study site in mountainous terrain
- P-band radiometer using signals of opportunity methodology
- High-altitude operations in challenging terrain (10,000 MSL, forested mountains)

## Damage Assessment

**Aircraft Damage:**
- Right wing: Fractured spar (major structural damage)
- Left wing: Minor damage only
- Fuselage: Intact with several internal brackets broken loose
- Both tail sections: Survived intact
- Detachable nose: Requires replacement
- Payload scaffolding: Requires replacement

**Payload Equipment Damage:**
- SDR: Unharmed
- LNA: Unharmed
- Antenna: Damaged (likely due to weight and forward position)

**Overall Assessment:** Damage to JPL equipment and aircraft determined to be "relatively minor" despite tree contact at flight speed

## Recovery and Follow-up

- Last known location noted and used for recovery
- Field team (Jack Elston, Maciej) recovered aircraft safely
- No immediate safety hazards found (battery in safe condition)
- All components collected; no items left behind
- Post-flight discussion conducted
- Incident summary sent to JPL via official "Close Call / Mishap Reporting Reference Sheet"
- Full incident analysis completed same afternoon

## Corrective Actions Undertaken

**Design Changes (implemented in latest aircraft version for future flights):**

1. **Structural Rigidity:** 
   - Much more rigid outer structure to prevent damage from handling and transport
   - Addresses pre-existing trim damage from transit/use that went undetected in pre-flight

2. **Protection:** 
   - Redesigned protective case for surface protection during transit

3. **Control System Updates:**
   - Increased maximum elevator deflection limits
   - **Critical change:** Manual control limits now set equal to autopilot limits (previously, manual limits set to pilot preference for comfort, creating mismatch that prevented adequate manual intervention)

## Notable Details

- All Flight Test Plan (FTP) procedures followed, including emergency procedures and incident reporting
- Official mishap reporting completed same day
- Armstrong review anticipated
- High-altitude mountainous operations present unique challenges (wind shear, terrain, density altitude effects on aircraft performance)
- Control system architecture consideration: pilot comfort vs. emergency capability trade-off identified and corrected# Details for Midsize from Hertz at $176.79 total

## Document Metadata
- Type: Presentation/Technical Update
- Client/Agency: Creare
- Program/Solicitation: 2019 VTOL Autopilot project
- Date: Created 2020-09-27, Modified 2020-10-20
- BST Products/Systems Referenced: Double Eagle (VTOL platform)
- Key Personnel: Maciej Stachura (last editor)

## Executive Summary
This presentation documents testing updates for a VTOL autopilot project with Creare, focusing on transition flight testing with the Double Eagle platform and troubleshooting of roll control saturation issues discovered during both full-scale and prototype aircraft testing.

## Technical Approach
Testing conducted in two phases:
1. **Full-scale Double Eagle transitions**: 7 transition flights to evaluate forward flight performance
2. **Small prototype iterations**: 9 flights dedicated to debugging roll control issues
3. **Control tuning**: Adjustments to elevon trim tabs to resolve saturation problems

## Products & Capabilities Described

**Double Eagle VTOL Platform:**
- Mass: 20.3 kg (with 2 batteries)
- Hover Power requirement: 2618W
- Forward Power @ 13 m/s: 1240W
- Identified inefficiency in forward flight due to maxed-out roll control authority

## Technical Issues & Solutions

**Roll Control Saturation Problem:**
- Initial issue: Forward roll control saturation in full autopilot mode, creating very narrow flight envelope
- Root causes identified:
  - Saturation in control channels during full automation
  - Rotor 3 saturation contributing to roll control issues
  - With elevons neutral: positive roll torque saturation
- Solution implemented: Elevon trim tab deflection (~5° up) eliminated saturation
- Result: Reduced rotor command spread, better control authority, improved tracking and orbit performance without oscillation

## Key Results
- Saturation effects demonstrated: decent tracking/orbit capability when saturated eliminated; oscillatory behavior observed with saturation present
- Elevon trim tab adjustment proved effective in expanding usable flight envelope
- Small prototype testing proved valuable for rapid iteration on control issues before full-scale validation

## Notable Details
- Inefficiency in Double Eagle forward flight attributed to control saturation rather than aerodynamic design
- Issue resolution required relatively minor hardware modification (trim tab deflection)
- Testing methodology: rapid iteration on small prototype followed by validation on full-scale platform# DARPA SBIR Direct to Phase II Technical Volume Template

## Document Metadata
- **Type:** Instruction template / Guidance document
- **Client/Agency:** Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA)
- **Program/Solicitation:** DoD SBIR BAA, Direct to Phase II opportunities
- **Date:** Not specified in document (appears to be FY25 based on file path)
- **Context:** This is an instruction and template document, not a completed proposal
- **Last Editor:** Beck Cotter
- **BST Products/Systems Referenced:** None

## Executive Summary
This document is a DARPA-issued instruction and template guide for Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Direct to Phase II proposals. It provides detailed formatting requirements, page limits, and content guidance for two alternative submission formats: (1) the Standard Format with Feasibility Documentation and Technical Proposal, and (2) the White Paper & Slide Deck Format. It is not itself a BST proposal or project document.

## Document Purpose and Content Structure

This is an **official DARPA template and instruction document** that establishes requirements for Direct to Phase II submissions. It does not describe a specific Black Swift Technologies project, proposal, or capability.

### **Part I: Standard Format Requirements**

**Technical Volume Structure (Two Parts):**
- **Part One: Feasibility Documentation** (max pages per DARPA Instructions)
  - Documentation substantiating Phase I feasibility achievement
  - Technical reports, test data, prototype designs, performance results
  - Commercial applications and DoD insertion opportunity analysis
  - One-page Commercialization Potential summary (required)

- **Part Two: Technical Proposal** (max pages per topic)
  - Problem/Opportunity identification and significance
  - Phase II Technical Objectives
  - Phase II Statement of Work (detailed approach, schedule, deliverables)
  - Phase II Option Statement of Work (if applicable)
  - Related Work (state-of-art awareness, previous relevant projects)
  - Relationship with Future Research/Phase III commercialization
  - Key Personnel (resumes, education, experience, publications)
  - Foreign Citizens disclosure (if applicable)
  - Facilities/Equipment description
  - Subcontractors/Consultants (minimum 50% work by prime contractor)
  - Prior/Current/Pending Support disclosure
  - Commercialization Strategy (5-page limit, doesn't count toward page limit)
  - Technical Data Rights assertions

**Commercialization Strategy Requirements (5 pages, not counted in page limit):**
- Phase I transition/commercialization activities and Technology Readiness Level (TRL) achieved
- Problem/Need Statement (DoD and/or private sector relevance)
- Product(s) and System Application(s) description
- Business Model(s)/Procurement Mechanism(s)
- Target Market analysis and competitive landscape
- Funding Requirements and history
- Transition and Commercialization Risks and mitigation
- Team Expertise/Qualifications and Company Readiness
- Anticipated Transition/Commercialization Results (quantitative schedule)
- Optional: Advocacy Letters and Letters of Intent/Commitment

**Optional Submission Elements:**
- Advocacy letters (substantiating customer interest)
- Letters of Intent/Commitment (from commercial, DoD, or prime contractor partners)

### **Part II: White Paper & Slide Deck Format**

**White Paper (max 20 pages):**
- Goals and Impact
- Phase I Feasibility documentation
- Technical Plan (objectives, metrics, milestones at 1-month or less intervals)
- Management and Capabilities (key personnel, team expertise, IP, facilities, BSL requirements)
- Transition and Commercialization Plan

**Slide Deck (max 15 slides, converted to PDF):**
- Topic relevance and proposed deliverables
- Technology approach and competitive landscape
- Technical and commercial value proposition
- Technical and commercial risks
- Market analysis
- Cost, schedule, and milestones
- Management overview
- Technical Summary Quad Chart (using SBIR template)
- Commercialization Summary Quad Chart (using DARPA TCSP template)

## Formatting Requirements

**General Format:**
- Standard 8.5" x 11" paper, single-spaced, single column
- Times New Roman font, minimum 10-point (smaller font allowable only for headers, footers, tables, figures, graphics)
- One-inch margins on all sides
- All content counts toward page limit unless otherwise specified
- Proprietary data must be marked with disclosure legend

**File Submission (White Paper & Slide Deck Format):**
- Single PDF file combining white paper and slide deck
- Consecutive page numbering
- Header: company name, topic number, proposal number
- Virus scanned before upload
- No locked/encrypted files
- No embedded videos or moving media

## Supporting Documentation Requirements

**Volume 1 (Cover Sheet):** Completed in DSIP system
- Proposal Summary (duration, abstract, commercial application, keywords)
- Proposal Certifications (% of work calculated from budget)
- Contact Information (PI, Corporate Official, Authorized Contract Negotiator)

**Volume 3 (Cost Volume):** Excel template required
- Personnel costs (by name and hours)
- Equipment and materials (with justification and market research)
- Travel (justified and project-related)
- Subcontractor and consultant costs (detailed substantiation)
- All costs require documentation of derivation

**Volume 4 (Company Commercialization Report):** Required for Phase I and Direct to Phase II
- Reporting of funding outcomes from prior SBIR/STTR awards

**Volume 5 (Supporting Documents):** MANDATORY uploads
- Contractor Certification Regarding Prohibition on Certain Telecommunications/Video Surveillance Services
- Disclosures of Foreign Affiliations/Relationships
- Disclosure of Funding Sources
- DARPA Milestones Template
- Technical Data Rights Assertions (table and supporting documentation)
- Letters of recommendation, CVs, and supplemental materials

**Volume 6 (Fraud, Waste & Abuse Certification):** Required for Phase I and Direct to Phase II
- Annual FWA training review and certification

## Key Submission Rules

- **Minimum 50% of work** (by direct and indirect costs) must be performed by proposing small business firm (unless waiver approved by Contracting Officer)
- Federal Laboratories and FFRDCs may be used without waiver; use must be certified on Cover Sheet
- Universities may be subcontractors; must certify that they will not publicly release Export Controlled/ITAR restricted information
- Cost sharing is permitted but not required
- Phase II Option Statement of Work (if applicable per topic)
- All proposed costs must include substantiation (quotes, market research, vendor justification)

## Technical Data Rights (Class Deviation 2020-O0007)

- Contractor retains rights to technical data and software developed under the contract
- Government obtains royalty-free license for Government purposes only during period from contract award through 20 years after project completion
- During 20-year license period, Government may not release/disclose SBIR data except: (1) for evaluation purposes, (2) with contractor permission, or (3) for emergency repair/overhaul
- After 20-year period, Government has unlimited rights
- Proposers may assert restrictions using Class Deviation 2020-O0007 framework
- All assertions must be identified in proposal; contract cannot be awarded until assertions approved

## Submission Portal and Process

**Defense SBIR/STTR Innovation Portal (DSIP):**
- Online submission system for all DoD SBIR/STTR proposals
- Training materials and job aids available at https://www.dodsbirsttr.mil/submissions/learning-support/training-materials
- Registration required
- "Start New Proposal" workflow for Direct to Phase II submissions
- Sequential volume uploads (Volumes 1-6)

## Notable Details

- **Advocacy letters and Letters of Intent/Commitment** are optional; should only be submitted if substantiating commercialization claims; do not count against page limits
- **Government personnel letters** are NOT considered during evaluation per DoD 5500.7-R Joint Ethics Regulation
- **Privacy Act protection** applied to foreign national information
- **Embedded Entrepreneurship Initiative (EEI)** eligibility may be determined separately following SBIR award selection based on commercialization strategy content
- **Compliance with environmental laws** (federal, state, local) must be addressed for proposed facilities
- **Technology Readiness Level (TRL)** progression must be demonstrated and tracked
- Document was last edited **October 1, 2025** by Beck Cotter (appears to be living template being updated for FY25 solicitation)

## Assessment

This is a **procedural instruction document, not a project proposal or capability brief**. It provides no information about Black Swift Technologies' projects, products, or capabilities. It should be retained as reference material for understanding DARPA SBIR Direct to Phase II submission requirements, but contains no substantive technical or business information about BST to extract into the knowledge base.# Bartington Instruments - Terms and Conditions of Sale and Services

### Defense-Related Use
- **Critical Restriction:** Any defense-related use must be "Passive Defence" only—solely to reduce probability and minimize effects of damage from hostile action, without initiating hostile action
- Buyer must provide written confirmation on request; must procure similar confirmations from all successors
- Breach is material, non-remediable breach

### Termination
- Either party may terminate with written notice if other party: (a) commits material breach not remedied within 30 days, or (b) becomes insolvent/ceases trading
- Force majeure clause: 90-day threshold for termination if delays continue

### Confidentiality & Schematics
- Standard confidentiality obligations for both parties
- Schematics are Confidential Information; non-exclusive, perpetual license granted only for designing electronics to work with Bartington goods
- Buyer may not use schematics for other purposes

### WEEE Compliance
- UK/EU buyers responsible for collection, treatment, recovery, environmentally sound disposal of electrical/electronic waste
- Non-EU buyers must comply with local law

### Dispute Resolution
- Governed by English law; exclusive jurisdiction of English courts

## Significance for Black Swift
This document establishes the terms under which Black Swift (as a buyer) would be purchasing Bartington magnetometer equipment for integration into its SBIR Phase II magnetometer project. The strict liability caps, 12-month warranty, passive-defense-only restrictions on any military applications, and requirements to disclose modifications are all contractual constraints that Black Swift must work within when using Bartington components in its Navy proposal.# Scott Tibbitts - Statement of Work: Methane Emission Detection Pilot Program

## Executive Summary
This document provides standardized instructions for completing a Research Performance Progress Report (RPPR) for Federal grant and cooperative agreement recipients. It establishes uniform reporting requirements across federal agencies to reduce administrative burden and enable consistent comparison of research outputs and outcomes. The RPPR is used for both interim and final progress reports.

## Document Purpose & Scope
This is a template/instruction document issued by the Department of Commerce for SBIR Phase I award recipients (including Black Swift Technologies on their NOAA 2019 SBIR Phase I project). It does not contain project-specific information but rather defines the standardized format and categories that recipients must use when submitting progress reports to federal agencies.

## Reporting Categories & Required Information

### Mandatory Section: ACCOMPLISHMENTS
Recipients must address:
- Major goals and objectives of the project
- What was accomplished under these goals
- Training and professional development opportunities provided
- How results were disseminated to communities of interest
- Plans for the next reporting period

### Optional Sections (as required by agency):
- **PRODUCTS**: Publications, conference papers, presentations, websites, technologies, inventions, patents, software, databases, educational materials, instruments, etc.
- **PARTICIPANTS & OTHER COLLABORATING ORGANIZATIONS**: Personnel involved, changes in active support, partner organizations, international collaborations
- **IMPACT**: Effects on the discipline, other disciplines, human resources development, teaching/education, infrastructure, technology transfer, society, and foreign countries
- **CHANGES/PROBLEMS**: Modifications to approach, delays, expenditure impacts, changes to human subjects/animal protocols, performance site changes
- **SPECIAL REPORTING REQUIREMENTS**: Award-specific requirements
- **BUDGETARY INFORMATION**: Financial data using standard forms
- **PROJECT OUTCOMES**: Cumulative findings (final report only, max 8,000 characters, written for general public)

## Cover Page Data Elements Required
- Federal agency and organization element
- Federal grant/identifying number
- Project title
- PD/PI name, title, contact information
- Submitting official information (if different from PD/PI)
- Submission date
- DUNS and EIN numbers
- Recipient organization name and address
- Project/grant period dates
- Reporting period end date
- Report frequency
- Final report designation (Yes/No)
- Submitting official signature

## Key Reporting Standards
- Recipients must obtain prior written approval for significant changes to project objectives or scope
- "Nothing to Report" option available when no significant activity in a category
- Instructions emphasize shift from reporting activities to reporting accomplishments as project progresses
- Results should be disseminated and evaluated based on excellence/significance, not quantity of publications
- Language should be accessible to lay audiences where possible

## Demographic Information (Optional)
Agencies may collect voluntary demographic data on significant contributors:
- Gender (Male/Female/Decline)
- Ethnicity (Hispanic/Non-Hispanic/Decline)
- Race (American Indian, Asian, Black, Native Hawaiian, White, Decline)
- Disability status (Yes/No/Decline)

Data collection must be direct from individual contributors and protected under Privacy Act requirements.

## Notable Details
- RPPR replaced previous agency-specific reporting formats to create uniformity
- Originally implemented FY2013, revised based on lessons learned
- Format applies to both interim and final progress reports
- Agencies may supplement with program-specific instructions only where necessary, subject to OMB clearance
- A "significant contributor" is defined as a PD/PI or individual working ≥1 person-month per year (approximately 160 hours) on the project
- Special emphasis on infrastructure development, technology transfer, and societal impact beyond traditional academic metrics
- International collaboration and foreign spending must be tracked and reported# RPPR Instructions - Department of Commerce

## Document Metadata
- Type: Compliance training presentation with certification requirement
- Client/Agency: U.S. Department of Commerce (DOC), Office of Inspector General (OIG)
- Program/Solicitation: Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Program
- Date: July 31, 2017 (training materials); applicable to SBIR proposals and awards
- BST Products/Systems Referenced: None
- Key Personnel: Not applicable (training material)

## Executive Summary

This is mandatory compliance training for all SBIR applicants, produced by the DOC Office of Inspector General. The training covers SBIR program requirements, fraud definitions, compliance obligations (particularly around "essentially equivalent work" and Principal Investigator employment), consequences of fraud, and administrative/record-keeping best practices. Completion and certification of this training is required to be attached to any SBIR proposal submission.

## Content Overview

### SBIR Program Structure
The SBIR Program is a federal initiative with three phases:
- **Phase I**: $150K–$225K awards (up to 6 months) to determine feasibility
- **Phase II**: $1M–$1.5M awards (up to 2 years) for development of prototypes
- **Phase III**: Commercialization with no funding limits and potential for sole-source awards

### Eligibility Requirements
- For-profit Small Business Concern (≤500 employees)
- >50% owned by U.S. citizens or permanent resident aliens
- Principal Investigator must have primary employment (>50%) with the SBC
- Work must be performed in the U.S.
- Phase I: minimum 2/3 of effort by SBC; Phase II: minimum 1/2 of effort by SBC
- Cannot receive funding for essentially equivalent work already funded by federal government

## Fraud Definitions & Compliance Requirements

### Key Fraud Types Outlined

1. **Essentially Equivalent Work**: Submitting and accepting funding for substantially the same research from multiple federal agencies or funding sources
   - Defined as: Research objectives and design that are "the same or closely related" regardless of funding source
   - Submitting similar proposals to multiple agencies is permitted, but accepting multiple contracts for the same work is fraud
   - Must disclose if similar proposals are submitted elsewhere

2. **Principal Investigator Employment Violations**: PI claiming primary employment with SBC while employed full-time elsewhere

3. **Misrepresentations**: Regarding SBC size, facilities, employee counts, percentage of work performed by SBC, or references

4. **Fund Misuse**: Using SBIR funds for personal expenses

5. **Fabrication/Falsification**: In proposals or reporting results

6. **Undisclosed Self-Dealing**: Subcontracting to entities in which PI or family has financial interest

7. **False Certifications**: Certifying compliance with material facts when in violation

### Required Certifications at Proposal Submission
- SBC meets size eligibility (≤500 employees)
- >50% U.S. citizen/permanent resident ownership
- Required percentage of work will be performed by SBC (2/3 Phase I, 1/2 Phase II)
- PI is primarily employed by SBC
- SBC facilities located in U.S.
- No other federal contracts/grants for essentially equivalent work
- Disclosure of family/academic relationships with owners, employees, subcontractors

### Certifications During Award Lifecycle (Phase I & II)
- At time of award
- Before final payment (Phase I)
- Before receiving >50% of total award and before final payment (Phase II)
- Certifications address: PI primary employment, no essentially equivalent work, work completed in U.S., required percentage performed by SBC

## Consequences of Fraud

### Criminal Prosecution
- **False Statements** (18 U.S.C. § 1001): Up to 5 years imprisonment, forfeiture, $250K fine
- **Theft of Federal Property** (18 U.S.C. § 641): Up to 10 years imprisonment, forfeiture, $250K fine
- **Wire Fraud** (18 U.S.C. § 1343): Up to 20 years imprisonment, forfeiture, $250K fine
- Criminal forfeiture = full contract/grant amount; personal assets can be seized

### Civil Liability
- **False Claims Act** (31 U.S.C. §§ 3729-3733): Up to treble damages (3x actual) plus civil penalty up to $21,916 per false claim
- Includes payments where government relied on false proposal information, certifications, or reports
- Knowledge includes "deliberate ignorance" or "reckless disregard of truth"
- Whistleblowers can recover up to 30% of settlement amount

### Administrative Remedies
- Contract/grant termination
- Suspension/debarment of SBC, owner, and/or employees (typically 3 years, can be longer)
- Results in prohibition from federal contracts/grants and work as subcontractor/subgrantee

## Case Examples Provided

1. **Essentially Equivalent Work Case**: SBC owner applied for NASA funding after receiving Air Force funding for same work; subcontracted major portions in violation of terms
   - Outcome: Pled guilty to mail fraud and tax evasion; 12 months home confinement, 5 years probation; $1.4M restitution; 5-year ban from federal funding

2. **PI Employment Case**: Subject employed full-time at university falsely certified full-time employment with SBC
   - Outcome: Pled guilty to wire fraud; 3 years probation; $133,333 restitution

3. **False Certifications Case**: University director's wife owned SBC; falsely represented SBC facilities and PI employment; falsified work identity and used university personnel without consent
   - Outcome: Both convicted of conspiracy and wire fraud; 6 months prison + 3 years supervised release for subject; $390,252 forfeiture and $100,000 fine; similar penalties for wife

## Best Practices & Recommendations

### Record-Keeping Requirements
- Timesheets for all involved employees
- Financial receipts, invoices, and statements for project-related expenses
- Laboratory notebooks
- Agreements for use of research facilities (if applicable)
- Personnel logs for assistance from institutions/students

### Government Oversight
- Government retains right to examine contract/grant status at any time
- Status checks include site visits and requests for records
- Good documentation is key to successful audits

## Additional Compliance Items

### ITAR (International Traffic in Arms Regulation)
- 22 C.F.R. §§ 120.1-130.17
- Restricts exports of military-related goods and technology
- SBIR awardees must ensure policies/processes to protect ITAR information
- Disclosure of defense-related technical data to unauthorized persons (e.g., foreign students) violates ITAR

### Whistleblower Protection
- Federal employees, applicants, and federal contractor/grantee employees making protected disclosures are protected from retaliation
- DOC OIG receives and investigates whistleblower reprisal allegations
- Contact: wpo@oig.doc.gov, 202-482-1099, or http://www.oig.doc.gov/

## Certification Requirement

Completion of this training requires signature and submission of a Certificate of Training Completion with the proposal, certifying:
- Full review and understanding of training content
- Authority to certify on behalf of the proposer/awardee
- Understanding that false/misleading information may result in criminal, civil, or administrative sanctions

- Training was created by DOC OIG and emphasizes fraud prevention and detection
- Multiple real prosecution examples demonstrate government enforcement activity
- Heavy emphasis on documentation and transparency as fraud prevention measures
- Training addresses both federal and state enforcement capabilities# DOC SBIR Mandatory Training Slides and Certification Form

## Document Metadata
- **Type:** Broad Agency Announcement (BAA) / Program Solicitation
- **Client/Agency:** U.S. Department of Defense (DoD)
- **Program/Solicitation:** Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Program 25.1 Annual Program BAA
- **Date:** December 2024 (Pre-release: December 4, 2024; Topics Open: January 8, 2025; Deadline: February 5, 2025)

## Executive Summary
This is the official DoD SBIR 25.1 Program Broad Agency Announcement (BAA), establishing the framework for small business innovation research proposals across three phases. It outlines eligibility requirements, proposal preparation instructions, evaluation criteria, and administrative procedures for companies seeking federal R&D funding. The program aims to stimulate technological innovation by small businesses, strengthen their role in meeting DoD R&D needs, and promote commercialization of defense-related research.

## Document Purpose & Scope
This document serves as the governing solicitation framework for the DoD SBIR 25.1 BAA. It is **not** a Black Swift Technologies proposal, report, or technical document. Instead, it is the government solicitation that establishes the rules and processes under which companies like BST would submit proposals to DoD SBIR opportunities.

### Key Program Dates
- **December 4, 2024:** Topics Pre-release
- **January 8, 2025:** Topics Open; DoD begins accepting proposals in DSIP
- **January 22, 2025:** DSIP Topic Q&A closes to new questions (12:00 p.m. ET)
- **February 5, 2025:** Topics Close; Proposal deadline (12:00 p.m. ET)

## Program Structure

### Three-Phase Program
1. **Phase I (6-12 months):** Determines scientific, technical, and commercial merit and feasibility; generally awards funds to prove concept viability
2. **Phase II (24 months):** Continues Phase I R&D development based on Phase I results; focuses on technical advancement
3. **Phase III:** Commercialization phase funded by non-SBIR sources (private sector or other federal agencies); focuses on bringing SBIR-funded technology to market

### Direct to Phase II Program
- Allows qualified SBCs to advance directly to Phase II without Phase I award
- Requires documentation demonstrating Phase I-level feasibility
- Cannot be based on prior federally funded SBIR/STTR work
- Must demonstrate ownership or licensure of underlying IP

## OUSD(R&E) Critical Technology Areas
Topics align with the following priority technology areas:
- FutureG
- Trusted AI and Autonomy
- Biotechnology
- Advanced Computing and Software
- Integrated Sensing and Cyber
- Directed Energy (DE)
- Hypersonics
- Microelectronics
- Integrated Network Systems-of-Systems
- Quantum Science
- Space Technology
- Renewable Energy Generation and Storage
- Advanced Materials
- Human-Machine Interfaces

**Supporting Technology Areas:**
- Advanced Infrastructure & Advanced Manufacturing
- Combat Casualty Care
- Emerging Threat Reduction
- Military Infectious Diseases
- Military Operational Medicine
- Mission Readiness & Disaster Preparedness
- Nuclear
- Sustainment & Logistics

## Eligibility Requirements

### Small Business Concern (SBC) Requirements
- Must meet Small Business Administration (SBA) definitions per 13 C.F.R §§ 701-705 at time of award
- Must be U.S.-owned and controlled per 13 CFR § 121.702
- SBC must be registered in SAM (System for Award Management) with valid UEI
- SBC must be registered in SBA Company Registry

### Work Performance Requirements
- **Phase I:** SBC must conduct minimum 2/3 of research and analytical work (measured by direct and indirect costs)
- **Phase II:** SBC must perform minimum 50% of research and analytical work
- **Principal Investigator (PI):** Must have primary employment with proposing SBC (>50% time) at time of award and during performance
- **Location:** All R&D work must be performed in the United States

### Joint Ventures
- Permitted if entity qualifies as small business per SBA size and ownership requirements
- Must disclose relationships with foreign entities or foreign government-controlled companies
- Must submit representations for small business status per FAR provisions

### Ownership Restrictions
- Proposing SBCs majority-owned by multiple venture capital firms, hedge funds, or private equity firms are **ineligible** (unless Service/Component authorizes)
- No single venture capital, hedge fund, or private equity firm may own >50% unless that entity itself qualifies as a small business

## Performance Benchmark Requirements
- **Phase I to Phase II Transition Rate:** Addresses extent to which awardee progresses from Phase I to Phase II
- **Commercialization Benchmark:** Addresses extent to which awardee moves past Phase II toward commercialization
- **Penalty for Non-Performance:** Experienced firms failing benchmarks limited to maximum of 80 total Phase I and Direct to Phase II awards across DoD:
  - Army: 20 awards maximum
  - Navy: 20 awards maximum
  - Air Force: 20 awards maximum
  - All other DoD Components combined: 20 awards maximum

## Proposal Submission Requirements

### Required Registrations & Certifications
1. **SAM (System for Award Management):** Must register to obtain Unique Entity ID (UEI)
2. **SBA Company Registry:** Must register using UEI; provide Control ID and Proof of Registration at submission
3. **DSIP (Defense SBIR/STTR Innovation Portal):** All proposal preparation and submission through DSIP
4. **Login.gov Account:** Required for DSIP access; account sharing prohibited

### Required Certifications at Proposal Submission
- SBC size, ownership, and program requirement compliance
- Certification of work percentages per SBIR requirements
- Disclosure of foreign affiliations/relationships
- FOCI (Foreign Ownership, Control, or Influence) compliance
- Organizational Conflicts of Interest (OCI) disclosure per FAR 9.5
- SETA/A&AS conflicts disclosure if applicable
- FASCA (Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act) compliance

### Security & Due Diligence Review
- DoD conducts risk-based due diligence to assess national security risks
- Reviews cybersecurity practices, patent analysis, employee analysis, foreign ownership/ties
- May request documentation of contractual/financial obligations with foreign entities
- May disqualify proposals posing unacceptable national security risk regardless of technical merit

## Proposal Volumes & Content

### Volume 1: Proposal Cover Sheet
- Prepared in DSIP
- Brief technical abstract (max 3,000 characters)
- Anticipated benefits and commercial applications (max 3,000 characters)
- Certification of SBC eligibility and work percentage compliance
- Topic number and proposal number (auto-assigned)

### Volume 2: Technical Volume (Phase I)
**Required sections in order:**
1. Identification and Significance of Problem/Opportunity
2. Phase I Technical Objectives
3. Phase I Statement of Work
4. Related Work
5. Relationship with Future Research or R&D
6. Commercialization Strategy
7. Key Personnel
8. Foreign Citizens
9. Facilities/Equipment
10. Subcontractors/Consultants
11. Prior, Current, or Pending Support
12. Identification and Assertion of Restrictions on Government Use, Release, or Disclosure

**Format Requirements:**
- Single PDF file (graphics embedded)
- No password protection, encryption, or active media
- Type size minimum 10-point
- Standard 8.5" x 11" paper with 1-inch margins
- Consecutive page numbering
- Header on each page with SBC name, topic number, and DSIP proposal number
- Page limit set by Service/Component (SBC responsible for verifying compliance)

### Volume 3: Cost Volume
- Completed using DSIP cost form
- List all key personnel with hours dedicated to project
- Detail special tooling, test equipment, materials
- Justify travel costs and relation to project
- Detail all subcontractor and consultant costs at prime contractor level
- Equipment title vests with DoD unless cost-effectiveness favors contractor transfer

### Volume 4: Company Commercialization Report (CCR)
- Required for SBCs with prior SBIR/STTR awards
- Firm admin must download CCR PDF from SBIR.gov
- Upload to DSIP "Firm Forms" (applies to all firm's proposals)
- **Warning:** Updating CCR in DSIP reopens all active proposals under open BAAs/CSOs for recertification
- Not required for first-time SBIR applicants

### Volume 5: Supporting Documents
- Joint venture representations (if applicable)
- OCI disclosure and mitigation plans
- Additional cost substantiation
- Export control compliance (DD Form 2345 for ITAR/EAR topics)
- Foreign affiliation/relationship disclosures

### Volume 6: Fraud, Waste and Abuse Training
- Certification of completion

### Volume 7: Disclosures of Foreign Affiliations or Relationships to Foreign Countries
- Identify foreign nationals, entities, government entities with >5% equity stake
- Identify ultimate parent owners
- Identify other entities/individuals with >5% equity stake
- Used for national security risk assessment

## Special Requirements & Considerations

### Export Control
- ITAR/EAR-marked topics require certified DD Form 2345 or evidence of application submission
- DD Form 2345 approval required if ITAR/EAR proposal receives award

### Classified Proposals
- **Not accepted** under DoD SBIR Program
- If Phase II requires classified work, proposing SBC must possess facility clearance
- Facility/personnel clearance info: DCSA website (dcsa.mil)

### Human Subjects Research (RIHS/HSR)
- Must comply with federal/state law and agency policy
- Require HHS federal-wide assurance (FWA) or equivalent
- Personnel must complete appropriate training
- IRB approval required (exemptions possible per 32 CFR 219.101)
- Approval timeline: 1-3 months IRB + 3-6 months DoD review
- **No funding for human subjects research until ALL approvals granted**

### Animal Subjects Research
- Comply with federal/agency rules on animal care, handling, use
- IACUC approval required
- Secondary/HQ approval from DoD veterinarian required
- No animal research funding until all approvals granted

### Recombinant DNA Research
- Institutional biosafety committee approval required

### Organizational Conflicts of Interest (OCI)
- FAR 9.5 compliance required
- Full disclosure of potential OCIs for proposing SBC and team members
- OCI mitigation plan required addressing FAR 9.505-1 through 9.505-4
- Disclosure required if providing SETA, A&AS, or similar support to DoD offices (current or within 1 year)
- Government evaluates and may grant waiver if in government interest
- Failed disclosure or waiver may result in proposal rejection

## Intellectual Property & Rights

### Patents
- SBIR awardees receive patent rights per standard SBIR provisions
- Details covered in resulting contract

### Technical Data Rights
- Government retains rights to use technical data as specified in contract

### Copyrights
- SBIR awardees may retain copyright in works developed under SBIR funding
- Government retains unlimited rights to data produced under SBIR

### Invention Reporting
- All inventions must be reported per SBIR/STTR requirements

## Award Information & Contract Terms

### Award Limitations
- DoD not obligated to make awards under Phase I, II, or III
- All awards subject to risk-based due diligence security review and funds availability
- DoD not responsible for costs incurred before award issuance
- Proposals must conform to BAA terms
- No obligation to fund any proposal or specific number per topic

### Phase II Enhancement Policy
- Some DoD Services/Components offer Phase II Enhancement
- Additional Phase II funding if awardee matches with non-SBIR DoD or private sector funds
- Details in Service/Component instructions

### Commercialization Readiness Program (CRP)
- Army, Navy, and Air Force each have CRP
- OSD Transitions SBIR Technology (OTST) Pilot Program available
- Info: osd.ncr.ousd-r-e.mbx.sbir-sttr# DoD 25.2 SBIR BAA Preface

## Executive Summary
This is the preface document for the DoD FY2025.2 Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Program Broad Agency Announcement. It establishes the framework, eligibility requirements, certifications, and proposal preparation instructions for small business concerns (SBCs) seeking Phase I, Direct to Phase II, or Phase III SBIR funding from the Department of Defense. The BAA runs from April 23, 2025 (topics open) through May 21, 2025 (proposal deadline).

## Important Dates
- **April 2, 2025:** Topics Pre-release
- **April 23, 2025:** Topics Open; DoD begins accepting proposals in DSIP
- **May 7, 2025:** DSIP Topic Q&A closes to new questions at 12:00 p.m. ET
- **May 21, 2025:** Topics Close; Deadline for receipt of proposals is 12:00 p.m. ET

## Program Overview

### Objectives
The SBIR Program aims to:
- Stimulate technological innovation
- Strengthen small business role in meeting DoD R&D needs
- Foster and encourage minority and disadvantaged persons' participation in technological innovation
- Increase commercial application of DoD-supported research results

### Three-Phase Structure
- **Phase I:** 6-12 months; Determines scientific, technical, and commercial merit/feasibility; typically funded amount not specified in this document
- **Phase II:** ~24 months; Continues and further develops Phase I R&D effort; generally follows successful Phase I completion
- **Phase III:** Non-SBIR funded work deriving from or extending prior SBIR funding; focused on commercialization with private sector or other non-SBIR federal funding

### Direct to Phase II Program
Available under 15 U.S.C. §638(cc) as amended; allows SBCs to submit Phase II proposals without prior Phase I award if they provide feasibility documentation demonstrating Phase I-level technical merit. Feasibility work cannot be based on prior federally funded SBIR/STTR work.

### Open Topics Program
Established under 15 U.S.C. §638(ww); uses generalized mission requirements or technology areas to adapt commercial solutions rather than specifying exact technical objectives. Single submission per SBC allowed per open topic.

## OUSD(R&E) Critical Technology Areas
The BAA aligns with Office of the Under Secretary of Defense, Research & Engineering (OUSD(R&E)) critical technology areas:
- FutureG
- Trusted AI and Autonomy
- Biotechnology
- Advanced Computing and Software
- Integrated Sensing and Cyber
- Directed Energy (DE)
- Hypersonics
- Microelectronics
- Integrated Network Systems-of-Systems
- Quantum Science
- Space Technology
- Renewable Energy Generation and Storage
- Advanced Materials
- Human-Machine Interfaces

Additional supporting areas:
- Advanced Infrastructure & Advanced Manufacturing
- Combat Casualty Care
- Emerging Threat Reduction
- Military Infectious Diseases
- Military Operational Medicine
- Mission Readiness & Disaster Preparedness
- Nuclear
- Sustainment & Logistics

## Eligibility Requirements

### Small Business Concern (SBC) Qualification
- Must meet SBC definition per 13 C.F.R §§ 701-705 at time of award
- Must meet small business ownership and control requirements (13 CFR § 121.702)
- Must be U.S.-owned and controlled

### Work Performance Requirements
- **Phase I:** SBC must conduct minimum 2/3 of research and analytical work (measured by direct and indirect costs)
- **Phase II:** SBC must perform minimum 50% of research and analytical work
- Deviations may be permitted with Funding Agreement Officer's written approval after SBIR/STTR program manager consultation

### Principal Investigator (PI) Requirements
- PI's primary employment must be with proposing SBC at time of award and during performance
- Primary employment defined as >50% of time with SBC (based on 40-hour work week)
- Precludes full-time employment elsewhere
- Changes/deviations subject to Funding Agreement Officer approval

### Performance Location
- All R&D work must be performed in the United States by SBC and subcontractors

### Joint Ventures and Partnerships
- Permitted if entity qualifies as SBC per ownership and size requirements
- Must disclose relationships with foreign entities or foreign government-controlled companies

### Venture Capital/Private Equity Restrictions
- SBCs with multiple venture capital operating companies (VCOCs), hedge funds, or private equity firms as majority owners are generally ineligible unless Service/Component authorizes participation
- Single VCOC/hedge fund/private equity firm cannot own >50% unless that firm is itself a small business >50% directly owned and controlled by U.S. citizens or permanent resident aliens
- Foreign ownership thresholds: Must disclose foreign nationals, foreign entities, or foreign government ownership >5% (direct or indirect)

## Performance Benchmark Requirements

For SBCs with multiple prior SBIR/STTR awards:
- **Phase I to Phase II Transition Rate:** Extent of progression from Phase I to Phase II
- **Commercialization Benchmark:** Progress toward commercialization beyond Phase II work

Increased minimum performance standards apply per SBIR and STTR Extension Act of 2022 (Pub. L. 117-183).

**Consequences for firms failing either benchmark:**
Maximum 80 total Phase I and Direct to Phase II awards across DoD, allocated as:
- Army: 20 awards maximum
- Navy: 20 awards maximum
- Air Force: 20 awards maximum
- All other DoD Components combined: 20 awards maximum

## Certifications and Registrations Required

### System for Award Management (SAM)
- SBC must register in SAM to receive Unique Entity ID (UEI) and Commercial and Government Entry (CAGE) code
- Required for SBA Company Registry registration

### SBA Company Registry
- SBC must be registered; must provide SBC Control ID and Proof of Registration/Certification during proposal submission

### Defense SBIR/STTR Innovation Portal (DSIP)
- All individuals from proposing SBC must register in DSIP
- Uses Login.gov authentication
- Designated DSIP Firm Admin responsible for Firm PIN creation, user access control, and firm-level forms
- Account sharing/password sharing prohibited per Login.gov Terms of Use and DoD policy
- **Accessibility Note:** DSIP only accessible from within the United States (50 states, territories, possessions, Puerto Rico, Marshall Islands, Federated States of Micronesia, Palau, District of Columbia)

### Required Certifications
Per SBIR and STTR Extension Act of 2022, SBCs must certify at:
- Time of Phase I and Phase II award
- Prior to final payment on Phase I award
- Prior to receiving 50% of Phase II total award amount
- Prior to final payment on Phase II award

## Due Diligence Program - National Security Risk Assessment

Per 15 U.S.C. §638(vv), DoD must assess and mitigate national security risks from SBCs seeking federal funding.

### Assessment Areas
- Cybersecurity practices
- Patent analysis
- Employee analysis and foreign ownership
- SBC's financial ties and obligations (surety, equity, debt)
- Employee ties to foreign countries, persons, or entities
- Open-source analysis to confirm accuracy of disclosures

### Information Required
- "Disclosures of Foreign Affiliations or Relationships to Foreign Countries" (Volume 7 of proposal)
- DoD may request copies of contractual/financial obligations or agreements with foreign state-owned or foreign entities (5-year lookback period)

### Risk Determination
- DoD may not make awards posing unacceptable national security risk
- If risk deemed unmitigable, proposal rejected regardless of technical merit review
- Reference: "Defense Small Business Innovation Research and Small Business Technology Transfer Due Diligence Program" memo (May 13, 2024) with Common Risk Matrix

### FOCI Training
DoD offers online course on Understanding Foreign Ownership, Control, or Influence (FOCI) via Project Spectrum at projectspectrum.io

## Organizational Conflicts of Interest (OCI)

### FAR 9.5 Requirements
- SBCs must identify and disclose all facts relevant to potential OCIs
- Must include OCI mitigation plan describing actions taken/intended to:
  - Prevent conflicting roles biasing judgment
  - Prevent unfair competitive advantage
- Must address OCIs in context of FAR 9.505-1 through 9.505-4 limitations

### DoD Supplemental OCI Policy
- Contractors cannot concurrently provide SETA (Scientific Engineering Technical Assistance), A&AS (Advisory and Assistance Services), or similar support while being technical performer
- Must affirm whether SBC or proposed team members provide such support under:
  - Current awards/sub-awards
  - Past awards/sub-awards ending within one calendar year prior to submission
- If applicable, must disclose:
  - DoD Service/Component office receiving support
  - Prime contract number
  - Team member providing support
  - OCI mitigation plan per FAR 9.5

### Government Evaluation
- Per FAR 9.503, 9.504, 9.506, government evaluates OCI mitigation plans for proposals determined selectable and with funding available
- May require additional information to support OCI mitigation plan evaluation
- May reject proposals with failed full disclosure, missing government waiver, or failure to reasonably provide requested information

## Research Protections and Compliance

### Human Subjects Research (RIHS/HSR)
- Must comply with federal/state laws and agency policy for human subject protection
- Requires documentation of federal assurance of compliance (e.g., HHS Office for Human Research Protections federal-wide assurance)
- All subcontractors must also have valid assurance
- Personnel must provide documentation of completed human subjects protection training
- May be exempt if meeting criteria in 32 CFR 219.101
- Institutional Review Board (IRB) approval required; typical timeline 1-3 months
- DoD review of approved protocol: 3-6 months
- **No funding for human subject research until ALL approvals granted**
- Recommended: Separate human subject research tasks in technical and cost proposals

### Animal Subjects Research
- Must comply with federal and agency rules on animal acquisition, transport, care, handling, use
- Requires Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) approval
- Requires secondary/headquarters-level approval from DoD veterinarian
- **No animal research using DoD funding until all approvals granted**
- Recommended: Separate animal use tasks in technical and cost proposals

### Recombinant DNA Research
- Must comply with federal/state law, regulation, and agency guidance
- Institutional biosafety committee approval required

## Proposal Preparation - Structural Requirements

### DSIP Proposal Volume Structure
- **Volume 1:** Proposal Cover Sheet
- **Volume 2:** Technical Volume
- **Volume 3:** Cost Volume
- **Volume 4:** Company Commercialization Report
- **Volume 5:** Supporting Documents
- **Volume 6:** Fraud, Waste and Abuse Training
- **Volume 7:** Disclosures of Foreign Affiliations or Relationships to Foreign Countries

### Cover Sheet (Volume 1)
- Prepared in DSIP
- Brief technical abstract (max 3,000 characters)
- Anticipated benefits and potential commercial applications (max 3,000 characters)
- No proprietary or classified information
- May be publicly released if selected for award
- DSIP assigns proposal number upon save; may modify until BAA closes
- Includes Percentage of Work (POW) certification derived from cost volume entries
- If POW falls below eligibility requirements, Funding Agreement Officer must upload explanatory letter or approval

### Technical Volume (Volume 2)
**Format Requirements:**
- Single PDF file with graphics
- Must include virus check before upload
- No password protection, encryption, or locked files
- No active graphics (videos, moving pictures, etc.)
- File size and page limits per Service/Component-specific instructions

**Layout:**
-# DoD 25.4 SBIR BAA Preface_Release 4
