## Executive Summary
This is a NASA SBIR Phase I proposal preparation instruction document outlining formatting requirements, submission guidelines, and evaluation criteria for small business applicants. It specifies proposal structure, page limits, required forms, technical content organization, and compliance requirements for both SBIR and STTR (Technology Transfer) proposals.

## Technical Approach
Not applicable—this is an instruction document, not a proposal or technical document. It describes the framework within which proposals should be submitted.

## Products & Capabilities Described
None. No BST products or capabilities are referenced in this document.

## Use Cases & Applications
Not applicable.

## Key Results
Not applicable.

## Notable Details

### Proposal Structure Requirements
- **Total Page Limit:** 23 pages maximum (8.5" x 11", 1-inch margins)
  - Forms A, B, C: 1 page each (pages 1-3)
  - Technical content: 20 pages max for SBIR; 19 pages for STTR
  - Briefing chart: not counted toward limit
  - Firm-level forms (certifications, audit, prior awards, metrics survey): not counted toward limit
- **Type size:** Minimum 10-point font
- **Header/footer:** Must include firm name, proposal number, project title, and page numbers

### Required Components (in order)
1. Cover Sheet (Form A)
2. Proposal Summary (Form B) – public information, no proprietary data
3. Budget Summary (Form C) – maximum $125,000 Phase I funding
4. Technical Content (11 parts):
   - Part 1: Table of Contents
   - Part 2: Identification and Significance of Innovation
   - Part 3: Technical Objectives
   - Part 4: Work Plan (detailed description of R&D plan, schedules, milestones)
   - Part 5: Related R&D
   - Part 6: Key Personnel and Bibliography
   - Part 7: Relationship with Future R&D
   - Part 8: Facilities/Equipment
   - Part 9: Subcontracts and Consultants
   - Part 10: Potential Post Applications (Commercialization)
   - Part 11: Essentially Equivalent and Duplicate Proposals and Awards
5. Research Agreement (STTR only)
6. Briefing Chart (one page, non-proprietary)
7. Firm-level forms: Certifications, Audit Information, Prior Awards Addendum, Commercial Metrics Survey

### Key Submission Rules
- Maximum 10 proposals per firm per program (SBIR or STTR)
- NASA selection limit: no more than 5 SBIR and 2 STTR proposals from any single offeror
- Each proposal must be unique and limited to one subtopic
- Substantially equivalent proposals to multiple subtopics will result in rejection
- Electronic submission via Electronic Handbook (EHB) required
- Proposals with classified information are not accepted
- Website references, product samples, videotapes not considered during review

### Principal Investigator (PI) Requirements
- PI must make substantial commitment to project
- PI functions: planning/directing project, technical leadership, personal contributions, primary NASA contact
- PI must spend acceptable amount of time (to be determined by Contracting Officer)
- NASA has sole right to accept or reject PI based on qualifications, experience, demonstrated ability
- PI cannot work more than half-time for academic/nonprofit organization (with STTR exception allowing PI employed by either SBC or RI)

### Subcontracting Restrictions
**SBIR Phase I:** Subcontracts/consultants cannot exceed 33% of research/analytical work (calculated as subcontractor cost + G&A / total contract price less profit)

**STTR Phase I:** 
- Minimum 40% of work by SBC
- Minimum 30% of work by RI
- Other subcontracting (excluding RI work) cannot exceed 30% of research/analytical work

### Federal Facilities Policy
- NASA generally does not provide facilities or equipment for SBIR/STTR work
- Proposals requiring use of Federal facilities (non-laboratory) or personnel require SBA waiver and must include:
  - Letter from SBC official explaining necessity
  - Data verifying absence of non-Federal alternatives
  - Statement from Government official verifying facility availability
- Federal laboratory use requires justification letter from SBC and availability verification
- No SBIR/STTR funds may pay for Federal facility use or personnel; charges require alternative funding
- Selected contractors must provide executed facility use agreement within 10 business days of notification

### Deliverables
- Phase I reports must present: work accomplished, scientific/technical/commercial merit and feasibility, relevance to NASA needs, strategy for development and transition
- Deliverables may include demonstration, prototype, test unit, or product for NASA testing
- Submission via EHB in PDF or MS Word format

### Post-Award Requirements (if selected)
- Within 10 business days of selection notification:
  - Provide signed financial institution statement
  - Provide three references with contact information
  - Provide contractor responsibility information
  - STTR: Submit signed Allocation of Rights Agreement (ARA)

## Important Notes
- The Government is not responsible for monies expended before contract award
- Proposals not following formatting requirements subject to rejection during administrative screening
- All required 11 technical content parts must be included or proposal rejected as non-responsive
- No proprietary data on Forms B or briefing chart
- Classified information will result in rejection# Aircraft Selection and Requirements Analysis Report

## Document Metadata
- **Type:** Requirements analysis and aircraft selection report
- **Client/Agency:** SPEC Inc (Stratton Park Engineering)
- **Program/Solicitation:** Not specified
- **Date:** September 7, 2016
- **BST Products/Systems Referenced:** SwiftPilot autopilot, SwiftTab user interface
- **Key Personnel:** Nick Krause (SPEC Inc - CAD/mechanical validation)

## Executive Summary
This report presents Black Swift Technologies' analysis of airframe and systems selection for a payload-carrying UAS mission planned for Arctic operations in Ny Alesund, Svalbard. BST evaluated four candidate airframes and recommended the Penguin B from UAV Factory, along with the SwiftPilot autopilot and supporting avionics and communications systems, to meet mission requirements for high-altitude (15 kft), long-duration (2 hour) operations with up to 9 kg payload in icing-prone conditions.

## Technical Approach

### Airframe Selection Process
BST evaluated four airframes against mission requirements:
1. **Penguin B (UAV Factory)** - Selected
2. TBM UAV-4 (Troy Built Models) - Rejected (lower quality/reliability)
3. Cryowing - Rejected (non-COTS, sourcing/parts challenges; under consideration as for-hire service through Andoya Space Center)
4. Arcturus Jump 15 - Rejected (tractor configuration blocks sensor airflow)

**Tiger Shark UAS** was also reviewed but deemed beyond BST's operational capability; BST recommended client contact Navmar Applied Science Corporation if preferred.

### Penguin B Selection Rationale
- **Maximum payload capacity:** 11.5 kg total (fuel + payload)
- **Fuel capacity:** 3000 cc standard tank = 2.3 kg
- **Usable payload:** 9.2 kg with full fuel tank (0.2 kg margin above 9 kg requirement)
- **Fuel type:** 98 octane (readily available in Europe)
- **Mechanical validation:** Nick Krause (SPEC Inc) performed Solidworks CAD analysis confirming payload volume, center-of-gravity within spec, and sensor inlet port integration feasibility

### Propulsion System
**Engine Requirements Met:**
- No maintenance required during 10-20 hour initial testing phase (service interval considerably >20 hours per UAV Factory)
- Arctic-rated operation at temperatures below -20°C (extensively tested in Arctic regions)
- 15 kft density altitude capability (achievable with Electronic Fuel Injection [EFI] upgrade; 10 kft without)

**Engine Details:**
- Fuel consumption: 450 g/hour nominal at MTOW; range 200-700 g/hour depending on density altitude
- EFI system and Electronic Control Unit (ECU) supplied by Currawong Engineering (CE367B model)
- Interfacing: RS232 connection for throttle command from autopilot; optional engine diagnostics downlink possible

### Performance Specifications
- **Maximum climb rate (at MTOW):** 1.2 m/s (236 fpm)
- **Cruise speed:** 43 kts
- **Endurance capability:** Worst case (700 g/hr at 15 kft) requires 1.4 kg fuel for 2-hour mission; full 3000cc tank enables 3.3 hours worst-case or 5.1 hours nominal flight time
- **Wind capability:** 15 kts sustained (within design envelope; not limiting)
- **Note:** SPEC Inc required to verify climb/descent rates meet sensor mission requirements (rates not provided in this report)

## Products & Capabilities Described

### SwiftPilot Autopilot
**Specifications & Features:**
- Fixed-wing autopilot control with up to 128 actuator interfaces (only 7 needed for Penguin B)
- Capable of operating gas-powered vehicles
- Can execute ascent/descent while maintaining orbit maneuvers
- Telemetry output: 20 Hz onboard, at least 1 Hz available externally
- Payload data downlinking capability (tagged with autopilot telemetry)
- Command uplink capability from Ground Control Station (GCS)
- Waypoint-based flight plan execution with graphical interface (SwiftTab)

**Comparison to Alternative (Piccolo Autopilot):**
- SwiftPilot preferred due to lower training/operational cost
- Both systems meet core requirements
- Piccolo requires significant NRE for implementation; uses Microhard Nano n920 radio (60+ mile range, -108 dBm sensitivity)
- Piccolo integrates directly with Currawong CE367B ECU

### SwiftTab (Ground Control Station Interface)
- Allows graphic boundary definition for flight planning (e.g., balloon operation avoidance)
- Provides waypoint-based mission planning
- Receives autopilot telemetry and payload data

### Communications System: Xeta9m-T Radio (XetaWave)
**Specifications:**
- Manufacturer: XetaWave (Boulder, Colorado)
- Frequency: 900 MHz (recommended for Ny Alesund operations; 2.4 GHz restricted; 900 MHz typical for Europe requires special approval, obtainable through Andoya Space Center)
- Power output: 1 W standard; 3 W boost option available (harder to license)
- Receiver sensitivity: -110 dBm at 57 kbps (MSK modulation)
- Published range: 70+ miles (verified for 20 miles Svalbard link analysis)
- Software-defined radio with modulation flexibility
- Local manufacturer support from XetaWave

**Radio Analysis for Svalbard (20 nm requirement):**
- Link budget analysis using Radio Mobile Online tool
- 6.12 dB fade margin (note: low margin requiring real-world testing validation)
- Antenna: 2.1 dBi omnidirectional
- Critical requirement: Maintain line-of-sight with terrain in Svalbard

**Sensitivity vs. Throughput Trade (Xeta9m-T):**
| Sensitivity (dBm) | Modulation | Throughput (kbps) |
|---|---|---|
| -110 | MSK | 57 |
| -107 | MSK | 114 |
| -106 | MSK | 153 |
| -103 | MSK | 229 |
| -99 | BPSK | 530 |
| -98 | 2FSK | 663 |
| -97 | QPSK | 1061 |
| -95 | QPSK | 1768 |
| -90 | 8PSK | 2651 |
| -86 | 16QAM | 3535 |
| -81 | 32QAM | 4419 |

**Payload Radio Challenges:**
- SPEC Inc requested SSH (3 sessions) and FTP client capability
- Bandwidth requirements not provided in report
- BST recommends payload data downlink via SwiftPilot/Piccolo payload channel over 900 MHz rather than separate SSH/FTP radio due to:
  - Robustness and data tagging with autopilot telemetry
  - Reduced RF interference and system complexity
- Alternative (if dedicated payload radio required): 433 MHz or 5.8 GHz, but both inadequate (insufficient bandwidth and range respectively)

### Power System for Payload
**Total System Mass:** 0.7 kg

**Alternator: S676-300F-01 (Sullivan Unmanned Vehicle)**
- Dimensions: 76 mm diameter × 21 mm thickness
- Power output: 120 W @ 2500 RPM to 475 W @ 7500 RPM
- Mass: 350 g

**Voltage Regulator: SREGS-350U-01 (Sullivan Unmanned Vehicle)**
- Max output: 350 W
- Voltage: 20-30 VDC, 13A (factory set to 24 VDC)
- Backup battery capable: 24-32 VDC
- Dimensions: 139 mm × 48 mm × 48 mm
- Mass: 350 g
- Temperature range: -20°C to 55°C ambient

**Power Delivery:**
- Designed to meet SPEC Inc requirement of 200-300 W continuous payload power
- 300 W capacity selected for minimal weight penalty vs. lower-capacity systems
- Note: Penguin B manufacturer standard options only 80-100 W; external system required

## Use Cases & Applications

### Mission Profile (Ny Alesund, Svalbard)
- **Duration:** 2 hours flight time (takeoff to landing)
- **Altitude:** 0-15 kft density altitude capability
- **Payload:** Up to 9 kg (SPEC Inc sensor package)
- **Launch/Recovery:** "Soccer Field" adjacent to airport at Ny Alesund
- **Environmental conditions:** Arctic temperatures (-20°C and below), potential icing conditions
- **Operational constraint:** Avoid balloon operations (1.5 nm exclusion radius)

### Environmental/Science Operations
- High-latitude Arctic atmospheric sampling
- Operations in icing-prone conditions
- Extended endurance requirements for scientific measurement

## Key Results

### Icing Analysis and Recommendations
**Icing Types and Temperature Ranges:**
| Type | Temperature (°C) | Characteristics |
|---|---|---|
| Clear | 2 to -10 | Worst form; changes airfoil shape; stall risk |
| Mixed | -10 to -15 | Clear + rime combination |
| Rime | -15 to -20 | Forms when droplets freeze immediately; less airflow disturbance |

**Key Finding:** No reliable method currently exists for icing detection/mitigation on small UAS despite significant DoD/other investments.

**BST Recommended Icing Risk Mitigation Strategy:**
1. Use airport weather service and other sources to forecast and avoid/minimize icing areas
2. Heated pitot tube (provided by UAV Factory) to maintain airspeed measurement
3. Onboard Outside Air Temperature (OAT) sensor with ground monitoring (or ground-based visual observation) to avoid clouds below 5°C
4. ECU engine performance downlink with real-time monitoring for performance degradation
5. Escalating response protocol if icing encountered:
   - Primary: Fly reciprocal path out of icing environment
   - Secondary: Climb or descend to safer altitude
   - Tertiary: Return home immediately and land

**Critical Conclusion:** No guaranteed icing avoidance exists; field team must weigh aircraft risk vs. scientific data value with available information.

### Avoidance/Prevention Assessment
- Icing prevention systems (heated surfaces, anti-ice chemicals, special coatings) **not feasible** on Penguin B due to SWAP constraints
- Fault detection algorithms for ice buildup on aerodynamic surfaces possible but would constitute new R&D requiring validation before operational use
- Lessons learned from Navy small UAS operations incorporated into recommended CONOPS

### Flight Duration Validation
**Worst-case scenario analysis (700 g/hour at 15 kft density altitude):**
- 1.4 kg fuel required for 2-hour mission → 10.1 kg payload capacity (exceeds 9 kg requirement with margin)
- Full tank (2.3 kg fuel) → 3.3 hour worst-case flight time or 5.1 hour nominal flight time

### Radio Range Validation
- 20-mile requirement for Svalbard verified through Radio Mobile Online analysis
- 6.12 dB fade margin adequate but tight; **requires real-world testing validation**
- Terrain line-of-sight maintenance critical in operational area

- **Andoya Space Center:** BST discussing Cryowing for-hire operations; awaiting pricing/schedule for summer Svalbard integration/flights
- **XetaWave:** Local Boulder-based radio manufacturer with ongoing support relationship with BST

## Document Metadata
- **Type:** Phase I Final Report (SBIR)
- **Client/Agency:** NASA Langley Research Center (LaRC)
- **Program/Solicitation:** NASA SBIR 2022-I, Subtopic S16.04 "Unpiloted Aerial Platforms and Technologies for NASA Science Missions"
- **Contract Number:** 80NSSC22PA964
- **Date:** January 2023
- **BST Products/Systems Referenced:** S2, S2-VTOL, S3 (proposed), SwiftCore avionics, OAK/Luxonis vision platform
- **Key Personnel:** Jack Elston (PI), Maciej Stachura (Lead Engineer)

## Executive Summary
Black Swift Technologies completed Phase I of an SBIR contract to develop an "All Weather UAS" capability for long-term environmental observations in extreme conditions. The work focused on designing the S3 platform—an enhanced version of the proven S2 UAS—with new capabilities for operating safely in severe weather including high winds, heavy precipitation, icing, and turbulent conditions. Phase I achievements include aerodynamic redesigns for improved performance, a prototype heated/drained pitot-static system, weatherproofing plans, and a vision-based monitoring system design.

## Technical Approach

### Design Philosophy
BST's strategy was to leverage the proven S2 UAS platform and incrementally enhance it to create the S3 system capable of routine operations in extreme environments without concern for weather conditions. Key design objectives:

1. **Aerodynamic Redesign:** New wing and tail designs optimized for:
   - Sustained dash speed of 45 m/s (100 mph)
   - Climb rate of 10 m/s (2,000 ft/min)
   - Maintained cruise efficiency (~20 m/s optimal speed)
   - Improved L/D and reduced sink rate

2. **Severe Weather Systems:**
   - Dual redundant pitot-static system with heating for icing mitigation
   - IP55 waterproofing rating (dust/water protection)
   - Structural changes for turbulence tolerance

3. **Vision and Monitoring:**
   - Onboard machine vision for icing detection and terrain monitoring
   - Real-time 3D terrain mapping capability
   - Automated landing area detection and selection

### Technical Work Completed

**Aerodynamic Analysis (XFLR5 & AVL):**
- Redesigned wing planform with 1° washout for elliptical lift distribution
- Twin-boom inverted V-tail configuration to avoid propeller wash on fuselage
- Wing loading held constant with existing S2 (42.9 oz/ft²)
- Aspect ratio limited to 18:1 for structural and handling constraints
- New airfoil selection with 9.5% thickness at root, 8.5% at tip

**Performance Gains Identified:**
- Full redesign option: 22.8% improvement in sink rate, 23.3% in L/D vs. S2-3m (11.2% and 10.6% vs. S2-4m)
- Compromise "tip panel only" option: 97% of full redesign gains by replacing just wing tip panels
- Potential 10% additional gains from concealed linkages, construction improvements, and propulsion optimization

**S2-VTOL Prototype Development:**
- Extended wingspan by 32" to maintain wing loading with added VTOL mass (~2.8 kg increase)
- Extended tail boom by 10" with V-tail angle adjusted from 35° to 40° from horizontal
- Four rotor configuration with 1.5:1 thrust-to-weight ratio minimum
- Flight validation showed ~299W power draw at cruise (19 m/s IAS), supporting ~90-100 minute endurance with 5 lbs payload

## Products & Capabilities Described

### S2 UAS (Baseline System)
- **Description:** Proven small electric fixed-wing platform for scientific missions
- **Specifications:**
  - Mass: 9.3 kg
  - Endurance: ~90 minutes at 20 m/s cruise
  - Payload capacity: 5 lbs
  - Operating altitude: 0-14,000 ft
  - Temperature range proven: -20°C to +40°C
  - Typical power draw: 250W cruise
- **Use Cases in Phase I:** Baseline for aerodynamic analysis and flight validation testbed for new systems

### S3 UAS (Proposed)
- **Description:** Enhanced S2 with extreme weather and long-duration capabilities
- **Key Features:**
  - Redesigned wing and tail for high-speed dash and climb performance
  - Heated, dual-redundant pitot-static system for icing/precipitation
  - IP55 waterproofing for dust and water intrusion
  - Onboard vision system (5 cameras planned)
  - Solar panel integration for extended operations
  - Planned capability: weeks to months of mission duration
- **Planned Specifications:**
  - Dash speed: 45 m/s (100 mph)
  - Climb rate: 10 m/s (2,000 ft/min)
  - Cruise speed: ~20 m/s (optimized)

### Pitot-Static System (New Development)
- **Design:** Dual redundant heated pitot with selective switching
- **Components:**
  - Port 1: High-accuracy thin pitot tube for clear-air operations
  - Port 2: Larger-opening pitot with drain hole for rain/icing mitigation
  - 3D-printed metal heated tip (target: maintain >0°C down to -25°C ambient)
  - Temperature and humidity sensors
  - Automatic switching controller with microcontroller logic for failure detection
  - Heating element with thermal management
- **Validation Completed:**
  - Heating system tested in lab environment
  - Rain tunnel testing performed showing drain system functionality
  - Flight comparison tests planned with calibrated 5-hole probe on S2

### Vision System (Machine Vision Monitoring)
- **Core Hardware:** OAK/Luxonis platform (selected after evaluation)
- **Planned Camera Configuration:** 5 total cameras
  - 3 wing/tail monitoring cameras for icing detection (full field of view coverage)
  - 2 downward-looking stereo cameras for terrain mapping and landing
- **Capabilities:**
  - Real-time 3D terrain model generation
  - Automated landing area detection and classification (11 terrain classes)
  - Icing detection via visual monitoring plus atmospheric sensor fusion
  - GPS-denied navigation using SLAM algorithms
  - Forward-looking obstacle detection and tracking
- **Processing:** Jetson Nano single-board computer with Luxonis inference engine; evaluation of Coral AI tensor processing units

### SwiftCore Avionics System
- **Description:** Distributed, modular onboard monitoring architecture (separate from this SBIR but integrated into S3 plans)
- **Capabilities:**
  - Monitors all critical electromechanical systems as sensor network
  - Real-time failure detection and mitigation
  - Preventative maintenance prediction via machine learning
  - Redundant communications (satellite and wireless) with automatic switching
- **Current TRL:** 5 (component TRL ranges 2-8)

### Autonomous Landing System
- **Current Status:** Prototype demonstrated at TRL 5
- **Planned Phase II Implementation:**
  - Automated landing area identification from altitude
  - Real-time landing site selection
  - Obstacle detection and tracking in landing area
  - Specific landing point selection
  - Automatic abort capability
  - Leverages NASA Safe2Ditch research for obstacle detection

2. **Atmospheric Science:** Cloud sampling, severe storm research, hurricane research with extended duration capabilities
3. **Satellite Calibration:** Multi-day campaigns over diverse terrain (grassland, desert, alpine forests) via expanded operational envelope

## Executive Summary

Black Swift Technologies proposes to modify and integrate its high-TRL S0 UAS (air-deployable, disposable platform) for USAF hurricane sampling missions aboard C-130 aircraft operated by the 53rd Weather Reconnaissance Squadron. The S0 has been validated through extensive operational deployments from NOAA's P3 aircraft into multiple high-wind hurricanes (2023-2024 season). The effort will enhance the system to meet DOD cybersecurity and network integration requirements while optimizing deployment mechanisms and flight profiles for military operations.

## Technical Approach

**Core Problem Addressed:** Current hurricane data collection relies on disposable dropsondes that provide only discrete data points during descent, with limited spatial and temporal coverage. The lower boundary layer and eyewall—critical regions for determining storm intensity—are historically under-sampled.

**BST's Solution:**
- Deploy the S0 UAS as a disposable, autonomous platform capable of remaining in storm environments for extended periods
- Collect continuous 3D wind vectors, pressure, temperature, humidity, and sea surface temperature data
- Autonomously navigate through hurricanes following pre-programmed or adaptive flight paths
- Integrate into existing C-130 deployment procedures and USAF command systems
- Implement DOD-grade cybersecurity and secure communications protocols

**Key Technical Advantages Over Baseline:**
- **Continuous Data Collection:** Unlike dropsondes (brief descent-based data), S0 provides extended autonomous sampling with significantly more data points
- **Autonomous Flight:** Actively navigates storm regions vs. passive drift; enables precise lower boundary layer and eyewall sampling
- **Customizable Architecture:** Proprietary SwiftCore flight management system enables real-time data streaming, secure communication, and mission-specific adaptation
- **Extreme Condition Design:** Purpose-built for high wind speeds and turbulence characteristic of tropical cyclones

## Products & Capabilities Described

### S0 UAS
- **What it is:** Air-deployable, disposable autonomous UAS designed for boundary layer observations in extreme weather environments
- **Operational Heritage:** Successfully deployed from NOAA P3 aircraft into Hurricanes Tammy (2023), Ernesto, Francine, Helene, and Milton (2024)
- **Sensors/Measurement Capabilities:**
  - Flush-air sensing nose cone
  - High-rate 3D wind measurement
  - In-situ atmospheric probe (pressure, temperature, humidity)
  - Surface temperature measurement
  - Wave height measurement
  - Long-range communications
- **Proposed Military Application:** Deployment from USAF C-130 aircraft; autonomous hurricane sampling within lower boundary layer and eyewall
- **Key Specifications:**
  - Compact, low-cost design
  - Autonomous flight with targeted maneuvers
  - Real-time data streaming to aircraft
  - Extended operational duration within storms
  - Designed for C-130 air-deployment

### SwiftCore Flight Management System
- **What it is:** Proprietary flight management system enabling autonomous operations
- **Capabilities:** Real-time data streaming, secure communication protocols, mission-specific customization, integration with host aircraft systems
- **Military Application:** Secure data transmission meeting DOD cybersecurity requirements; integration with USAF C-130 command architecture

### S2 UAS
- **Referenced for:** Prior development demonstrating BST expertise in autonomous operations and low-altitude atmospheric data collection
- **Commercial Success:** $362,732 in sales
- **Relevance:** Lessons learned applicable to S0 hurricane mission

## Use Cases & Applications

**Primary Mission:** Hurricane reconnaissance and atmospheric data collection for the USAF 53rd Weather Reconnaissance Squadron

**Specific Use Cases:**
1. **Lower Boundary Layer Sampling:** Autonomous data collection in critical under-sampled storm regions
2. **Eyewall Observation:** Continuous measurements in storm's most intense region (critical for intensity forecasting)
3. **Model Initialization and Validation:** High-resolution data for improving hurricane intensity forecast accuracy
4. **Extended Duration Monitoring:** Track dynamic storm changes over longer time periods than dropsondes
5. **Risk Reduction for Manned Crews:** Replace dangerous manned aircraft penetrations in most hazardous storm regions with disposable autonomous platforms
6. **Operational Planning Support:** Real-time meteorological intelligence for DOD decision-making

**Dual-Use Applications Mentioned:**
- ISR (Intelligence, Surveillance, Reconnaissance) operations with adaptable camera solutions
- Cooperative control and swarming applications
- Ground cargo drop support (wind column measurement near drop sites)

## Key Results (Previous Deployments/Operational Evidence)

**Operational Validation:**
- Successful deployments from NOAA P3 aircraft into 5 hurricanes during 2023-2024 season (Tammy, Ernesto, Francine, Helene, Milton)
- Demonstrated survivability in extreme high-wind, turbulent environments
- Validated data quality for scientific hurricane research

**Commercial Traction:**
- Ongoing collaboration with NOAA AOML (Atlantic Oceanographic and Meteorological Laboratory) since 2018
- University of Colorado partnerships generating steady validation data
- Recognition from NOAA for filling critical data gaps in hurricane research

**Prior SBIR/Government Funding Success:**
- S2 UAS (NASA): $362,732 in commercial sales
- Soil moisture mapping services: $284,004 in sales
- Methane detection services: $46,088 in sales
- **Total SBIR-Funded Project Commercialization:** >$690,000 in revenue
- Previous DOD SBIR funding for ground-launched UAS wind sampling
- AFWERX funding for ML-based UAS maintenance scheduling (2022)
- AFWERX runway integrity validation project (ongoing through mid-2025)

## Technical Feasibility Plan (Phase I)

**Phase I Scope:** Determine technical feasibility of S0 for C-130 deployment with DOD integration

**Five Major Work Tasks:**

1. **System Integration Requirement Development**
   - Identify modifications needed for S0 UAS and flight control station
   - Determine autonomous flight software changes for hurricane sampling
   - Define integration requirements with C-130 command systems
   - Assess airborne deployment system modifications

2. **Cybersecurity Compliance Requirement Development**
   - Identify required secure communication and data transfer protocols
   - Conduct vulnerability analysis
   - Ensure compliance with DOD cybersecurity standards

3. **Flight Profile Requirement Development**
   - Develop process for custom flight profiles for autonomous hurricane boundary layer navigation
   - Test profiles for eyewall operations
   - Determine deployment mechanism modifications for C-130

4. **Stakeholder Identification and Requirements Modification**
   - Interview current stakeholder list to understand benefit optimization
   - Identify additional stakeholders through interview process
   - Compile customer list for Phase II follow-on
   - Secure MOU signer commitments for Phase II

5. **Final Reporting**
   - Submit final report with SF 298 and DD Form 882

**Phase I Deliverables:**
- Preliminary Report (post-integration and initial testing)
- Final Report with feasibility results, testing outcomes, Phase II recommendations, SF 298, and DD Form 882

**Phase I Timeline:**
- Kickoff meeting within 30 days of contract award
- Stakeholder travel planned to Keesler Air Force Base, Biloxi, MS (late April 2025)
- Estimated travel cost: $1,107 (airfare, car rental, meals/lodging)

## Phase II Transition Plan

**Integration with Existing Operations:**
- Leverage current 53rd Squadron C-130 dropsonde deployment procedures
- Seamless integration with existing deployment and command systems
- Extended continuous data collection capability over current methods

**Planned Phase II Activities:**
1. **System Integration and Testing:** Ground and flight tests to validate C-130 integration
2. **Cybersecurity Implementation:** Collaboration with DAF cybersecurity specialists for secure communications
3. **Operational Deployment and Training:** Development of training programs and operational procedures for DAF personnel
4. **Ongoing Support:** Technical support for evolving operational requirements; enhancement for additional weather reconnaissance missions

**Success Metrics for End-Users (53rd Squadron):**
- Improved data quality and coverage (continuous vs. discrete dropsonde data)
- Increased crew safety through reduced manned aircraft exposure to dangerous storm regions
- Integration with USAF and NOAA weather models for actionable forecasting
- Operational efficiency through autonomous operations and C-130 platform integration

### DoD vs. Civilian Variants
The proposal notes two variants:

- **Civilian Variant (NOAA):** Emphasis on maximizing scientific data collection and reducing costs; fewer cybersecurity requirements

### Competitive Positioning
- **vs. Dropsondes:** S0 provides continuous, high-resolution data with longer collection windows and extended spatial coverage
- **vs. Other UAS Platforms:** S0 balances cost-effectiveness with performance optimization for disposable extreme-weather use; more affordable and storm-optimized than longer-duration platforms
- **Market Differentiation:** Modularity, cost-effective production, scalability through advanced manufacturing; ability to serve both defense and commercial sectors

- **Cargo Drop Support:** Potential to measure wind columns near drop zones, eliminating need for ground operators
- **Terrain Sampling:** Lessons from prior runway integrity project applicable to other landing site assessments

## Document Metadata
- Type: Guidance document / procedural guidance
- Client/Agency: NAVAIR SBIR/STTR Program Management Office (PMO)
- Program/Solicitation: Navy SBIR Phase II
- Date: 2026-03-13
- BST Products/Systems Referenced: None
- Key Personnel: Beck Cotter (last editor)

## Executive Summary
This document is guidance from the Navy SBIR/STTR PMO to small businesses preparing full Phase II proposals. It identifies common submission issues and provides specific hints and tips to minimize back-and-forth corrections, accelerate cost negotiations, and reduce time to award. The guidance covers templates, compliance, deliverables, cost structure, and administrative requirements.

## Technical Approach
Not applicable—this is procedural guidance, not a technical proposal.

## Products & Capabilities Described
None. This is administrative/contracting guidance for Navy SBIR Phase II proposals.

## Use Cases & Applications
Not applicable.

## Key Results
Not applicable.

## Notable Details

### Formatting & Templates
- Technical volume must adhere to provided formatting/numbering structure
- Cost volume must use Navy's Phase II Cost Volume template exclusively; no alternative templates accepted
- Templates available at: https://www.navysbir.com/links_forms.htm

### ITAR/EAR Restrictions
- Question 7 (SBIR) or 8 (STTR) on Volume I Proposal Certification in DSIP asks about ITAR/EAR data
- Check original topic description in BAA for ITAR/EAR-restricted status
- Contractor's DSIP response must match Government's understanding; resolve discrepancies with TPOC

### Deliverables Section
- Must not be deleted from Volume II Technical Proposal
- Must list all items produced and delivered throughout effort (progress reports, test reports, manuals, etc.)
- Must include tangible/productized deliverable (prototype/hardware/software)

### Government Participation (GFP/GFI)
- If none requested, write "No GFP, GFI or Facilities/Personnel requested at this time"
- If resources needed, clearly articulate what is needed and why
- Must explain necessity of resources

### Security Classification
- Section must remain in Volume II even if work is unclassified
- Must identify whether work anticipated to be classified or unclassified
- Consult TPOC if uncertain

### Data Rights Assertions
- Question 11 (SBIR) or 12 (STTR) on Volume I asks about DFARS 252.227-7017 assertions
- If "yes" answered, corresponding assertions table required in Technical Proposal
- **No need to assert rights on data from previous contracts under same topic** or data developed during upcoming Phase II
- Assert rights only on technical data from external contracts or privately funded development
- Descriptions must clearly distinguish pre-contract data from execution-phase development
- If answering "no," write "none" rather than deleting section

### Equipment
- Complete Equipment tab in Cost Proposal with maximum detail
- Must identify equipment type
- **No fee applied to Plant Equipment (PE) or General Purpose Equipment (GPE)/Contractor Acquired Property (CAP)**
- Must complete all table sections: description, vendor/source, country of origin, basis of estimate
- If CAP proposed, **Property Management System Approval (PMSA) Letter from DCMA required**
- If PMSA letter doesn't exist, contact cognizant DCMA office and provide confirmation to NAVAIR contracting officer (Dina Marinelli: dina.m.marinelli.civ@us.navy.mil)
- DCMA office locator: https://www.dcma.mil/DCMA-Pricing-Support/

### TABA (Technical and Business Assistance)
- **Must be included within NTE amount, not in addition to it**
- Maximum $25,000 per Phase II award; $50,000 per project (all phases combined)
- Reviewed and approved by DON SBIR/STTR Program Office
- Final report with TABA report required: http://www.navysbirprogram.com/navydeliverables/

**TABA Requirements if proposed:**
- TABA provider firm name
- Provider point of contact, email, phone
- Explanation of provider's unique qualifications
- Detailed tasks to be performed (purpose/objective)
- Total cost, hours, labor rates (blended rate acceptable)

**TABA Prohibitions:**
- No profit/fee by SBIR proposer
- Cannot be the SBIR proposer
- Cannot be affiliate of SBIR proposer
- Cannot be investor of SBIR proposer
- Cannot be subcontractor/consultant otherwise required for paid research effort

**TABA Consequences:**
- If awarded TABA, firm eliminated from DON SBIR/STTR Transition Program (STP), Forum for SBIR/STTR Transition (FST), and other Phase II assistance
- If NOT awarded TABA, must participate in virtual DON STP Kickoff in first or second year (up to full day, no travel costs)
- **Failure to include TABA details in Volume 5 results in disapproval**

### Period of Performance (PoP)
- Standard: 30-month base + 12-month option
- Deviations require written justification from Government TPOC
- Base and option periods can overlap
- **Goal: minimize no-cost extensions**—propose sufficient time to complete base and option tasking
- All PoP dates must match across technical volume sections
- Cost volume: break base and option into yearly increments (calendar or fiscal years)
- Year-to-year breakdown must cover entire PoP and show obvious labor rate escalation

### Teaming Partners/Subcontractors
- Question 13 (SBIR) or 14 (STTR) on Volume I asks about teaming/subcontractors
- Answer "yes" only if subcontractors proposed; consultants alone don't require "yes"
- Complete consultant and subcontractor tabs in cost volume with maximum detail
- Volume 5 must include competitive quotes or agreement letters for subcontractors/consultants with agreed-upon rates/costs for **this specific** Phase II effort
- Do not rely on past history or old estimates

### Labor Category
- All key personnel must be in cost volume with labor category, rate, and hours
- PI labor category: "Principal Investigator"

### Human/Animal Testing
- Research involving human, animal, or recombinant DNA must be proposed for **Option period only**
- If proposed during base period, contract cannot be awarded until review board approvals completed
- **This may significantly delay contract award**

### Contract Type & Fee
- NAVAIR generally awards Phase II as **Cost-Plus-Fixed-Fee (CPFF)**
- **Must include fee in cost volume**
- Firm Fixed Price (FFP) requires justification; CPFF more appropriate for R&D due to uncertainty and flexibility
- CPFF shifts financial risk to government, allows funding increases based on transition potential

### Labor Escalation
- If proposing escalation, "Labor&Ind Rates" tab must be thoroughly completed
- For 42-month PoP, expect **minimum 3 escalation instances** across 3+ calendar/fiscal years
- Year-to-year breakdown required so escalation can be verified
- While not required, escalation is typical and expected
- If no escalation proposed, Government will request confirmation this was intentional

### Materials/Vendor Quotes
- **Strongly recommend domestic materials and vendors** per SBIR/STTR Policy Directive and Buy American clause
- Foreign vendors/materials: if proposed, must identify domestic source or provide justification if domestic unavailable or cost-prohibitive
- Foreign materials require funding agreement officer review/approval—takes additional time, approval not guaranteed
- **Basis of estimate required for all materials, supplies, equipment**
- Provide support documentation in Volume 5: vendor quotes, correspondence, website screenshots
- Complete Materials-Supplies tab with detail: country of origin, reference document numbers, unit/total price
- Arrange quotes in order they appear on table if possible

## Executive Summary
This publication documents the development and testing of the Coyote sonobuoy-launched unmanned air vehicle (SLUAV) for atmospheric and ocean boundary layer profiling. Over ~6 years and nearly 50 test flights, the team integrated meteorological sensors into the Coyote to collect data compatible with AMDAR (Aircraft Meteorological Data Relay) formats for use in COAMPS® weather prediction models operated by NOAA and the US Navy. The platform demonstrated capability to profile atmospheric conditions from launch altitude to near sea level while operating from conventional P-3 aircraft sonobuoy launch tubes.

## Technical Approach
- **Platform Design**: Coyote SLUAV designed to fit in standard A-sized sonobuoy launch tubes (4.875" diameter, 36" length, max 39 lbs); deployable from P-3 aircraft at 170-220 knots at altitudes up to 30,000 feet
- **Flight Characteristics**: ~60-minute endurance; nominal cruise speed 45 knots (sustainable ~90 min) with dash capability to 75 knots; minimum 20 nautical mile range
- **Control System**: UTC Aerospace Systems Piccolo autopilot provides real-time command/control and data links to ground control station (GCS); autopilot gathers time, position, barometric pressure, wind speed, turbulence
- **Launch/Recovery**: Canister-based deployment with parachute descent; launch-to-flight sequence <0.5 seconds; aircraft remains on parachute in steady descent for 10 seconds during GPS lock; parachute released after 15 seconds when platform commences climb
- **Data Format**: Sensor data converted to FM-42 AMDAR message format for direct integration with COAMPS® weather models; WMO standard format compliance
- **Development Blocks**: Five major design iterations (prototypes, Block A1, A2, A2-1, B1, B1-1, B2); 41 total aircraft fabricated

## Products & Capabilities Described

### Coyote SLUAV
- **Purpose**: Provide on-demand atmospheric profiling without requiring manned aircraft to change altitude; extend sensor range and aircraft on-station time; improve survivability
- **Key Features**: 
  - Stores in standard sonobuoy launch tube
  - Real-time telemetry to GCS
  - Can operate <100m above sea surface
  - ~60-minute flight duration
  - Compatible with existing P-3 launch protocols

### Integrated Sensor Suite
**Operational (Green - tested on Coyote):**
- Piccolo autopilot (time, position, pressure, wind, turbulence)
- Pressure-Temperature-Humidity (PTHU) sensor - reconfigured from commercial aerosondes; approximately 3.5" × 2.5" × 1.5" with extended flexible sensors (~8" total length); produces continuous altitude profiles
- EO/IR imagery (640×480 or 320×240 cameras; dual gimbaled systems available from vendors like Trillium)
- Micro-Tesla magnetometer

**Tested on Surrogate (Yellow - Silver Fox UAV):**
- Ocean temperature profiling (capability to measure vertical temperature profiles)
- Sea surface temperature
- Sea wave height and periodicity (inertial measurement unit + GPS-based approach)
- Ocean surface currents

**Deferred/Future (Orange/Red):**
- Hyperspectral imaging (HSI)
- Radar
- Altimeter
- Aerosol sensors

## Use Cases & Applications

### Primary Mission: Meteorological Data Collection
- **Tropical Cyclone Monitoring**: Planned Caribbean field testing summer 2014 to collect data directly within tropical cyclones; offers extended data duration (>1 hour vs. dropwindsondes' minutes) with flexible positioning capability
- **Boundary Layer Profiling**: Detailed atmospheric profiles from launch altitude to sea surface to better assess boundary layer tropical cyclone structure
- **COAMPS® Model Augmentation**: Provide "actionable data" (AMDAR-compatible) to complement AMDAR streams from commercial aircraft and improve Navy/NOAA weather prediction models

### Secondary Missions
- Anti-submarine warfare (ASW)
- Intelligence, Surveillance, Reconnaissance (ISR)
- Magnetic field mapping

### Operational Integration
- Complement Aircraft Meteorological Data Relay (AMDAR) system which generates 300,000+ high-quality observations per day
- Augment Coupled Ocean Atmospheric Mesoscale Prediction System (COAMPS®) - Navy's two-way coupled atmospheric/ocean prediction model
- Support COAMPS-OS® visualization and scheduling interface

## Key Results

### Flight Test History
- **2007-2009**: Nine flights with Coyote A2-1 block; ~3.4 hours total flight time; testing focused on launch protocols and sonobuoy procedures
- **2013**: Seven flights with Coyote B2 block; ~4.7 hours flight time without incident
- **2014 (through publication date)**: Three flights with Coyote B1-1 block; ~2.63 hours flight time without incident
- **Total to Date**: ~49 flight tests and sorties; approximately 10+ hours cumulative flight time

### PTHU Sensor Data
- Successfully tested on Silver Fox surrogate UAV in 55-minute flights
- Demonstrated continuous atmospheric profiling with altitude increases in 500'-1000' increments to 4,000'
- Captured air temperature oscillations and humidity variations
- Confirmed ability to gather METOC data in WMO standard format

### Magnetometer Testing
- Commercial micro-Tesla magnetometer integration verified as feasible
- Test flights at 50 feet AGL altitude over known magnetic targets (parked vehicles)
- Initial testing showed insufficient sensitivity; identified need for 3-axis pico-Tesla magnetometer for future flights
- More sensitive magnetometer identified for future evaluation

### Wave Height & Current Measurement
- Successfully demonstrated use of Piccolo autopilot IMU and GPS to measure ocean surface conditions after platform ditching
- December 2011 test off Monterey Bay captured:
  - 14-second wave periodicity corresponding to 4.9-foot wave height
  - 11-second periodicity corresponding to 3.1-foot wave height
  - Platform drift tracking over 17.4-minute duration
- Confirmed feasibility of collecting ocean state data with autopilot sensors suite

### Data Format Conversion
- Successfully converted sensor data to FM-42 AMDAR message format
- AMDAR decoder tested at NRL Monterey; conversion deemed successful
- Custom .log file at GCS generates AMDAR records directly for COAMPS® ingestion
- AMDAR records include: OBS Type, VEH Code, Latitude, Longitude, Clock D/H/M, Altitude, Air Temp, Rel. Humidity, Wind Direction, Turbulence, Icing, Additional Data, Pitch, Roll, Pressure, E-Lat, E-Long

## Notable Details

### Development Philosophy
- Focused on mission-specific sensor integration without significantly escalating platform cost or schedule
- Emphasized data compatibility with existing operational systems (AMDAR, COAMPS®) for immediate operational utility
- Miniaturized commercial sensors where possible (e.g., PTHU probe from aerosondes)
- Leveraged existing aircraft infrastructure (P-3 sonobuoy launch tubes) for deployment

### Partnership & Support
- Multi-agency collaboration: US Navy (primary funder across multiple contracts from 2004-2014), NOAA (Hurricane Sandy funding), US Air Force Research Laboratory (2013 testing)
- University and private sector partnerships: Sensintel Inc., Itri Corporation, Hydronalix

### Competitive Advantages
- First sonobuoy-launchable UAV with integrated METOC sensors
- Compatibility with existing aircraft platforms and launch procedures (no modification required)
- Extended observation duration compared to dropwindsondes while maintaining deployment flexibility
- Real-time data link and near real-time 3D atmospheric profiling capability
- Direct integration with Navy/NOAA operational weather models

## Document Metadata
- **Type:** Peer-reviewed journal article (IEEE Transactions on Geoscience and Remote Sensing)
- **Client/Agency:** NASA (SMAP mission)
- **Program/Solicitation:** SMAP (Soil Moisture Active Passive) mission
- **Date:** Published January 2014 (manuscript received September 2012, accepted June 2013)
- **BST Products/Systems Referenced:** None directly; this is a NASA/academic publication
- **Key Personnel:** Jeffrey R. Piepmeier (NASA GSFC, lead author), Joel T. Johnson (Ohio State), Priscilla N. Mohammed (GESTAR/GSFC), Damon Bradley (University of Maryland/NASA GSFC), Christopher Ruf (University of Michigan), Mustafa Aksoy (Ohio State), Rafael Garcia, Derek Hudson, Lynn Miles, Mark Wong (all NASA GSFC)

## Executive Summary
This paper describes NASA's comprehensive approach to radio-frequency interference (RFI) mitigation for the SMAP spaceborne L-band microwave radiometer. Because SMAP operates in the protected 1400–1427 MHz spectrum vulnerable to out-of-band emissions and illegal transmitters, the mission employs an innovative digital back-end radiometer with ground-based signal processing algorithms to detect and remove RFI. The system collects ~1000× more data than conventionally necessary, enabling multi-domain RFI detection and removal while maintaining soil-moisture measurement accuracy of <0.04 m³/m³.

## Technical Approach

### RFI Environment Characterization
SMAP conducted a multifaceted characterization:
- **Prediction modeling:** Simulations of out-of-band (OOB) emissions from known L-band radar facilities in North America, predicting received power levels up to 2 W
- **Ground-based observations:** Measured RFI characteristics at fixed locations, identifying narrow-band spurious emissions (1 MHz or less)
- **Aircraft-based observations:** 9 flights (~24 hours) during SMAPVEX08 (2008) using digital and analog back-end systems to map RFI across North America
- **Satellite data analysis:** Leveraged SMOS and Aquarius L-band observations to characterize global RFI environment

**Key Finding:** RFI environment includes pulsed radar emissions, continuous-wave (CW) sources, wideband and narrow-band interference. Low-level RFI equivalent to 0.1–10 K brightness temperature would jeopardize mission without aggressive mitigation.

### Radiometer Digital Back-End Design
Rather than conventional square-law diode detectors, SMAP uses:
- **Two Analog Processing Units (APU):** One per polarization, with 14-bit ADCs sampling at 96 megasamples/second (MSPS)
- **One Digital Processing Unit (DPU):** Coordinates signal processing and data management
- **Seven radiation-tolerant FPGAs** performing:
  - **Digital Downconverter (DDC):** Shifts 24 MHz bandwidth (96 MSPS) to baseband, applies 63rd-order low-pass filter with on-orbit programmable coefficients
  - **16-channel Polyphase Filter Bank:** Separates full-band data into 1.5 MHz subbands; uses custom pipelined FFT
  - **Statistics Calculation Unit (SCU):** Computes first four raw moments of signal for full-band and all 16 subbands

**Key Capability:** Outputs the first four raw moments of receiver-system noise voltage (enabling kurtosis calculation and Stokes parameter measurement) rather than simple detector counts. Synchronous integration with radar pulse-repetition interval (~350 μs).

### RFI Detection Algorithms (Ground Processing)
Four complementary detectors, each producing binary RFI flags:

1. **Pulse Detection (Time Domain):** Searches for impulsive RFI via anomalous antenna temperatures
   - Compares individual T_A against mean m and standard deviation σ_td
   - Detection: T_A − m ≥ β_td · σ_td
   - Best for large-amplitude, short-duration, low-duty-cycle sources

2. **Cross-Frequency Detection:** Identifies RFI spanning multiple frequency channels
   - Operates on 16 subband channels at 1.4 ms integration
   - Uses 16−N channels with smallest T_A values to estimate mean/σ
   - Flags channels >β_cf standard deviations above mean, plus adjacent subbands
   - More sensitive to CW interference

3. **Kurtosis Detection:** Tests for non-Gaussianity of received signals
   - Computes kurtosis K = (fourth central moment) / (second central moment)²
   - Detection: |K − K_nom| > β_K · σ_K
   - Applied independently to I and Q components of every subband and polarization
   - Effective for both CW and pulsed RFI classification

4. **Polarization Detection:** Thresholds third and fourth Stokes parameters (T₃, T₄)
   - Detects anomalous linear and circular polarization signatures
   - T₄ expected ~0 over land; T₃ varies with Faraday rotation
   - Detection: |T₃,₄ − T_nom| ≥ β₃,₄ · σ₃,₄

**Maximum Probability of Detection (MPD) Flag:** Logical OR of all four detector outputs maximizes probability of catching RFI; outputs combined for removal of contaminated time–frequency samples.

### Data Collection Strategy
- **Full-band measurements** at 350 μs interval (~44 samples per 15.4 ms L1B product)
- **Subband measurements** at 1.4 ms interval (11 time samples × 16 frequency channels per product)
- **Total data multiplier:** ~1000× more measurements than minimum needed for single Stokes vector measurement
- **Single-product NEDT:** 0.96 K (nominal system temperature 540 K, 24 MHz bandwidth)

## Products & Capabilities Described

### SMAP Microwave Radiometer
- **What it is:** Spaceborne L-band (1400–1427 MHz) radiometer with digital back-end for soil-moisture measurement
- **Specifications:**
  - Operates in protected Earth Exploration Satellite Service band
  - Full bandwidth: 24 MHz
  - 16 frequency subbands of 1.5 MHz each
  - Dual-polarization (V and H)
  - Measures full Stokes vector + kurtosis
  - Radiometric accuracy requirement: <1.3 K uncertainty
  - Soil-moisture retrieval requirement: <0.04 m³/m³ uncertainty
  - 40° nominal incidence angle

- **Proposed Use:** Global high-resolution active–passive L-band observations of Earth from space; primary objective is soil-moisture measurements
- **Key Innovation:** First spaceborne digital radiometer with raw-moment outputs (vs. detector counts) enabling advanced RFI detection on ground

### Engineering Test Unit (ETU)
- **What it is:** Fully functional pre-flight radiometer with identical RF and digital electronics (minus antenna)
- **Use in context:** Verified RFI detection and mitigation performance before flight
- **Test Capability:** Accepts injected RFI signals (pulsed sinusoids at various widths: 2, 30, 450 μs, and continuous) with controllable power levels (0.1 K to >1000 K brightness temperature)

## Use Cases & Applications

### Primary Mission
- **Global soil-moisture measurement:** Daily, high-resolution observations of Earth's surface soil moisture with <0.04 m³/m³ uncertainty
- **Application areas:** Agriculture, hydrology, climate modeling, drought monitoring
- **Requirement context:** Must maintain measurement fidelity despite ubiquitous RFI in global L-band environment

### RFI Environment Characterization Uses
- **North American validation:** SMAPVEX08 aircraft campaign mapped RFI spatial distribution
- **Global RFI assessment:** Leveraged SMOS and Aquarius satellite data to extend beyond regional (North America-centric) predictions
- **Regulatory/spectrum management:** Results inform international radio spectrum management for passive remote sensing

## Key Results (Measurements & Demonstrations)

### RFI Environment Findings
1. **Global RFI distribution (Aquarius data, April–May 2012):**
   - Large RFI sources observed on every continent
   - North America less corrupted than Europe and Asia
   - Emphasizes importance of global characterization vs. North America-only studies

2. **RFI Statistics (SMOS analysis):**
   - Generalized Extreme Value (GEV) distribution fits RFI brightness-temperature tail behavior
   - GEV parameters fitted from SMOS data: a=0.77, σ=3.75 K, μ=3.2 K
   - SMOS-derived RFI levels significantly higher than SMAPVEX08 airborne campaign (due to global coverage)
   - **Conservative SMAP assumption:** 10% of observations will contain RFI ≥20 K

3. **RFI Source Types Observed:**
   - Pulsed radar emissions (wide-band)
   - Narrow-band continuous-wave (CW) emissions (<1 MHz bandwidth)
   - Spurious emissions from communication systems
   - Likely illegally operating emitters within protected band

### Radiometer Hardware Performance (ETU Testing)

**Kurtosis Measurements:**
- Full-band kurtosis measured at 350 μs resolution in presence of injected sinusoidal RFI
- Good theoretical agreement for mean kurtosis; measured standard deviations slightly higher (due to fourth-moment discretization)
- Kurtosis values <3 for sinusoidal interference; >3 for pulsed interference (enables source classification)

**Cross-Frequency RFI Mitigation (Low-Level CW Example):**
- Injected 1413.5 MHz sinusoid at 17.3 K brightness temp in center channel (1.08 K integrated effect)
- Cross-frequency detector at 15.4 ms resolution removed corrupted channel + adjacent channels
- Result: 46 of 176 measurements discarded; 16.3% NEDT increase; **mitigated brightness 114.6 K vs. true 114.7 K (0.1 K error)**
- Successful detection/mitigation demonstrated from <1 K to >100 K RFI power levels

**Pulsed RFI Removal (2 μs Pulses at 596 Hz):**
- **High-amplitude case (3.84 K RFI contribution):**
  - Original: 120.01 K → Mitigated: 116.15 K (after 0.19 K bias correction)
  - Mitigated 3.86 K vs. true 3.84 K RFI (**excellent agreement**)

- **Low-amplitude case (1.74 K RFI contribution):**
  - Original: 117.75 K → Mitigated: 117.12 K
  - Mitigated only 0.63 K vs. true 1.74 K (**1.11 K uncorrected bias**)
  - Note: Full-band measurements used primarily for land flagging; spectrogram-based (subband) detectors perform better at low amplitude

**Simulated Global Performance:**
- Integration of simulated SMAP mitigation biases with SMOS-derived RFI pdf enables prediction of global expected RFI impact
- Example: Pulsed RFI at 1.74 K brightness temp → <0.1 K post-mitigation bias (after algorithm improvements from initial testing)
- NEDT increase from RFI mitigation quantified as function of RFI brightness temperature

### Detection Threshold & False-Alarm Rate
- Prelaunch threshold (β) set to limit false-alarm rate to **9.3%**
- This corresponds to **5% increase in effective NEDT** when no RFI present
- Threshold varies geographically via 1° × 1° lookup table to account for regional RFI likelihood/type
- Expected revision post-launch based on actual on-orbit RFI environment

### Data Loss from RFI Removal
- Trade-off between RFI mitigation and measurement noise: discarding contaminated samples increases# PIMS 7837 - Budget Justification

## Executive Summary
Black Swift Technologies is evaluating participation in a Navy STTR to develop an improved expendable profiling system for atmospheric and air-sea observations in hazardous weather conditions (tropical cyclones, polar lows, heavy precipitation). The effort aims to advance beyond current radiosonde capabilities in quantity, quality, spatial/temporal coverage, cost per unit, durability, and uncertainty characterization. BST's S0 system appears positioned as the candidate technology, though internal questions remain about capability alignment, deployment mechanisms, and Navy operational requirements.

## Technical Approach
The RFP seeks a compact, deployable, cost-effective alternative to radiosondes that improves observations of:
- Vertical, horizontal, and temporal variations in atmospheric profiles (dynamics and thermodynamics)
- Air-sea interface phenomena
- Hazardous weather environments (tropical cyclones, polar lows, sea ice formation/break-up in marginal ice zones)

**Phase I Deliverables Required:**
- State-of-science review of current observing platforms, measurement uncertainties, and logistical challenges
- Concept design for improved measurement techniques addressing identified limitations
- Comparative analysis with radiosondes and remote sensing (uncertainty specifications, real-world validated results)
- Engineering, hardware, software, and/or platform upgrades proposal
- Discussion of competitive advantages vs. radiosondes in cost, longevity, sampling rate, spatial/temporal coverage

**Phase II Focus:**
- Development, fabrication, demonstration, validation, and iteration of expendable profiling technology
- Calibration and accuracy demonstration in hazardous conditions
- Multiple prototype development spirals with real-world field demonstrations
- Leverage existing delivery systems (ground, ship, aircraft-based)
- Data ingest and assimilation into operational forecast models with added-value analysis

**Phase III Commercialization:**

## Document Metadata
- Type: Science magazine article / research feature
- Publication: PNAS (Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences)
- Published: July 2, 2013
- Key Personnel: David Pieri (California Institute of Technology / Jet Propulsion Laboratory)
- Subject: UAV applications in volcanology

## Executive Summary
This article describes how geologist David Pieri and colleagues at JPL are using small unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to collect detailed measurements from volcanic plumes and lava flows, addressing limitations of traditional helicopter and satellite-based observation methods. The work aims to improve volcanic activity prediction and aviation safety.

## Technical Approach
- **Multiple simultaneous UAVs**: Flying 6+ Dragon Eye UAVs concurrently to track chemical characteristics at multiple locations in ash clouds simultaneously
- **Small electric-powered platforms**: Electric engines minimize ash ingestion compared to jet aircraft
- **Miniaturized sensor payload**: Integrated multiple instruments into 500-gram payload limit
- **Real-time ash cloud sampling**: Direct in-plume measurement versus relying on unvalidated satellite infrared data

## Products & Systems Described

### Dragon Eye UAVs
- **Specifications**: 5.9 lbs weight, 3.75 ft wingspan, 500-gram payload capacity
- **Sensor suite**: 2 cameras, SO₂ sensor, particulate sensor, nanoparticle counter, vacuum sampling bottle for ash/gas collection
- **Source**: Retired US Marine Corps units managed by NASA Ames Research Center (~90 total available)
- **Advantages**: Reduced cost, lower risk than crewed aircraft, immunity to ash clogging (electric engines), ability to operate inside volcanic plume

## Use Cases & Applications
1. **Volcanic plume chemistry tracking**: Monitor chemical composition changes over time and distance from volcano
2. **Ash plume characterization**: Quantitative measurement of ash cloud thickness and density
3. **Lava flow monitoring**: Detailed observations of lava flow routes and length prediction
4. **Aviation safety**: Validation of ash plume data to determine safe flight corridors
5. **Volcanic activity prediction**: Support model development for eruption forecasting and damage prediction
6. **Future concept**: Landing UAVs directly on lava flows for ground-level measurements

## Field Demonstrations
- **March 2013**: Trial deployment of 6 Dragon Eye UAVs into volcanic plume of Turrialba volcano, Costa Rica
- **Historical context**: David Pieri's earlier frustration with 1984 Mauna Loa (Hawaii) helicopter survey limitations motivated the research

## Key Advantages Cited
- "Whole new arena of detailed observations and new kinds of data that we could never get before"
- Relatively inexpensive approach compared to crewed aircraft
- Eliminates risk to human pilots from harsh volcanic environment conditions
- Addresses satellite data validation gap (infrared measurements largely unvalidated and not quantitative)

## Notable Details
- Resolves historical challenge where helicopter could only observe single location at a time; 22-km Mauna Loa lava flow couldn't be fully surveyed in single flight
- Helicopter turbulence from 800°C lava made data collection difficult and dangerous
- Jet aircraft vulnerability: blades clogged by melted ash, preventing safe operation near dense ash plumes
- Pieri emphasizes technology has "limitless possibilities" for volcano research

## Relevance to BST Context
This article appears in BST's 2016 NASA SBIR volcano proposal supporting materials, suggesting Pieri's work with small UAVs in volcanic environments was a reference point for Black Swift's own volcano monitoring technology development.# Purchase Order 108020 - Black Swift Technologies Subcontracting Services

## Document Metadata
- Type: Purchase Order with Statement of Work (SOW)
- Client/Agency: By Light Professional IT Services LLC (DISA Global Operations)
- Program/Solicitation: Mustang Program; Project Number 15423.00.0001.000001
- Date: 10/8/2025
- BST Products/Systems Referenced: SwiftCore (flight computer), Mustang (fixed-wing UAS platform)
- Key Personnel: Jack Elston (Black Swift Technologies), Josh Whetstine (By Light POC), Bryan Sparling (By Light SVP Strategic Programs), Beck Cotter (BST contact)

## Executive Summary
Black Swift Technologies will conduct a nine-week engineering effort to design, build, and flight-test a next-generation Mustang UAS (G2) meeting specified requirements: ≤55 lb gross takeoff weight, 400–450 km range, full-electric propulsion, and integration with government-provided launcher and GOTS autopilot systems. The work leverages SwiftCore flight computer for rapid data-driven design iteration and flight validation.

## Technical Approach

### Phase Structure (Effort 1 + Effort 2)

**Effort 1: Rapid Initial Validation (10/6–10/17, 2 weeks)**
- Integrate SwiftCore into existing Mustang Unit 3
- Execute truck launch and flight operations
- Collect ground/air video and flight telemetry
- Analyze data to validate airframe and propulsion baseline

**Effort 2: G2 Design, Build, and Flight Test (10/6–12/5, 9 weeks)**

1. **G2 Conceptual Design (Weeks 3–4, MS1)**
   - Mission & constraints freeze: payload, range, endurance, launch method
   - SwiftCore-enabled rapid design loop: real-time telemetry, logging, and system-identification tools feed aerodynamic and power data directly into sizing models
   - Power-to-weight optimization: trade studies on motor Kv, propeller diameter/pitch, ESC efficiency, battery energy density to achieve target cruise power and climb margins
   - Aerodynamic configuration selection: evaluate BST in-house wings, CU "Mistral" wing, and COTS 4–5 m options using lift/drag estimation and Reynolds-scaled polars
   - Structural analysis: quasi-static launch load calculations; safety factors for wing joiners, fuselage attachment, landing gear
   - Deliver design package with aerodynamic coefficients, propulsion selections, and predicted range vs. payload curves

2. **COTS Procurement (Weeks 3–4, MS1)**
   - Vendor down-select for wings, tails, test fuselage meeting geometric and structural requirements
   - Dimensional and structural verification (mass properties, stiffness, joiner fit, control-surface play)
   - CAD/drawings for wing-to-fuselage and tail interfaces

3. **Assembly & Ground Integration (Weeks 5–7, MS2)**
   - Install SwiftCore flight computer, avionics, wiring, sensors, telemetry
   - Bench and ground power testing
   - Launcher fit-checks and dry runs
   - CG verification, battery placement, sensor alignment
   - Thermal validation using onboard sensors

4. **Flight Testing & Performance Validation (Weeks 8–9, MS3–4)**
   - Staged flight cards: manual launch stabilization, speed sweeps, climb/descend
   - Incremental weight loading: 42, 48, 52, 55 lb GTOW
   - Power-vs-speed testing: controlled speed points recording voltage, current, ESC temperature, airspeed
   - SwiftCore data logging: extract thrust-to-power ratios, trim states, control effectiveness
   - Range modeling: SwiftCore power logging and analysis scripts to compute Wh/km and extrapolate endurance under mission profiles
   - Minimum 3 consecutive successful flights meeting stability and endurance metrics

5. **GOTS Integration**
   - Mechanical/electrical accommodation for EchoMAV FC, payload, gimbal, cameras
   - Design power buses and harnesses isolating SwiftCore from GOTS payload power systems
   - Data compatibility: SwiftCore NetCDF export interface for By Light to translate into Cube/ArduPilot parameters
   - Environmental verification: structural mounting, vibration isolation, EMI cleanliness
   - Note: Physical EchoMAV/Cube installation and tuning by By Light (out of scope)

6. **Government Launcher Integration (MS4)**
   - Launcher interface design: adapter or rail-mount solution for GOV launcher
   - Launch envelope characterization: acceleration, exit speed via SwiftCore IMU/GPS
   - Safety limits definition: abort thresholds, environmental limits (wind, temperature, battery state-of-charge)
   - Minimum three successful GOV-launcher flight sequences with video and data logs

## Products & Capabilities Described

### SwiftCore Flight Computer
- **What it is:** BST's flight computer and data acquisition system with real-time telemetry, high-rate logging (IMU, GPS, power, ESC telemetry), and open data interface (NetCDF export)
- **Proposed use:** Primary flight computer for Mustang G2; enables rapid iterative design via system-identification tools feeding aerodynamic and power data into sizing models; high-fidelity onboard logging for performance validation and thermal monitoring
- **Key capabilities:**
  - Real-time telemetry and onboard logging at high sample rates
  - System-identification tools for aerodynamic coefficient extraction
  - Power logging for range/endurance modeling
  - Thermal sensor integration for subsystem monitoring
  - NetCDF data export for downstream autopilot adaptation
  - Vibration/launch dynamics characterization

### Mustang Platform
- **What it is:** Fixed-wing tactical UAS, existing Units 3 and 4; G2 variant is redesigned full-electric evolution
- **Effort 1 use:** Unit 3 retrofitted with SwiftCore for rapid baseline validation
- **Effort 2 use:** G2 design based on COTS airframe components (wings, tail, fuselage) optimized for 55 lb GTOW and 400–450 km range; truck-launch compatible
- **Specifications (G2 targets):**
  - GTOW: ≤55 lb (minimum required for 450 km range)
  - Range: 400–450 km (full electric)
  - Launch method: truck launch + GOV government launcher
  - Endurance: modeled via SwiftCore power telemetry
  - Propulsion: electric (motor, ESC, propeller trade studies; battery energy density TBD)
  - Payload: TBD per mission requirements; design loop includes payload accommodation

## Use Cases & Applications

1. **Long-range tactical reconnaissance:** 450 km range enables extended-range ISR missions
2. **Rapid prototyping & design validation:** SwiftCore-enabled iterative loop compresses development cycle (9 weeks from concept to flight-proven prototype)
3. **Government platform adaptation:** Designed for integration with GOTS EchoMAV/Cube autopilots and government-supplied launcher for future By Light operational deployment
4. **Electric propulsion validation:** Demonstrates full-electric long-range platform; battery draw modeling provides confidence bounds for mission planning

## Key Results / Deliverables

**Effort 1 (by 10/17/25):**
- Ground and air video of Unit 3 flying reliably with SwiftCore
- Flight data logs and technical summary
- Baseline performance validation

**Effort 2 (by 12/5/25):**
- **G2 Mustang prototype:** ≤55 lb GTOW, 400–450 km range, full-electric, truck-launch and GOV-launcher compatible
- **Design package:** aerodynamic coefficients, propulsion selections, structural analysis, range vs. payload curves
- **Flight test data:** minimum 3 successful flights; power-vs-speed data; thermal logs; launcher integration validation
- **Range model:** validated Wh/km performance curves and endurance predictions under mission profiles
- **System identification data:** control responses, trim states, aerodynamic parameters extracted from SwiftCore telemetry
- **Integration documentation:** CAD/interface drawings for GOTS component accommodation; power bus schematics; thermal validation report
- **Video and data package:** flight test footage, consolidated SwiftCore logs, analysis plots
- **Government-purchasable IP:** all deliverables and designs become non-proprietary property of By Light upon completion

## Notable Details

1. **IP Terms:** Black Swift explicitly waives all proprietary claims; all deliverables and design data become sole property of client upon payment, enabling By Light to adapt for government purchase and operational deployment.

2. **Rapid Iterative Design Loop:** SwiftCore's real-time telemetry and system-identification tools are central to the technical approach, enabling BST to compress traditional design-build-test cycles by feeding live flight data directly into aerodynamic models and propulsion sizing.

3. **Data-Driven Battery Modeling:** Flight tests will include controlled speed sweeps with full power logging to establish Wh/km consumption and extrapolate reliable 400–450 km range with confidence margins and recommended cruise speeds.

4. **Modular Autopilot Accommodation:** Design isolates SwiftCore from GOTS EchoMAV/Cube payloads via power bus separation and uses NetCDF export to enable By Light's later parameter translation, decoupling BST's role from downstream autopilot tuning.

5. **Launcher Flexibility:** Effort 2 includes both truck-launch (Effort 1 baseline) and government launcher integration, with IMU/GPS characterization of launch dynamics and abort threshold definition.

6. **Schedule Risk Mitigation:** Effort 1 (immediate 2-week Unit 3 validation) funded at $100K up-front to validate approach before committing full Effort 2 resources; remaining $350K contingent on milestone completion. Schedule contingency notes dependency on personnel availability and long-lead component delivery.

7. **Subcontractor References:** CU "Mistral" wing option mentioned; no COTS vendors named but wing/tail procurement from standard suppliers anticipated.

8. **Budget:** $450K fixed labor + actual cost for materials, supplies, and travel; payment milestones tied to design review, assembly completion, flight test, and final package delivery.# Potential Proposals - 2014

## Document Metadata
- Type: Internal planning document / proposal brainstorm
