## Document Metadata
- Type: Technical specification/requirements document
- Client/Agency: NASA
- Program/Solicitation: 2018 SBIR - Terrain Following (Phase I)
- Date: 2018-10-01 to 2018-10-08
- BST Products/Systems Referenced: None explicitly (document evaluates sensor options for potential integration)
- Key Personnel: Austin Anderson (commentator)

## Executive Summary
This document evaluates sensor technologies suitable for autonomous terrain-following flight, establishing long-range and short-range obstacle detection requirements and comparing performance, SWaP-C (Size, Weight, Power, Cost), and processing needs across multiple sensor families including cameras, thermal imagers, lidar, radar, and lasers.

## Sensing Architecture
The document establishes a two-tier detection strategy modeled on automotive ADAS systems:
- **Long-range detection**: Coarse detection of large obstacles at distance for early corrective action
- **Short-range detection**: Fine detection of smaller obstacles at close range for terminal collision avoidance

---

## Long-Range Sensor Requirements

| Parameter | Value | Type |
|-----------|-------|------|
| Min Range | 10 m | Minimum |
| Max Range | 100 m | Maximum |
| Obstacle Size | 10 m² | Minimum |
| Obstacle Height | 5 m | Minimum |
| Range Resolution | 50 cm | Minimum |
| Field of View (Az, El) | 45°, 17° | Minimum (TBR) |
| Update Rate | 5 Hz | Minimum |
| Detection Rate | 99.9% | Minimum |

*Note: Internal comments indicate 50m min range was "ludicrously conservative" and FOV values are placeholder estimates requiring review.*

---

## Short-Range Sensor Requirements

| Parameter | Value | Type |
|-----------|-------|------|
| Min Range | 1 m | Minimum |
| Max Range | 20 m | Maximum |
| Obstacle Size | 1 m² | Minimum |
| Obstacle Height | 2 m | Minimum |
| Range Resolution | 5 cm | Minimum |
| Field of View (Az, El) | 60°, 20° | Minimum (TBR) |
| Update Rate | 20 Hz | Minimum |
| Detection Rate | 99% | Minimum |

---

## Products & Capabilities Described

### Single Cameras (Visible Light)

**Characteristics:**
- Small, light, low power consumption
- Require substantial processing for obstacle detection
- Performance highly dependent on visual diversity and lighting conditions

**Performance by Mission Type:**
- **Good performance**: Canopy sampling, mountain sampling, farm sampling (clear weather, good visual diversity), safe landing/takeoff with visual diversity
- **Poor performance**: Arctic/oceanic missions (lack visual diversity), volcanic plumes, fog, heavy rain, snow, icing, water on lens

**Obstacle Performance:**
- Large obstacles (structures, boulders, ridges, wind turbines): easily identified
- Vegetation/trees: detectable in multi-image depth maps
- **Challenge**: Small/thin structures (power lines)

**Processing Requirements:**
- Very high-density processing needed for depth maps and visual odometry
- Image data up to 50 Hz requires USB 3.0, GigE, or PCIe
- Deep learning: requires GPUs or dedicated accelerators with millions of computations per estimate
- Significant RAM and storage for image buffering

**Example Parts & SWaP-C:**

| Part | Size | Weight | Power | Cost |
|------|------|--------|-------|------|
| Ximea MC124CG-SY | 26×26×33 mm | 38g | 3.25 W | $3,055 |
| LI-USB30-C570X | 26×26×38 mm | 32g | 1.12 W | $699 |
| LI-USB30-M021 | 26×26×38 mm | 22g | 0.85 W | $229 |

**Critical Requirements:**
- **Shutter Type**: Global shutter (prevents motion blur critical for odometry/matching; rolling shutter may have higher pixel density but suffers from blur)
- **Focal Length**: Inversely proportional to FOV and stereo range resolution; directly proportional to disparity resolution
- **Field of View**: Wider FOV shows more obstacles and aids digital stabilization, but maps fixed-size obstacles to fewer pixels (harder detection); narrow FOV requires tighter pointing/stabilization
- **Imager Size**: Affects maximum stereo disparity
- **Pixel Count**: Critical for algorithmic performance; dictates minimum realizable disparity and pixel occupancy of objects; scales processing requirements
- **Color vs. Monochromatic**: Monochromatic produces 1/3 data of color; reduces processing if sufficient for task
- **Dynamic Range**: Determines lighting scenario tolerance
- **Frames Per Second**: Higher rates identify obstacles faster but generate more data

**Target Specs:**
- Global shutter
- 2M pixels minimum
- 4.5 µm maximum pixel size
- 50 dB dynamic range (10 bits)
- 5 Hz minimum frame rate
- Color preferred for deep learning
- 5.5 mm focal length, f/1.8 aperture
- 76°/64.5°/51° FOV (D/H/V)
- Max 26×26×33 mm, 50g, 4W, $1,000

---

### Thermal Cameras

**Characteristics:**
- Produces temperature-based imagery
- Lower resolution and limited performance compared to standard cameras
- Simpler processing than visible light (binning sufficient for many tasks)

**Performance by Mission Type:**
- **Good**: Farm mapping (man-made structure identification), populated areas
- Unlikely suitable for odometry/depth mapping

**Obstacle Performance:**
- Excels at detecting warm objects: power lines, humans, man-made structures, vehicles
- Shows contrast against environmental background

**Processing Requirements:**
- Lower resolution (single channel) produces much smaller images than comparably-priced visible cameras
- Simple binning algorithm produces pixel maps of objects of interest
- Simpler identification algorithms than deep learning networks

**Example Parts & SWaP-C:**

| Part | Size | Weight | Power | Cost |
|------|------|--------|-------|------|
| FLIR Lepton | 12.5×12.5×10 mm | 5g | 0.16 W | $239.95 |
| FLIR Duo | 41×59×29.6 mm | 84g | 3.3 W | $1,000 |
| FLIR Duo Pro R | 85×81.3×68.5 mm | 325g | 10 W | $7,600 |

**Target Specs:**
- 4.8k pixels minimum
- 17 µm maximum pixel size
- 40 dB dynamic range (8 bits)
- 5 Hz minimum frame rate
- 5.5 mm focal length, f/1.8 aperture
- 50°/60° FOV (H/D)
- Max 41×60×30 mm, 50g, 4W, $1,000

---

### Stereo Cameras (Visible Light)

**Characteristics:**
- Two synchronized cameras producing simultaneous depth images via visual disparity
- Many commercial systems available with integrated processing accelerators
- Simplified processing compared to single-camera depth mapping but less design flexibility

**Performance:** Same as single cameras

**SWaP-C:**
Smaller and cheaper than single cameras due to widespread mobile robotics use.

**Example Parts & SWaP-C:**

| Part | Size | Weight | Power | Cost |
|------|------|--------|-------|------|
| RealSense D435 | 90×25×25 mm | 72g | 3.5 W | $179 |
| ZED-M | 175×30×30 mm | 159g | 2 W | $449 |
| ZED | 124.5×30.5×26.5 mm | 63g | 2 W | $449 |

**Target Specs:**
- 10 m minimum range
- 10 Hz minimum update rate
- 1280×720 minimum pixels
- 80°×50° FOV (H×V)
- Max 200×40×40 mm, 160g, 4W, $500

**Processing:** Similar to single cameras with baseline requirement for stereo matching

---

### Structured Light Cameras

**Characteristics:**
- Similar to stereo cameras but include active structured light component
- Struggle in bright lighting and inclement weather

**Performance:** Same as single/stereo cameras

**Processing:** Same as stereo cameras

**Example Parts & SWaP-C:**

| Part | Size | Weight | Power | Cost |
|------|------|--------|-------|------|
| RealSense D435 | 90×25×25 mm | 72g | 3.5 W | $179 |

**Target Specs:** Same as stereo cameras

---

### 1D Lasers (Single Point Range Sensors)

**Characteristics:**
- Very accurate, rapid range measurements to fixed points
- Narrow beamwidth leaves large unmapped regions
- Multiple lasers can build sparse point clouds when corrected with IMU

**Performance by Mission Type:**
- **Excellent**: Areas without significant vegetation, farm sampling, mountain sampling, landing/takeoff
- **Challenging**: Canopy sampling (varied range response), arctic/oceanic sampling (snow/water reflectivity dependent), volcanic plumes
- **Weather-independent** (mostly)

**Obstacle Performance:**
- **Excellent**: Solid large obstacles (structures, utility poles, wind turbines, vehicles, boulders, ridge lines)
- **Challenging**: Foliage, dense vegetation, power lines (due to narrow beam width)

**Processing Requirements:**
- Minimal processing (single range measurements)
- Array systems or temporal filtering may require light estimation

**Example Parts & SWaP-C:**

| Part | Size | Weight | Power | Cost |
|------|------|--------|-------|------|
| LightWare LW20/C | 20×30×35 mm | 20g | 0.55 W | $370 |

**Target Specs:**
- 100 m minimum range
- 20 Hz minimum update rate
- 0.2° maximum beamwidth
- Max 20×30×35 mm, 20g, 1W, $400

---

### Lidar (Scanning Laser Rangefinder)

**Characteristics:**
- Single or multi-channel scanning laser producing point clouds
- Works well across most mission scenarios
- Larger, heavier, more expensive than single lasers

**Performance by Mission Type:**
- **Excellent**: All missions except potentially arctic/oceanic (surface reflection), volcanic plumes

**Obstacle Performance:**
- **Excellent**: All obstacle types
- Better than single lasers in canopies (point cloud catches minimum distances across canopy)
- **Excellent**: Power line detection

**Processing Requirements:**
- Point cloud filtering/clustering
- More significant data generation than single lasers
- Requires larger RAM and storage
- Does not require pixel matching or deep learning

**Example Parts & SWaP-C:**

| Part | Size (D/H) | Weight | Power | Cost |
|------|-----------|--------|-------|------|
| Velodyne PUCK VLP-16 | 103/72 mm | 830g | 8 W | $4,000 |
| LightWare SF40/C | 79/91 mm | 270g | 30 W | $1,000 |

**Target Specs:**
- 100 m minimum range
- 5 Hz minimum update rate
- 180° minimum horizontal FOV
- ±10° minimum vertical FOV
- Max 20×30×35 mm, 450g (ideally 225g), 10W typical, $5,000
- Weight is significantly over budget requirement

---

### Radar (Electronically Scanning)

**Characteristics:**
- Rapid volumetric scanning capability
- Works in all weather, day/night
- Can be coarse for fine obstacle avoidance
- May struggle with low-RCS targets and wind turbines (Doppler effects)

**Performance by Mission Type:**
- **Excellent**: All scenarios

**Obstacle Performance:**
- **Excellent**: Large RCS targets at great range
- **Challenging**: Small RCS obstacles (tree branches,# NightFOX SERTC Test Flight After Action Report

## Document Metadata
- Type: Situation Report / After Action Report
- Client/Agency: NOAA ESRL CSD (Earth System Research Laboratory, Chemical Sciences Division)
- Program/Solicitation: NOAA FIREX (Fire and Smoke Study) / NightFOX (Nighttime Fire Observations)
- Date: November 15, 2018 (report date); Test flight: November 8, 2018
- BST Products/Systems Referenced: S2 UAS
- Key Personnel: Ru-Shan Gao (NOAA), Troy Thornberry (NOAA), CU IRISS team (pilots)

## Executive Summary
A test flight of the S2 UAS with remote sensing payload was conducted on November 8, 2018, at SERTC facility in Pueblo, CO, to evaluate nighttime fire observation capabilities for the NightFOX project. While the mission was unable to observe the planned fire due to battery performance issues in cold weather conditions, the flight successfully demonstrated FAA-approved nighttime operations at 2000 ft AGL and validated the S2's lighting systems for night operations.

## Technical Approach
- Integration of remote sensing payload (infrared imaging system for fire detection) onto the S2 UAS
- Nighttime flight operations under FAA Certificate of Authorization (COA) with waiver approval
- Test flight planned at controlled burn site with wooden pallet and hay bale constructed fire
- Maximum authorized altitude: 2000 ft above ground level (still within line of sight)
- Flight conducted in severe cold weather conditions (near 20°F ambient temperature)

## Products & Capabilities Described

### S2 UAS
- Multi-rotor UAS platform modified with lighting systems for nighttime operations
- Capable of carrying remote sensing payloads
- Designed for UAS operations with in situ and remote sensing instruments
- Lighting system described as "clearly visible" and satisfactory for field operations
- Demonstrated ability to reach 2000 ft altitude with operational payload
- Right wing sustained minor damage from frost-related landing (remained flyable)

### Remote Sensing Payload
- Infrared imaging capability for fire/smoke detection
- Integration onto S2 successful based on prior Boulder test flights
- Objective: observe fire temperature and characteristics at night

### In Situ Payload
- Smoke plume sampling capability
- Not deployed in this test; planned for future laboratory fire sampling

## Use Cases & Applications
- Nighttime fire observation and monitoring (NightFOX program)
- Fire and smoke characterization during FIREX-AQ operations (planned for summer)
- Arctic operations and future NOAA ARL deployments

## Key Results

### Successes:
1. **FAA Authorization**: Obtained FAA COA for nighttime operations to 2000 ft AGL with support from Denver Approach
2. **Nighttime Flight Demonstrated**: Successfully conducted nighttime takeoff and landing with S2
3. **Lighting Validation**: S2 lighting systems proved adequate for nighttime operations visibility
4. **Maximum Altitude Achievement**: Reached authorized 2000 ft altitude with operating instrument payload
5. **Institutional Relationship**: Established working relationship with SERTC; future test opportunities planned for April

### Failures/Limitations:
- Fire observation not achieved due to operational constraints
- Smoke plume sampling not conducted
- UAS battery severely degraded by cold temperature (20°F), dropping from full charge to 70% during short flight
- Frost accumulation on aircraft during flight created icing hazard (pitco tube risk)
- Landing skid distance increased due to grass frost, resulting in minor wing damage
- Cancelled further flights due to icing conditions

## Notable Details

**Environmental Challenges:**
- Unexpected low temperatures (near 20°F) with unusually high relative humidity
- Frost formation on grass and aircraft wings during flight
- Brush at facility too damp for self-propagating fire; artificial fire constructed instead

**Operational Constraints:**
- Limited testing window due to: FAA COA/waiver processing time, CU IRISS crew duty time limits, site access legal negotiations, NOAA purchase order processing
- Crew duty time limit caused late afternoon arrival, reducing available test window

**Lessons Learned:**
1. Lighting systems critical for nighttime takeoff and landing safety
2. Adequate crew staffing necessary for desired operational tempo
3. Cold weather battery performance severely compromised; needs further investigation for operational limitation determination (noted as non-issue for FIREX-AQ in August, but important for future projects)

**Future Plans:**
- Advance instruments/payloads from prototype to operational status
- Laboratory fire sampling for in situ payload validation
- Proceed with FIREX-AQ deployment planned for summer operations# Service Agreement - Purchasing Website

## Document Metadata
- Type: Final Report (SF 298 - Report Documentation Page)
- Client/Agency: NASA / Shared Services Center (Stennis Space Center)
- Program/Solicitation: SBIR 2022-1-1118; Contract: 80NSSC22CA192
- Date: 07-08-2024 (Final Report submitted)
- Coverage Period: 08/09/2024 to 08/07/2024
- BST Products/Systems Referenced: Small UAS (uncrewed aircraft systems)
- Key Personnel: Jack Elston, Maciej Stachura, Josh Fromm (all 720-638-9656)

## Executive Summary
This final report documents Black Swift Technologies' SBIR Phase II-e work on developing a ruggedized UAS for scientific data gathering in harsh environments. The project focused on addressing limitations in atmospheric data collection for volcanic ash monitoring and other hazardous atmospheric phenomena by enabling small UAS to operate autonomously in difficult conditions without requiring extensive manual intervention and specialized expertise.

## Technical Approach
BST's approach centered on automating mission planning and flight management for small UAS operations in challenging atmospheric environments:

- **Autonomous Operations Focus**: Development of systems to conduct missions automatically in all-weather conditions, reducing reliance on highly trained teams and months of preparation
- **Real-Time Adaptive Management**: Implementation of software suite capabilities that can automatically observe wind conditions and adjust flight parameters to ensure adequate battery margin for safe return
- **Mission Planning Automation**: Reduction of manual flight planning burden that previously required months of preparation to account for communication constraints and rugged terrain navigation
- **Routine Capability**: Enabling the same level of operational capability that was demonstrated in Phase II-e to be performed repeatedly and globally without specialized expertise

## Products & Capabilities Described

### Small UAS Platform
- **Demonstrated Capability**: Previously achieved the only visual observations of target volcano during a calendar year during Phase II-e testing
- **Proposed Enhancement**: Automation of mission planning, wind observation, and adaptive flight management
- **Operational Constraint**: Prior missions required very knowledgeable and well-trained teams; proposed solution aims to democratize this capability

## Use Cases & Applications

### Primary Use Case: Volcanic Ash Monitoring
- Data collection for volcanic ash aviation hazards assessment
- In situ atmospheric measurements (wind, temperature) near volcanoes where ground stations are distant or at different elevations
- Validation data for atmospheric dispersion models used in volcanic hazard warnings

### Broader Applications
- Pollution alerts and toxic release response
- Dust storm monitoring
- Wildfire smoke hazard assessment
- General atmospheric model validation in remote/hazardous locations

## Problem Statement & Context
The document emphasizes critical safety implications:
- Existing atmospheric models (weather, dispersion) that inform public safety warnings rely on limited data sources
- Ground systems, crewed aircraft, balloons, and dropsondes have operational limitations
- Satellite data (ASTER, MODIS, AIRS, OMI) suffers from infrequent coverage, cloud masking, poor resolution, and validation gaps
- UAS theoretically can access airspaces too difficult or hazardous for crewed aircraft, but lack of all-weather autonomous capability prevents routine deployment

## Notable Details
- **Phase II-e Achievement**: Demonstrated the only visual observations of target volcano during an entire calendar year, proving concept feasibility
- **Operational Challenge Identified**: Despite proof of concept, the requirement for highly specialized teams and months of preparation severely limited practical deployment
- **Safety Case**: A key barrier to UAS adoption is the ability to automatically conduct missions in all weather conditions with appropriate safety margins
- **Geographic Scope**: Project intended to enable worldwide deployment of routine UAS volcanic monitoring missions
- **Distribution**: Report marked with SBIR Rights Notice (Dec 2007)

## Document Metadata
- Type: Final Report (SF 298 - Report Documentation Page)
- Client/Agency: NASA / Shared Services Center (Stennis Space Center, MS)
- Program/Solicitation: NASA SBIR 2022-1-1118
- Contract Number: 80NSSC22CA192
- Date: 07-08-2024 (report date); 08/09/2024 to 08/07/2024 (dates covered)
- Key Personnel: Jack Elston, Maciej Stachura, Josh Fromm (Black Swift Technologies LLC)
- Performing Organization: Black Swift Technologies LLC, Boulder, CO

## Executive Summary
This is a NASA SBIR final report documenting Black Swift Technologies' work on developing a ruggedized uncrewed aircraft system (UAS) for scientific data collection in harsh environments. The work emphasizes the need for automated flight capabilities in difficult conditions to improve atmospheric model validation and safety systems related to volcanic ash aviation hazards, pollution, and other atmospheric phenomena. Previous Phase II-e work demonstrated small UAS capability for volcano monitoring but revealed that autonomous operation in challenging conditions requires significant automation improvements.

## Technical Approach & Problem Statement
The report identifies a critical gap in UAS operational capability: while instrumented UAS can theoretically operate in airspaces too hazardous for crewed aircraft, the lack of autonomous/automatic operation in all weather conditions limits widespread adoption and safety validation. 

Key issues addressed:
- Current atmospheric models rely on limited ground station data, satellite observations (with gaps from cloud masking, infrequent coverage, resolution limits), and occasional in situ measurements
- Previous volcano monitoring missions required months of planning and real-time wind observation data to ensure safe battery margins and navigation
- Routine hazardous-environment missions require significant human expertise and cannot easily scale worldwide

The proposed solution involves automating much of the flight planning and real-time decision-making that previously required expert human operators.

## Products & Capabilities Described
**Small UAS for Scientific Missions**
- Demonstrated capability during Phase II-e volcano monitoring operations
- Achieved "only visual observations of the target volcano during that calendar year" (implying operational success in conditions that prevented other observation methods)
- Ability to operate in airspaces too difficult or hazardous for crewed aircraft
- Can carry instrumentation for atmospheric science measurements

## Use Cases & Applications
- **Volcano monitoring**: Primary demonstrated use case from Phase II-e; collecting data from volcanic regions
- **Atmospheric model validation**: In situ data collection to improve weather and dispersion models
- **Volcanic ash aviation hazards**: Improving warnings and safety systems
- **Pollution alerts and toxic release monitoring**: Supporting air quality and hazard notification systems
- **Dust storms and wildfire smoke hazards**: Data collection for improved forecasting
- **Wind and temperature measurement**: Basic atmospheric profiling in remote/hazardous locations

## Key Results
- Phase II-e successfully demonstrated small UAS for routine data gathering in harsh volcanic environments
- Achieved unique observational capability during a challenging year when other methods could not obtain visual observations
- Revealed critical need for automation: successful missions required:
  - Months of flight planning and preparation
  - Continuous expert monitoring and wind observation during flight
  - Custom software to manage battery margins and safe return planning
  - Highly trained, knowledgeable flight team

## Notable Details
- **SBIR Rights Notice**: Document includes standard SBIR rights notice (Dec 2007)
- **Atmospheric science focus**: Emphasis on improving model accuracy and validation for safety-critical systems
- **Satellite limitations**: Acknowledges that existing satellite systems (ASTER, MODIS, AIRS, OMI) provide valuable data but have significant constraints
- **Subject classification**: SAR 222 (Same as Report for limitation of abstract)
- **Distribution**: SBIR Rights Notice indicates controlled dissemination

The actual technical content, results, and detailed findings from the Phase II-e CCRPP work would be contained in a separate final report document. This form provides the framework and executive summary but not the complete technical narrative.# A3.02-1718 - Uncrewed Aircraft System Data Assimilation for Improved Wildland Fire Fighting Decision Support

## Document Metadata
- Type: SBIR Phase I Final Report
- Client/Agency: NASA (Shared Services Center, Stennis Space Center, MS)
- Program/Solicitation: NASA SBIR Phase I; Topic A3.02-1718
- Date: 02-02-2024 (report date); Period covered 07/25/2022 to 01/25/2023
- BST Products/Systems Referenced: UAS (uncrewed aircraft system) for atmospheric observation and data collection
- Key Personnel: Jack Elston, Maciej Stachura, Alex Lomis (all BST; phone: 720-638-9656)

## Executive Summary
Black Swift Technologies proposed and executed a pilot study to demonstrate the value of collecting UAS observations near active wildland fires and assimilating that data to improve low-level wind and turbulence forecasting. The work addressed a critical safety gap exposed by a fatal 2021 nighttime air tanker crash potentially caused by low-level turbulence, with the goal of enabling safer and more efficient wildland firefighting operations, including expansion to nighttime operations.

## Technical Approach
- **Observation Collection**: BST would deploy UAS to collect targeted atmospheric observations near wildland fires in complex terrain
- **Data Assimilation**: Partnership with NCAR/RAL to perform data quality assessments and assimilation experiments using an Ensemble Kalman Filter approach specifically tailored to assimilate UAS observations
- **Outcome Metrics**: Quantify improvements in accuracy of low-level winds and turbulence representation; determine critical wind/turbulence criteria required for safe operation of crewed and uncrewed aerial firefighting assets

## Products & Capabilities Described
**Black Swift Technologies UAS**
- Purpose: Collecting low-level atmospheric observations (wind, turbulence) in extreme fire environments
- Application Context: Near active wildland fires in complex terrain where traditional sensors unavailable
- Performance Goal: Provide accurate estimates of current low-level wind field and evolution over 3-12 hour windows

## Use Cases & Applications
- **Wildland Firefighting Operations**: Improved decision support for air tanker operations (both crewed and uncrewed)
- **Nighttime Operations**: Enabling safer nighttime aerial firefighting by providing real-time wind/turbulence data
- **Complex Terrain**: Areas where terrain-induced low-level turbulence poses hazards to conventional firefighting aircraft
- **Extreme Environments**: Operations in high-temperature, smoke-laden, turbulent conditions near active fires

## Partnerships & Collaborations
- **NCAR/RAL (National Center for Atmospheric Research / Research Applications Laboratory)**: Data assimilation and ensemble Kalman filtering expertise
- **Colorado Center of Excellence (CoE) for Advanced Technology Aerial Firefighting**: Coordination of field operations and permissions to collect data near active fires

## Notable Details
- **Triggering Event**: Fatal 2021 air tanker crash during nighttime operations, attributed potentially to strong low-level turbulence—established critical need
- **Safety Focus**: Project explicitly aims to improve safety of mixed (crewed and uncrewed) flight operations in extreme conditions
- **Data Assimilation Innovation**: Ensemble Kalman Filter approach tailored specifically for UAS observations (non-standard for this application)
- **Operational Envelope Expansion**: Goal to extend wildland firefighting operations to nighttime with improved situational awareness
- **Subject Terms**: Wildfire, Extreme Environments, UAS, Earth Science, Wind, Turbulence# SF 298 Form - AFWERX SBIR Phase I Soil Moisture Mapping

## Executive Summary
This document is a template and instruction guide for completing the Standard Form 298 (SF-298), the Report Documentation Page required by the Department of Defense. It provides definitions and guidance for all 19 data fields on the form, which is used to standardize the documentation and metadata for technical reports, research, and project deliverables submitted to government agencies.

## Document Purpose
The SF-298 is a mandatory administrative form used by DoD and other federal agencies to collect standardized metadata about technical reports. The form establishes uniform documentation practices across government-sponsored research and development projects.

## Form Fields & Instructions

1. **Report Date** - Full publication date (DD-MM-YYYY format, Year 2000 compliant)
2. **Report Type** - Category (final, technical, interim, progress, quarterly, etc.)
3. **Dates Covered** - Time period during which work was performed
4. **Title and Subtitle** - Full report title with volume/part numbers if applicable
5. **Identification Numbers** - Contract, grant, program element, project, task, and work unit numbers
6. **Author(s)** - Names of persons responsible for writing/research (format: Last, First, Middle Initial)
7. **Performing Organization** - Name and address of the organization conducting the work
8. **Performing Organization Report Number** - Unique alphanumeric identifier assigned by performing organization
9. **Sponsoring/Monitoring Agency** - Name and address of financially responsible organization
10. **Sponsor/Monitor Acronym(s)** - Agency abbreviations (e.g., BRL, ARDEC, NADC)
11. **Sponsor/Monitor Report Number(s)** - Report identifier assigned by sponsoring agency
12. **Distribution/Availability Statement** - Public availability or distribution restrictions (RD/FRD, PROPIN, ITAR, copyright info)
13. **Supplementary Notes** - Additional information (cooperative arrangements, translations, superseded editions)
14. **Abstract** - Brief factual summary (approximately 200 words) of significant information
15. **Subject Terms** - Keywords or phrases identifying major concepts
16. **Security Classification** - Classification level (U, C, S, etc.) for report, abstract, and page
17. **Limitation of Abstract** - Distribution limitation code (UU = Unclassified Unlimited; SAR = Same as Report)
18. **Number of Pages** - Total page count
19. **Responsible Person Contact** - Name and telephone number of point of contact

## Notable Details
- Public reporting burden estimated at 1 hour per form completion
- Document emphasizes Year 2000 compliance for date fields
- Form prescribed by ANSI Standard Z39.18
- Instructions note that respondents cannot be penalized for non-compliance with collection requirements that lack a valid OMB control number
- Template appears to be part of BST's NASA Autonomy project documentation procedures (based on file location)

## Assessment
This is an administrative reference document with no substantive technical content about BST products, capabilities, or projects. It serves as a procedural guide for completing mandatory federal documentation forms.# SF-298 Template Instructions Document

## Executive Summary
BST proposes the S3, a Group 2 tactical UAS designed for low-altitude persistent monitoring through solar-powered extended endurance (4-6 hours per flight), automated machine vision landing, and terrain-aware flight planning. The system enables month-long automatic monitoring campaigns without extensive pre-planning.

## Technical Approach
The S3 employs several integrated capabilities:
- **Solar power system**: Solar panels integrated on wings for extended flight endurance (4-6 hours per flight)
- **Ground recharging**: Between-flight recharging capability enabling month-long continuous campaigns
- **Automated landing**: Machine vision-based autonomous landing system eliminates need for pre-planned landing zones
- **Terrain-aware flight planning**: On-board elevation models allow low-altitude flight in rugged terrain with terrain-following capability
- **Wind-aware flight planning**: Active wind condition assessment to avoid infeasible flight paths and perform energy harvesting to extend endurance
- **Environmental hardening**: Ingress protection rated for extended temperature range (-40°F to +120°F)

## Products & Capabilities Described

**S3 (Tactical UAS)**
- Classification: Group 2 tactical unmanned aircraft system
- Primary capability: Low-altitude persistent monitoring
- Key features:
  - 4-6 hour endurance per flight with solar power
  - Autonomous machine vision landing
  - Terrain-aware and wind-aware flight planning
  - Rugged environmental protection (-40°F to +120°F operational range)
  - Capable of month-long automated monitoring campaigns

## Use Cases & Applications
- Persistent area monitoring
- Low-altitude surveillance missions
- Long-duration tactical operations in rugged terrain
- Automated monitoring campaigns requiring minimal human intervention

## Notable Details
- The S3 represents a new category of long-term UAS deployment by combining solar endurance with autonomous operations
- Emphasis on reducing operational complexity through automation (no need to pre-plan landing areas beyond identifying general monitoring regions)
- Designed for harsh environmental conditions (wide temperature range)

- Type: Technical datasheet / component specification
- Client/Agency: Internal BST reference (NASA SBIR context)

## Executive Summary
Technical datasheet for Silicon Microstructures SM9541 pressure sensor series, detailing I2C communication protocols, pin configurations, and product specifications. Document appears to be supporting material for a volcano monitoring application under NASA SBIR Phase I.

## Technical Approach
The document specifies I2C slave communication protocols for a pressure measurement device:
- **Measurement Request (IbC6Read_MR6)**: Slave initiates measurement and DSP calculation cycle
- **Data Fetch Options**:
  - **DF4 (4 bytes)**: Pressure data only
  - **DF8 (8 bytes)**: Pressure data + temperature high byte [hF:8]
  - **DF7 (7 bytes)**: Pressure data + full temperature bytes [hF:8] and [b:F]

All protocols follow standard I2C start/stop conditions with slave addressing [9:F], read/write bit control, ACK/NACK handshakes.

## Products & Capabilities Described

**SM9541 Pressure Sensor Series**
- **Configuration**: Modular product family with designation: SM 9541 [Rated Pressure] [Port Configuration] [Supply Voltage] [Shipping Configuration]
- **Port Configuration**: 
  - C = Vertical Port
  - S = Single-Ended (Dual Ported Gauge)
  - D = Differential
- **Supply Voltage**: 3.3V or 5.0V options
- **Pressure Units**: cmH2O (C), mBar (M), kPa (K), or PSI (default)
- **Shipping Options**: Sticks/Tubes (S) or Tape & Reel (T)
- **Interface**: I2C digital communication
- **Lot Number Format**: 95-00X with tolerance 0.20 +/- 0.10
- **Capacitive Coupling**: 0.1 µF capacitor required in close proximity
- **Pull-up Resistors**: 4.7 kΩ recommended for I2C lines

## Use Cases & Applications
Pressure measurement for volcano monitoring application (implied from file location in NASA SBIR volcano program folder).

## Notable Details
- Silicon Microstructures OEM component integrated into BST system
- Dual communication protocol options allow flexibility in data retrieval (pressure only vs. pressure + temperature)
- Decoupling capacitor and pull-up resistor requirements specified for proper I2C bus operation
- Document references "Silicon Microstructures Warranty and Disclaimer" (text cut off)

## Document Metadata

- **Client/Agency:** U.S. Air Force

- **Key Personnel:** Dr. Jack Elston (Principal Investigator, Founder and CEO)

## Executive Summary
Black Swift Technologies proposes to modify its existing Soil Moisture Mapping (SMM) UAS—developed in partnership with NASA for precision agriculture and scientific research—for Air Force applications. The system uses a high-resolution L-band radiometer to provide soil moisture maps at 15-meter spatial resolution down to ~10 cm depth. Phase I would establish specific Air Force customer needs, develop integration plans with Air Force weather models (particularly WRF), and document required modifications for deployment to support trafficability forecasts and runway operations.

## Technical Approach

**System Overview:**
- L-band radiometer mounted on BST's S2 UAS platform
- Provides local soil moisture measurements at 15-meter spatial resolution to ~10 cm depth
- Currently developed under NASA SBIR contract in collaboration with University of Colorado's Center for Environmental Technology (CET)
- System has been flight-tested at NASA SMAP calibration sites and commercial agriculture research farms with validation against in situ sensors

**Phase I Strategy:**
1. **Kickoff Meeting:** Establish contacts and map strategy with Air Force technical monitor
2. **Preliminary Integration Plan:** Collaborate with NOAA experts (Mimi Hughes, Rob Cifelli, Kelly Mahoney) and Professor Dev Niyogi (Purdue) to develop detailed WRF model integration plan
3. **Customer Discovery:** Reach out to 3 DoD end users to identify specific needs, focusing on Air Force forecast models and trafficability applications
4. **Requirements Documentation:** Document DoD user requirements and identify necessary instrument, CONOPS, and data structure modifications
5. **Integration Study:** Conduct detailed technical analysis to answer key questions about required resolution, accuracy, area coverage, data frequency, and format/interface requirements for seamless Air Force system integration
6. **Final Report:** Deliver comprehensive documentation for Phase II transition

**Key Research Questions to Address:**
- What resolution, accuracy, and area coverage is needed for meaningful WRF model contribution?
- What frequency and spatial coverage are required for sufficient Air Force user value?
- What are specific interfacing and format requirements for integration with existing Air Force systems?

## Products & Capabilities Described

### Soil Moisture Mapping (SMM) UAS
- **What it is:** Small unmanned aircraft system equipped with high-resolution L-band radiometer
- **Specifications:** 
  - 15-meter spatial resolution
  - ~10 cm soil moisture measurement depth
  - Lightweight airborne platform
  - On-demand, local measurement capability
- **Current Applications:** Precision agriculture, hydrological scientific studies, weather research
- **Proposed Air Force Applications:**
  - Integration into Air Force weather modeling (WRF)
  - Aircraft operations on unimproved runways (soil integrity assessment)
  - Army trafficability support
  - Battlefield environment characterization

### S2 UAS
- Airframe platform carrying the L-band radiometer payload
- Avionics developed by Dr. Elston with EMI reduction for measurement quality
- Interfaces with multiple sensors for soil moisture determination
- Flight control enabling safe near-ground operations
- Pilot-in-command operations demonstrated

## Use Cases & Applications

**Air Force:**
- Support for Air Force weather forecasts and climate analysis
- Aircraft operations on unimproved runways—soil integrity assessment for landing safety
- Integration with 557th Weather Wing (primary target customer)
- Support for both Air Force and Army weather requirements

**Army:**
- Trafficability forecasting (identified as top Army priority)
- Augmentation of existing Air Force weather data products

**Longer-term/Dual-use Applications:**
- Persistent theater soil moisture imagery via high altitude platform adaptation
- FEMA flash flood prediction (demonstrated in 2007 with older instrument version in North Texas/Oklahoma)
- Precision agriculture commercialization

**Competitive Advantage vs. Alternatives:**
- **vs. In situ probes:** Point-only measurements requiring considerable redeployment effort
- **vs. Satellites (SMAP):** Provides much higher spatial resolution (~15m vs. satellite coarse resolution) and on-demand capability vs. fixed satellite measurement cycles

## Executive Summary
Black Swift Technologies offers an integrated soil moisture mapping sUAS combining a passive L-band microwave radiometer with their SwiftCore avionics system to provide volumetric soil moisture measurements at 15m resolution and 5-20cm depth. The hand-launched system covers 1-2 km² per hour and is available as a turnkey solution with existing FAA and NASA approvals for U.S. operations.

## Technical Approach
The system integrates a calibrated passive L-band microwave radiometer sensor with:
- Precision GPS (10 Hz, raw measurements, <1m accuracy)
- High-rate IMU (100 Hz attitude updates, 9 DOF, 1 kHz sampling)
- Differential and static pressure sensing
- NDVI sensor (near-infrared and red wavelength, nadir and zenith)
- Thermal imaging (surface temperature)

Flight control via SwiftCore avionics provides real-time telemetry (10 Hz) through tablet/mobile interface (Swift Tab), enabling precision low-altitude operations for accurate soil moisture mapping.

- **L-band Microwave Radiometer**: Passive measurement at 15m resolution from 15m altitude; penetration depth 5-20 cm
- **NDVI Sensor**: Nadir and zenith measurement of near-infrared and red wavelengths

## Document Metadata
- Type: Peer-reviewed scientific journal article
- Publication: Geophysical Research Letters, Vol. 35, L13204
- Date: Published July 10, 2008 (received February 29, 2008; accepted June 2, 2008)
- Instrument/Mission: VIRTIS (Visible and InfraRed Thermal Imaging Spectrometer) on Venus Express (VEX)
- Lead Author: A. Sánchez-Lavega (Universidad del País Vasco, Bilbao, Spain)
- BST Connection: Referenced in 2018 NASA SBIR Phase I Venus proposal materials (Jack Elston added to library)

## Executive Summary
This paper presents the first comprehensive three-dimensional wind measurements of Venus's cloud layers using cloud tracking analysis of VIRTIS images from Venus Express, obtained between April 2006 and June 2007. The study maps zonal and meridional wind velocities at three altitude levels within the cloud layers and identifies key wind structure characteristics, including super-rotation at low latitudes, vertical wind shear patterns, poleward meridional circulation consistent with Hadley cell dynamics, and solar tide effects at high latitudes.

## Observational Data & Methodology

### Instrument & Orbital Parameters
- **Venus Express**: Highly elliptical polar orbit (apocenter 60,000 km over South Pole; pericenter 250 km over North Pole); 24-hour orbital period
- **VIRTIS Observations**: April 2006–June 2007
- **Cloud Tracking Method**: Identified cloud features across 20–74 minute image pairs
- **Total Cloud Elements Tracked**: 625 at 380 nm; 662 at 980 nm; 932 at 1.74 μm

### Three-Altitude Measurement Levels
1. **Upper Cloud (Dayside, 380 nm UV)**: 62–70 km altitude (~66 km nominal)
2. **Upper Cloud Base (Dayside, 980 nm near-infrared)**: 58–64 km altitude (~61 km nominal)
3. **Lower Cloud (Nightside, 1.74–2.3 μm infrared)**: 44–48 km altitude (~47 km nominal)

### Measurement Uncertainty
- Polar and mid-latitudes (30°S–90°S): ±4–12 m/s systematic uncertainty per tracked feature
- Equatorial latitudes (30°S–0°): ±13–20 m/s systematic uncertainty
- Mean RMS scatter: ±9 m/s for meridional velocity measurements
- Error bars in figures: ±10 m/s (standard deviation within each 2° latitude bin)

## Key Findings

### Zonal Winds (Westward Super-Rotation)

**Low Latitudes (0°–55°S):**
- Nearly constant with latitude
- Upper cloud (66 km): mean velocity ⟨u⟩ = 102 ± 10 m/s
- Upper cloud base (61 km): ⟨u⟩ = 62 ± 10 m/s (showing possible temporal variation; earlier April 2006 showed ~75 m/s closer to Galileo measurements)
- Lower cloud (47 km): ⟨u⟩ = 60 ± 10 m/s

**High Latitudes (55°S–90°S):**
- Wind speeds decrease linearly toward pole
- Drop to zero velocity at pole
- Meridional shear: ∂⟨u⟩/∂y = 0.026 m/s per km (upper cloud), 0.021 m/s per km (lower cloud)
- Indicates vertically coherent vortex structure with minimal vertical wind shear (∂⟨u⟩/∂z ~ 2 m/s per km or lower)

### Vertical Wind Shear
- **Equatorial/mid-latitudes (0°–55°S)**: ∂⟨u⟩/∂z = 8 ± 2 m/s per km between 61 and 66 km; <1 m/s per km between 47 and 61 km
- **Subpolar latitudes (50°S–60°S to pole)**: ∂⟨u⟩/∂z ≤ 2 m/s per km (weak or no shear)

### Meridional Winds (Poleward Motion)
- **Upper cloud (66 km)**: Increases from 0 m/s at equator to ~10 m/s peak at 55°S, then decreases to 0 m/s poleward
  - Interpreted as upper branch of Hadley circulation
  - Peak speed and rapid decrease toward pole related to polar vortex structure
- **Upper cloud base (61 km) and lower cloud (47 km)**: Mean values <5 m/s with no conclusive latitudinal trend due to measurement uncertainty

### Solar Tide Effect
- **Detection**: Present at high latitudes (50°S–75°S) in zonal wind at upper cloud level (66 km)
- **Magnitude**: ~2.5 ± 0.5 m/s/hr wind speed increase from morning (9 hr local time) to afternoon (15 hr)
- **Wave amplitude**: ~10 m/s
- **Altitude Confinement**: Confined to near cloud tops; not detected at 61 km level or on nightside at 47 km
- **Latitude Distribution**: Stronger at high latitudes than at equator (differs from some previous reports)

## Consistency with Previous Missions

The study compares results with:
- **Pioneer Venus** (1979–1985, 1990): Cloud tracking and in situ entry probe data
- **Galileo** (1990 Flyby): Cloud tracking northern hemisphere and equatorial measurements
- **Vega Balloons**: Middle-cloud drift measurements
- **Mariner 10**: Flyby cloud tracking

Finding: VIRTIS zonal wind profiles (2006–07) are broadly consistent with measurements from 1979–85, 1990, and earlier 2006 Galileo comparisons, within measurement uncertainties. Tentative detection of ~10 m/s decrease in mean equatorial speed at 61 km from April 2006 to later observations requires confirmation.

## Structural Conclusions

1. **Latitudinal Transition at ~55°S**: Sharp change in wind circulation character
   - Equatorward: Nearly constant zonal winds with strong vertical shear
   - Poleward: Linear decrease to pole with minimal vertical shear and vertically coherent vortex structure

2. **Polar Dipole Feature**: Vortex structure extends to poles forming dipolar feature observed at cloud tops

3. **Hadley Cell Dynamics**: Meridional wind pattern at upper cloud level consistent with upper branch of Hadley circulation; lower return branch not clearly detected at lower cloud level (may be below measurement sensitivity or weaker than 5 m/s)

## Notable Technical Details

- **Spatial Resolution**: Variable 15–105 km/pixel due to orbital characteristics and instrument constraints
- **Image Processing**: Defect correction, contrast enhancement, navigation, cylindrical and polar map projections
- **Homogeneous Dataset**: First study using same instrument with consistent methodology to retrieve winds at three wavelengths/altitudes
- **Temporal Coverage**: 14-month span allowed identification of both mean wind structure and temporal variability

## Relevance to Black Swift

This paper was included in BST's 2018 NASA SBIR Phase I Venus proposal reference materials, indicating its relevance to BST's proposed Venus atmospheric science mission. The three-dimensional wind mapping and cloud-tracking methodology documented here establishes baseline atmospheric characterization for Venus that would inform aerial platform operations and sensor design for BST systems proposed for Venus science missions.# SOCOM RFI Notes Jul24

## Executive Summary
Black Swift Technologies proposed its S2 fixed-wing and S3 VTOL uncrewed aerial systems to USSOCOM's LR/LE UAS Event, demonstrating compliance with most basic threshold requirements and many desired traits for Special Operations Forces missions. BST positioned its modular, open-systems platforms built on the SwiftCore FMS as suitable for rapid customization and autonomous operations in contested environments, with clear development pathways for enhanced endurance and GPS-denied navigation capabilities.

## Company Background
BST is a Boulder, CO-based small business founded in 2011, specializing in small unmanned aircraft platforms and technologies. The company has been awarded numerous federal contracts from NASA, DoD, NOAA, and USGS spanning small business, SBIR Phase I-III, and unrestricted awards. Key work areas include extreme environmental monitoring, volcano observation, atmospheric data collection, runway integrity assessments, and wildland firefighting decision support. BST collaborates with industry partners including Creare LLC, Orbital Micro Systems, and Anduril Industries.

**Key Competitive Advantages:**
- Proprietary modular SwiftCore™ FMS (autopilot, ground station, user interface, support electronics)
- Quality guarantee on critical components meeting NDAA and ASDA requirements
- Complete solutions from aircraft design and manufacturing through field operations
- ASDA (American Security Drone Act) compliant systems

## Document Metadata
- Type: SBIR Phase I presentation/overview
- Client/Agency: U.S. Air Force (AFWERX)
- Program/Solicitation: AFWERX SBIR Phase I - Soil Moisture Mapping
- Date: Created/Modified October 23, 2023
- BST Products/Systems Referenced: L-band soil moisture sensor system, UAS-based soil moisture measurement platform
- Key Personnel: Jack Elston (last editor)

## Executive Summary
Black Swift Technologies proposes an L-band based soil moisture mapping approach for rapid airfield evaluation and soil integrity assessment. The system leverages soil moisture measurement as the key variable to determine soil strength (Cone Index), addressing inefficiencies in current manual and localized assessment methods used by the Air Force.

## Technical Approach
- **Core Measurement**: L-band based soil moisture sensing with 5-7cm measurement depth
- **Key Principle**: Soil moisture is the primary unknown variable needed for soil integrity mapping; soil type knowledge is also required
- **Calculation Method**: Cone Index (CI) calculated using formula incorporating:
  - mg = percent moisture content (expressed as weight of soil)
  - a, b = coefficients specified for each USCS (Unified Soil Classification System) type
- **Platform**: UAS-based deployment for automated, efficient coverage vs. manual point measurements

## Products & Capabilities Described
**L-band Soil Moisture Sensor**
- Measurement depth: 5-7 cm
- Technology type: L-band radar
- Application: Rapid, automated soil integrity mapping
- Advantage: Replaces inefficient manual methods and localized point measurements (Dynamic Cone Penetrometer, Rapid Assault Zone Terminal Evaluation Kit)

## Use Cases & Applications
- **Primary (AFWERX focus)**: Airfield evaluation and rapid assessment of landing zones
- **Dual-use applications** (prior NASA SBIR program):
  - Wildfire mitigation (USGS - Jonathan Stock, ongoing)
  - Watershed characterization (NOAA - Gijs DeBoer, ongoing)
  - Sod/turf health monitoring (Turf Scout - Dana Sullivan, ongoing)
  - Phase II-E SBIR and CCRPP development (NASA - Geoffrey Bland, ended 2017)

## Technical Justification
- Related peer-reviewed research demonstrates that L-band soil moisture measurement with soil type knowledge is sufficient for trafficability assessment
- Two cited studies validate the approach:
  - Flores et al. (2013) on hillslope-scale soil moisture data assimilation for military trafficability
  - Carranza et al. (2019) on monitoring field trafficability using Sentinel-1 radar

## Notable Details
- Technology leverages prior NASA SBIR program results, now adapted for Air Force applications
- Replaces both manual approaches (inefficient) and limited automated approaches
- Dual-use technology with established government and commercial partnerships
- Multiple ongoing validation projects across federal agencies (USGS, NOAA) and commercial sector (Turf Scout)# Soil Moisture Concepts of Employment

## Executive Summary
This document outlines Black Swift Technologies' proposed Soil Moisture Measurement (SMM) system for three Air Force operational concepts: unimproved runway integrity assessment, base civil engineering projects, and ground trafficability assessment. The SMM system uses UAS-mounted remote sensing (NDVI, IR thermal, and L-band radiometer) to replace manual cone penetrometer measurements, reducing personnel exposure to threat in contested environments while providing spatially distributed soil integrity mapping.

## Technical Approach

### Sensor Suite
The SMM system comprises three integrated sensors:
- **NDVI (Normalized Difference Vegetation Index)**: Measures health and quantity of vegetation
- **IR Thermal**: Measures ground surface temperature (degrees Celsius)
- **LDCR (Lobe Differencing Correlating Radiometer)**: Measures brightness temperature (L-band energy, degrees Kelvin)

**Processing**: Onboard processing calculates both soil moisture maps and soil integrity maps from sensor data.

**Platform Flexibility**: System can be mounted on multirotor or fixed-wing UAS.

**Technical Basis**: Approach leverages established research showing correlation between soil moisture and soil integrity, and demonstrated capability of space-based and aircraft-mounted radiometers to measure soil moisture remotely.

## Products & Capabilities Described

### Soil Moisture Measurement (SMM) System
- **What it is**: UAS-mounted remote sensing system for real-time soil integrity and soil moisture assessment
- **Key advantage over current method**: Provides spatially distributed measurements across entire runway/route rather than point measurements; reduces personnel exposure to threat
- **Proposed platforms**: Multirotor or fixed-wing UAS
- **Output**: Soil moisture maps and soil integrity maps

## Use Cases & Applications

### 1. Unimproved Runway Integrity Assessment
**Current approach**: Air Force Special Tactics Teams (contested) or Civil Engineering units (uncontested) use cone penetrometer to measure soil integrity at multiple points across prospective runway.
- Drop weight on rod driven 36 inches into ground
- Measure blows per inch, convert to California Bearing Ratio (CBR) or Cone Penetration Index (CPI)
- Takes ~5 minutes per measurement point
- Exact number of measurements required unknown

**Contested scenario**: Team covertly inserted to austere location (e.g., dry lake bed in hostile territory); provides own security during insertion and assessment; reports results via radio/SATCOM after measurement; exfiltrates on first available aircraft.

**Uncontested scenario**: Typically humanitarian relief after natural disaster; performed by civil engineering units with administrative/logistical infrastructure support; results reported via telephone or email.

**Problem addressed**: Current approach time-consuming and exposes servicemembers to enemy threat in contested environments.

**Proposed SMM advantage**: Remote measurement from UAS reduces personnel exposure; provides comprehensive coverage across runway surface rather than point samples.

### 2. Base Civil Engineering Projects
Document outlines this use case but content incomplete/underdeveloped (template structure provided without substantive detail).

### 3. Ground Trafficability Assessment
**Mission**: Assess soil conditions along routes for vehicle convoy transit to prevent vehicles becoming stuck in mud/soft soil/waterlogged areas.

**Current challenges**: Lack of real-time soil stability data forces convoys to take longer alternative routes or use trial-and-error navigation, risking delays, mechanical strain, delays, vulnerability to ambush/exposure.

**Proposed solution**: UAS-mounted SMM system performs on-call measurement of soil integrity along ground routes using fixed-wing unmanned platform; provides soil integrity maps across width and length of prospective route.

**Problem addressed**: Enables predictive terrain assessment before transit; reduces risk of vehicles becoming stuck.

## Key Results
None provided. Document is a prospective concepts paper, not a report of completed work or testing.

## Notable Details

### Current System Limitations
- **Cone penetrometer**: Purely mechanical; low maintenance (corrosion prevention only); no batteries/electronics; but time-consuming and personnel-intensive
- **Point vs. distributed measurement**: Current approach yields only point measurements at discrete locations; exact number required for certification unknown
- **Personnel exposure**: Both contested and uncontested scenarios require personnel on the ground; contested operations expose Special Tactics Teams to enemy threat during insertion, assessment, and exfiltration

### Soil Types and Accuracy Specifications
Document indicates uncertainty in specifications:
- Soil types: "All natural soil types? Not rock?" (unknown whether rock surfaces supported)
- Soil integrity accuracy: "???" (not specified)
- Soil moisture accuracy: Listed in specification tables but values not filled in

### Operational Flexibility
- Works in both contested (covert insertion) and uncontested (humanitarian relief) scenarios
- Applicable to different operational personnel: Air Force Special Tactics Teams vs. Civil Engineering units
- Compatible with existing military communication infrastructure (radio, SATCOM, digital, telephone, email)

### Document Status
Document is incomplete/draft stage. Three major use cases outlined but:
- "Base Civil Engineering Projects" section is template-only (section headers with no content)
- "Ground Trafficability" section has significant placeholder text ("Ipsum lorem...")
- "System Analysis" sections across all use cases are unfilled
- Many specification fields marked unknown or incomplete ("???")

## Document Metadata
- Type: Project overview presentation
- Client/Agency: U.S. Air Force, Air Force Research Laboratory (AFRL)
- Program/Solicitation: AFWERX SBIR Phase II (Topic: Soil Moisture Mapping)
- Date: Created May 28, 2024; Last modified January 28, 2025
- BST Products/Systems Referenced: L-band radiometer, E2 Group 1 Quadrotor UAS
- Key Personnel: Daniel Prendergast (last editor)

## Executive Summary
Black Swift Technologies, in partnership with CU Technology Transfer Company (CET) and Operational Management Services (OMS), is developing a UAS-based L-band radiometer system to map soil integrity via soil moisture measurements for the U.S. Air Force. The system will enable rapid assessment of landing zones for C-130 aircraft operations by computing cone index (a measure of soil strength) from remotely sensed soil moisture data, replacing time-consuming manual field surveys.

## Technical Approach

**Core Technology:**
- L-band radiometer originally developed under NASA SBIR for SMAP (Soil Moisture Active Passive) Cal/Val
- Patented technology penetrates vegetation and measures volumetric soil moisture (VSM) in top soil layer
- Integrated onto E2 Group 1 Quadrotor UAS for high-resolution mapping

**Key Technical Elements:**
- Radiometer modifications for DAF requirements (refined instrument, auxiliary sensors)
- UAS modifications including surface temperature and NDVI (Normalized Difference Vegetation Index) sensors for real-time soil moisture calculation
- Soil Integrity Algorithm: Cone Index (CI) calculated from VSM and soil type using formula: **CI = a + b × mg**, where a and b are coefficients specific to USCS soil types
- Integration of geophysical sensing methods (EMI, CRI, GPR, tTEM) for subsurface characterization
- Survey capability: 1 km² per hour mapping rate

**Performance Specifications:**
- Soil moisture measurement accuracy: within 3% of true volumetric soil moisture
- Validated at test sites with NASA, USGS, and NOAA

## Products & Capabilities Described

**L-Band Radiometer**
- What: Patented remote sensing instrument measuring soil moisture through vegetation
- Use case: Primary sensor for computing soil integrity/cone index on unimproved landing zones
- Development history: Originally developed for NASA SBIR SMAP Cal/Val project; validated across multiple agencies

**E2 Group 1 Quadrotor UAS**
- What: Small unmanned aircraft system developed and validated for soil moisture mapping
- Capabilities: Carries radiometer and auxiliary sensors (thermal, NDVI, DEM generation, orthorectified imagery)
- Operational history: 6 field campaigns (golf courses, high-altitude alpine, grasslands) for NOAA and commercial users
- Use case: Platform for C-130 landing zone assessment; operates in demanding environments

**Soil Moisture-to-Integrity Conversion**
- Converts volumetric soil moisture (VSM) percentage to cone index via empirical relationship
- Leverages soil type database to tailor coefficients

## Use Cases & Applications

**Primary Use Case:**
- Mapping landing areas for C-130 operations on unimproved landing zones
- Rapid airfield evaluation to provide forward air controllers decision-critical data on soil integrity for landing operations

**Operational Context:**
- Replaces inefficient manual approaches (local point measurements with Dynamic Cone Penetrometer) and automated approaches (Rapid Assault Zone Terminal Evaluation Kit)
- Enables "on the move" measurements for global rather than local soil strength characterization
- Intended for field campaigns at locations including Tyndall Air Force Base

## Executive Summary

The Department of Interior seeks multiple IDIQ contracts for on-call Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS) to provide non-emergency resource flight services throughout the contiguous 48 states. Services include survey and mapping, video, LiDAR, thermal operations, and logistical/reconnaissance activities in support of public safety and resource management. Successful offerors must provide fully contractor-operated and maintained fixed-wing or VTOL UAS with dual-sensor (EO/IR) gimbals, certified pilots, maintenance capabilities, and support personnel. Contractors must demonstrate FAA and DOI compliance and be available 14 hours daily for mission operations.

## Technical Approach & Requirements

### UAS Aircraft Requirements (Section B2.1)
- **Platform Type**: Fixed-wing with assisted launch/landing OR VTOL unmanned aircraft system
- **Altitude Capability**: 12,000 feet Density Altitude (DA); 8,500' launch site DA for VTOL at max payload
- **Endurance**: Sufficient fuel/batteries for 16-hour shift duration
- **Wind Performance**: Capable of takeoff/landing in 20-knot winds; sustained operations in 25-knot winds
- **Operations**: Day and night capable with anti-collision lighting visible from ≥3 statute miles
- **Minimum Quantity**: Two (2) UAS required per contractor; three or more may be offered for consideration

### Sensor Requirements (Section B2)
- One stabilized dual sensor (EO/Infrared) gimbal per aircraft
- Capable of capturing still EO and IR images with geo-tagging (latitude/longitude)
- Payload operator must have minimum 25 logged flight hours on offered UAS make/model/GCS

### Command and Control (Section B2.2)
- **Secure Uplink**: Digital data uplink frequency-hopping at 2.4, 5.8, or 900 MHz ISM band or proprietary spectrum with WPA2 or 128/192/256-bit AES encryption (FIPS compliant)
- **Secure Downlink**: Digital data downlink frequency-hopping at 2.4, 5.8, or 900 MHz ISM band or proprietary spectrum with WPA2 or 128/192/256-bit AES encryption (FIPS compliant)
- **Loss of Link Capability**: Autonomous LOL capability to return to designated location and terminate flight
- **Ground Station**: Programmable VHF AM and VHF FM radios (FCC compliant) for communication with incident and aviation resources
- **Compliance**: Operations must comply with DOI, FAA policy, and Executive Order 13981

### Regulatory & Certification Requirements (Section B2.1.1)
- All aircraft and personnel must comply with DOI OPM-11 and 14 CFR Part 107
- UAS pilots must possess FAA remote pilot certificate
- Pilots must be approved by DOI Office of Aviation Services (OAS)
- Aircraft must be FAA airworthy certified (or equivalent DOD/NASA flight release)

### Maintenance & Airworthiness (Section B5-B6)
- All maintenance by manufacturer-authorized personnel
- Routine/preventive maintenance before/after scheduled daily use or as COR-approved
- Contractor must maintain list of field-replaceable components
- Functional maintenance check flights required after installation, overhaul, major repair, or engine/flight control changes
- Immediate notification required for any major component changes or repairs following incidents/accidents

## Products & Capabilities Described

### Aircraft/UAS
- **What**: Contractor-furnished fixed-wing or VTOL UAS with dual EO/IR sensor gimbal, spare parts, certified pilots, and maintainers
- **Operational Use**: Non-emergency resource support missions including survey/mapping, video collection, LiDAR operations, thermal imaging, logistical/reconnaissance activities
- **Performance Specs**: 
  - 12,000 ft DA capability; 16-hour endurance
  - Day/night operations with anti-collision lighting
  - 20-knot takeoff/landing; 25-knot sustained wind operations
  - Secure encrypted C2 links (AES 128/192/256-bit, FIPS compliant)
  - Autonomous loss-of-link return capability

### Support Services
- UAS operation and piloting
- Maintenance and repair
- Personnel (pilots, maintainers, payload operators)
- Service vehicles (reimbursable at FTR rates: Class 1 auto, Class 2-4 trucks at $1.71-$3.14/mile)
- Per diem for multi-day deployments
- Ground support equipment and fuel

### Gimbal/Sensor System
- Stabilized dual-sensor (EO and Infrared) configuration
- Capable of still image capture with geolocation
- Zoom/focus/EO/IR manipulation to "best picture available"
- Make/model to be specified by offeror; subject to government approval

## Use Cases & Applications

1. **Survey and Mapping Operations**: Aerial reconnaissance and data collection for resource assessment
2. **Video Collection**: Tactical situational awareness (day/night operations)
3. **LiDAR Operations**: Terrain and structure analysis
4. **Thermal/Infrared Imaging**: Heat signature detection and monitoring
5. **Logistical and Reconnaissance Activities**: Support for incident management and resource deployment
6. **Public Safety Support**: Coordination with DOI, USFS, and partner agencies
7. **Incident Management**: Potential augmentation of manned aviation fleet for emergency response coordination
8. **Multi-location Deployment**: Coverage across contiguous 48 states with aircraft based at designated locations

## Personnel Requirements

- FAA Part 107 Remote Pilot Certification required
- Minimum 25 logged flight hours on offered UAS make/model and GCS
- Subject to government flight evaluation if deemed necessary
- Must demonstrate proficient operation of all aircraft equipment
- FAA airworthiness action notification required

### Duty & Flight Hour Limitations (Section B11)
- **Daily Duty Limit**: Maximum 14 consecutive duty hours per assigned duty period
- **Rest Requirements**: 
  - Minimum 2 calendar days off-duty within any 14 consecutive calendar days
  - Minimum 8 consecutive hours rest prior to assigned duty period
- **Flight Hour Limits**:
  - Maximum 8 flight hours per pilot per duty period
  - Maximum 42 flight hours in any consecutive 6-day period
  - When 36+ hours flown in 6-day period, pilot gets 1 calendar day off before new cycle

### Personnel Availability
- Contractor must provide 14-hour daily availability for all calendar days as required

## Inspection & Approval Process (Section B13)

### Initial Inspection Timeline
- Scheduled within 30 calendar days of award
- Conducted at designated base, contractor facility, or mutually agreed location
- Monday-Friday, 0730-1630 local time (unless otherwise agreed)

- Verification of compliance with all contract requirements

### Non-Conformance

- Failure to have approved aircraft/pilots may result in exclusion from orders, removal from master listing, or contract termination

## Data Rights & Intellectual Property (Section B17)

- **Government Ownership**: All documents and materials produced are government-owned with exclusive ownership and copyright rights
- **Restriction on Use**: Contractor may not use, sell, or disclose data without written CO permission
- **Data Classification**: All sensor and ground control data acquired is government property and must be stored per government policy
- **Proprietary Data**: Contractor shall not disclose proprietary data bearing restrictive legends except as required for performance or with written CO approval
- **Non-Disclosure**: Contractor personnel cannot divulge or release developed data until made public by government

## Insurance & Liability Requirements (Section B15)

### Public Liability Insurance
- Contractor must procure and maintain aircraft public liability insurance per 14 CFR 298
- Both Contractor and United States of America named as insured parties
- Coverage may be primary and excess policies with combined coverage ≥ combined minimums required
- Insurance policy or company certification must be submitted to CO prior to work commencement

### Damage Responsibility
- Contractor responsible for all damage to public/private property and persons (including third parties and government employees) resulting from contractor fault, negligence, or equipment failure
- Environmental damages: Contractor responsible for cleanup of fuel, oil, chemical contamination from contractor activities;# Sole Source Justification for Ultra Maritime Subcontractor Selection

## Document Metadata

- Phase I Contract Number: N6833525C0492
- Date: 2026-03-23
- BST Products/Systems Referenced: S0-Acoustic (airframe)
- Key Personnel: Paul DeMond (Ultra Maritime); Beck Cotter (BST, last editor)

## Executive Summary
Black Swift Technologies justifies the selection of Ultra Maritime (UM) as sole-source subcontractor for Phase II development of acoustic and Electric-field (E-field) sensor payloads on a Sonobuoy-Launched Unmanned Aerial System (SL UAS). The justification centers on UM's unique, mature sensing technologies and direct integration with BST's Phase I airframe design, making replacement impractical.

## Technical Approach
**Sensor Integration Architecture:**
- BST's S0-Acoustic airframe was custom-engineered around Ultra Maritime's specific sensor architecture during Phase I
- UM defined precise physical dimensions, weight profiles, and electrical interface requirements
- BST designed complex features to accommodate UM's payload: elastically-loaded belly compartment, cable compliance assembly, and gravity-assisted deployment mechanism

**SWaP and Performance Constraints:**
- Development constrained by Navy's stringent Size, Weight, and Power (SWaP) requirements
- Acoustic sensitivity thresholds specified by Navy requirements

## Products & Capabilities Described

### Ultra Maritime Acoustic Sensors
- **Calibrated Omnidirectional (CO) sensor**: Modified version derived from UM's Q53H production sonobuoy
- **Performance improvement**: Self-noise reduction and acoustic performance improvement of 6-8 dB achieved using textured ceramic materials
- **Development precedent**: Technique successfully demonstrated during Digital Vertical Line Array (DVLA) 2.0 sonobuoy development

### Ultra Maritime E-Field Sensing
- **Frequency range**: 0.01 Hz – 5 Hz (low-frequency)
- **Specialized bands**: Extremely Low Frequency Electromagnetic (ELFE) and Ultra Low Frequency (ULF)
- **Navy validation**: Demonstrated under two relevant PMA-264 SBIRs:
  - N091-019: Multi-Modal Sensor for Tactical Marine Surveillance / EA Buoy (UM as large business partner with Information Systems Lab)
  - N192-060: Multi-Sensor Sonobuoy (MSS) (UM as exclusive large business partner)

### Black Swift S0-Acoustic Airframe
- Custom-engineered to integrate UM sensor suite
- Features elastically-loaded belly compartment for payload accommodation
- Cable compliance assembly for sensor integration
- Gravity-assisted deployment mechanism

## Use Cases & Applications
- **Primary Mission**: Sonobuoy-Launched Unmanned Aerial System (SL UAS)
- **Operational Context**: Navy Air Anti-Submarine Warfare Systems (ASW), specifically under Program Executive Officer for Air Anti-Submarine Warfare Systems (PMA-264)
- **Sensing Applications**: Acoustic and electric-field detection for submarine/marine surveillance

## Key Justification Arguments
1. **Specialized Technology Maturity**: UM possesses flight-ready, production-derived acoustic hardware (Q53H/DVLA-derived) and Navy-validated E-field technology
2. **Recent Relevant Performance**: Direct past performance developing identical sensing modalities under PMA-264 program
3. **Design Integration Lock-in**: S0-Acoustic airframe was engineered specifically around UM's sensor specifications; replacing UM would require:
   - Discarding validated Phase I CAD models
   - Complete re-engineering of S0-Acoustic airframe
   - Massive duplication of engineering effort
   - Unacceptable schedule delays to Phase II
4. **Unique Qualification**: No known alternative vendor possesses the combination of flight-ready Q53H/DVLA-derived acoustic hardware, PMA-264 validated E-field technology, and pre-integrated Phase I form factors

## Notable Details
- This is a Phase II effort following successful Phase I development
- The justification emphasizes the validated integration between BST's airframe and UM's sensors as key reason for continued partnership
- Document references specific SBIR contract vehicles and program codes indicating Navy acquisition framework
- The 6-8 dB acoustic performance improvement via textured ceramic materials represents a specific technical innovation
- Frequency range for E-field sensing (0.01-5 Hz) represents low-frequency maritime detection capability critical for ASW operations# Sole Source Justification for Ultra Maritime Subcontractor Selection

## Executive Summary
This document justifies the selection of Ultra Maritime (UM) as the sole-source subcontractor for developing acoustic and Electric-field (E-field) sensor payloads on BST's Phase II Sonobuoy-Launched Unmanned Aerial System (SL UAS) effort. Ultra Maritime is the only known source with the required combination of mature acoustic hardware, Navy-validated E-field technology, and Phase I-integrated form factors necessary to meet Navy Size, Weight, and Power (SWaP) and acoustic sensitivity requirements.

## Technical Approach
The Phase II effort involves integrating specialized sensor payloads into BST's S0-Acoustic airframe. Ultra Maritime provides:

**Acoustic Sensor Architecture:**
- Modified Calibrated Omnidirectional (CO) sensor derived from UM's production Q53H sonobuoy
- Textured ceramic material technology that reduces self-noise and improves acoustic performance by 6-8 dB (proven in Digital Vertical Line Array 2.0 sonobuoy development)

**E-Field Sensing Architecture:**
- Low-frequency E-Field sensing capability (0.01 Hz – 5 Hz)
- Dual-band approach: Extremely Low Frequency Electromagnetic (ELFE) and Ultra Low Frequency (ULF) bands

## Products & Capabilities Described

**S0-Acoustic Airframe:**
- BST's custom-engineered airframe designed specifically around UM's sensor architecture
- Features elastically-loaded belly compartment with cable compliance assembly
- Includes gravity-assisted deployment mechanism
- Integrated during Phase I with validated CAD models and precise physical/electrical specifications

**Ultra Maritime Sensors:**
- **Q53H Sonobuoy:** Production-grade acoustic sensor platform
- **Digital Vertical Line Array (DVLA) 2.0:** Advanced sonobuoy with ceramic-enhanced acoustic performance
- **E-Field Sensors:** PMA-264 validated technology for submarine detection

## Use Cases & Applications
- **Primary Mission:** Air Anti-Submarine Warfare (ASW) operations via sonobuoy-launched UAS
- **Navy Program:** Air Anti-Submarine Warfare Systems Program (PMA-264)
- **Detection Capability:** Submarine detection via acoustic and electromagnetic signatures

## Notable Details

**Unique Qualification Factors:**
- UM has direct, recent past performance on Navy PMA-264 programs
- Successfully demonstrated E-field sensors under two previous SBIR efforts:
  - **N091-019:** Multi-Modal Sensor for Tactical Marine Surveillance / EA Buoy (partner with Information Systems Lab)
  - **N192-060:** Multi-Sensor Sonobuoy / MSS (exclusive large business partner)

**Sole-Source Justification Basis:**
- UM provided precise physical dimensions, weight profiles, and electrical interface requirements used to design the S0-Acoustic airframe's complex mechanical systems
- Airframe is now validated and integrated to UM's specifications
- Switching vendors would require discarding Phase I CAD models and completely re-engineering the S0-Acoustic airframe
- Replacement would cause unacceptable program schedule delays and massive engineering duplication
- UM is "the only known source" possessing the specific combination of flight-ready Q53H/DVLA-derived hardware, PMA-264-validated E-field technology, and pre-integrated Phase I form factors

**Key Performance Requirements Met:**
- Navy's stringent SWaP (Size, Weight, Power) constraints
- Acoustic sensitivity thresholds
- Integration compatibility with existing Phase I design# STTR AFX24.E AMENDMENT 1
