## Document Metadata
- Type: Proposal/Application
- Client/Agency: World Wildlife Fund (WWF)
- Program/Solicitation: WWF Wildlife Crime Technology Project
- Date: Submitted June 2, 2013 (created); last modified January 10, 2017
- BST Products/Systems Referenced: SwiftSentinel, SwiftPilot (autopilot), SwiftStation (ground control station), SwiftTab (user interface tablet)
- Key Personnel: Jack Elston (President/Co-founder, Support Engineer), Oier Penagaricano-Munoa (Project Manager), Raymond Oung (Lead Engineer), Maciej Stachura (Support Engineer/CTO), Coby Leuschke (Training Lead, Rocketship Systems President), Moses Gichanga (Maintenance Lead, ASR CEO), Lian Pin Koh (Advisor/Training Coordinator, Conservation Drones), Serge Wich (Advisor/Training Coordinator, Conservation Drones)

## Executive Summary
Black Swift Technologies proposes the SwiftSentinel small unmanned aerial system (sUAS) as a solution for the WWF Wildlife Crime Technology Project. The company offers either a complete system for purchase or operating the platform as a service, leveraging established partnerships with Autonomous Systems Research in Africa and Conservation Drones in Asia to provide training, maintenance, and operational support for wildlife surveillance and monitoring missions.

## Technical Approach

**Core System Architecture:**
The SwiftSentinel is a fixed-wing sUAS comprising five major components:

1. **Airframe (Nurf)**: 2-meter wingspan fixed-wing aircraft constructed from expanded polypropylene foam (EPP)
   - Designed for durability and rapid setup/teardown (5-10 minutes with two-person crew)
   - 60-minute flight endurance at ~10 km/h wind speeds
   - 72 km maximum range per mission
   - 60-minute battery charging (via car battery or solar panels)
   - Capable of light precipitation and sand operation; designed for potential modification to heavy precipitation, water landings, parachute deployment
   - Operating ceiling: 3,000 meters (10,000 ft) above sea level

2. **Autopilot (SwiftPilot)**: Patent-pending proprietary autopilot system
   - Fully autonomous capability (autonomous take-off, flight, landing)
   - Proven in extreme weather conditions (tornadoes, arctic, storms)
   - Stall recovery capability
   - Optional radio-controlled mode via multiplexer add-on for aggressive maneuvers
   - Integrated removable microSD card for onboard telemetry logging
   - Interchangeable wireless transceiver modules supporting multiple frequency bands and ranges

3. **Payload Options**:
   - Electro-optical (EO) HD wireless imaging/video camera with optional two-axis gimbal
   - Forward-Looking Infrared (FLIR) thermal camera with optional two-axis gimbal for heat signature detection (night/rain/fog/canopy conditions)
   - Optional single-board computer for computationally intensive operations (RF triangulation, target tracking, route optimization)

4. **Ground Control Station (SwiftStation)**:
   - All communication electronics in hard-shell, waterproof case
   - Ruggedized Panasonic Toughpad with Android OS interface (SwiftTab)
   - Car battery or wall outlet powered
   - Mission planning with hardware-in-the-loop simulation capability (X-Plane compatible)
   - Support for 100+ waypoints and multiple flight parameters
   - Real-time flight plan adjustment
   - Multi-format map and geo-referenced data import

**Wireless Transceiver Options:**
| Transceiver Type | Frequency | Max Range |
|---|---|---|
| Digi XBee Pro Series | 868/900 MHz | 40 km |
| Digi XTend | 900 MHz | 64 km |
| Microhard Products | 900 MHz/2.4 GHz/3.4 GHz | 100 km |

## Products & Capabilities Described

### SwiftSentinel sUAS
- **What it is**: A complete small unmanned aerial system specifically developed for wildlife monitoring and surveillance, joint project between BST, Rocketship Systems Inc., and Autonomous Systems Research, partially IEEE-funded
- **Design philosophy**: End-user focused, affordable, easy-to-use for novice operators, physically robust, low maintenance
- **Modular architecture**: Customizable to specific end-user requirements
- **Key capabilities**: 
  - Intuitive Android tablet interface with autonomous flight
  - 5-10 minute operational setup
  - Thermal and electro-optical imaging payloads
  - Mission planning with simulation capability
  - Multiple simultaneous sUAS operation capability
  - Robust autopilot proven in extreme weather

### SwiftPilot Autopilot
- **Suppliers**: InvenSense (IMU), Measurement Specialties (pressure sensor)
- **Specifications**: Patent-pending design; proven in tornadoes, arctic conditions, storms; stall recovery capability
- **Flexibility**: Rapidly integrates various payloads; supports multiple wireless transceiver modules

### SwiftStation Ground Control Station
- Packaged with communication electronics and Panasonic Toughpad tablet
- SwiftTab interface for mission planning and real-time flight control
- Simulation capability and multi-format map support
- Total system weight with case: just over 20 kg

## Use Cases & Applications

- **Wildlife surveillance**: Primary application for IFAW and Kenya Wildlife Service
- **White rhinoceros monitoring**: Currently under evaluation by IFAW and Kenya Wildlife Service in East Africa; successfully completed initial flight tests in Kenya
- **Wildlife crime detection**: Monitoring of illegal human activities (logging, poaching, forest fires)
- **Large animal species surveying**: Mapping and census applications
- **Land use/cover mapping**: Near real-time geo-referenced mapping
- **Illegal forest activity monitoring**: Video and still photography documentation

## Key Results (Project Status)

- SwiftSentinel successfully completed initial field tests in Kenya
- System currently under evaluation for purchase by IFAW and Kenya Wildlife Service
- Meets expectations of both organizations according to proposal
- Established operational partnerships and training networks in Africa (via ASR in Kenya) and Asia (via Conservation Drones in Nepal, Cambodia, Indonesia)

## Notable Details

### Company Background & Expertise
- Black Swift Technologies founded 2011 as spinoff from University of Colorado Boulder's RECUV
- Leadership team: 5 Ph.D. graduates in Aerospace/Electrical Engineering, 1 Ph.D. candidate in business, 1 MBA graduate
- Combined team experience: 1000+ hours UAV flight time, 70+ peer-reviewed publications, 65 FAA Certificates of Authorization
- Extensive operational experience across diverse missions and challenging conditions

### Platform History & Track Record
BST team designed/developed the Tempest sUAS that performed the first-ever sUAS intercept of a tornadic supercell thunderstorm (VORTEX2, 2010); 21 missions in extreme weather

### Partnership Ecosystem
1. **Rocketship Systems Inc.** (USA): Airframe design/manufacturing (Nurf airframe), custom precision components, FlyingFoam division for CNC foam cores
2. **Autonomous Systems Research** (Kenya): African operations, maintenance, logistics hub, training; CEO Moses Gichanga
3. **Conservation Drones** (International): Asian operations, maintenance, logistics, training network; Co-founders Lian Pin Koh and Serge Wich; 10+ countries of operational experience; systems distributed to Jane Goodall Institute, WWF Nepal, Sumatran Orangutan Conservation Programme, WWF Netherlands, Google Inc., Flora and Fauna International, Greenpeace International, RSPB

### Maintenance & Logistics Model
Three-tier distributed model (Organizational/Intermediate/Depot levels) designed to reduce costs, minimize downtime, and build local capacity

**African Model**: Depot-level facility in Nairobi, Kenya (operated by ASR); I-level centers near operational areas; O-level at host organizations

**Asian Model**: Conservation Drones leverages existing network (Sabah/Malaysian Borneo, Sumatra) to establish integration, maintenance, training facilities

### Training Program
- 2-day course deemed sufficient for novice users
- Day 1: Classroom instruction and simulator flight
- Day 2: Practice flights with realistic mission scenarios
- Covers system manuals, documentation, O-level maintenance tasks
- Additional training available upon request
- Ongoing support provided by ASR (Africa) and Conservation Drones (Asia)

### Export Compliance
- Base-level SwiftSentinel not subject to known ITAR or export restrictions (uses COTS and open-source technology)
- Some payloads (thermal FLIR cameras) potentially subject to ITAR; BST will work with export regulation specialist to ensure compliance

### Delivery Options Proposed

**Option 1: Purchase**
- Complete system includes: 2 Nurf airframes with SwiftPilot, EO video camera, optional FLIR camera, 1 SwiftStation, battery chargers, secondary batteries
- Ruggedized hard-shell waterproof transport case
- Total system weight: just over 20 kg
- 3 years of software/firmware updates included
- On-site training and maintenance provided

**Option 2: Service Model**
- Operating platform as a service leveraging existing partnerships
- Cost varies based on user needs (available upon request)
- Access to established African and Asian operational networks

### Competitive Advantages
- Proven extreme weather capability (tornado intercept experience)
- Modular, customizable design
- Robust, low-maintenance construction (EPP foam)
- Intuitive user interface designed for novices
- Established operational and training partnerships in target regions
- Rapid deployment capability (5-10 minute setup)
- Extended mission capability with dual airframes and solar charging

### Component Suppliers
InvenSense (IMU), Measurement Specialties (pressure sensors), Airborne Innovations (wireless video/command links), Digi International (wireless transceivers), Microhard Corporation (wireless systems), Panasonic Toughpad (ruggedized tablet), Pelican (transport cases)# WWF Wildlife Crime Technology Project - RFP Q&A

## Document Metadata
- Type: Request for Information/Proposal (RFI/RFP) Frequently Asked Questions
- Client/Agency: World Wildlife Fund (WWF)
- Program: Wildlife Crime Technology Project
- Date: June 24, 2013 (document created July 3, 2013)
- BST Products/Systems Referenced: None explicitly mentioned
- Key Personnel: Not named in this document

## Executive Summary
This Q&A document clarifies the WWF's Wildlife Crime Technology Project RFP requirements for potential suppliers. The project seeks aerial surveillance systems to detect wildlife crimes across four international deployment sites (Namibia, Nepal, and two additional Asia/Africa locations). The RFP was flexible regarding system type (not limited to fixed-wing UAVs), emphasizing integration with SMART database and animal tracking technologies, with initial field deployment expected October 2013.

## Technical Approach & Requirements

**System Specifications:**
- Fixed-wing electrical UAV preferred but alternative solutions accepted
- Minimum 60-minute endurance with video transmission and continuous telemetry
- Operating temperature range: primarily 10-30°C (acceptable under -5°C to +40°C in emergencies)
- Launch capability in winds up to 16 m/s (with flexible takeoff direction)
- Landing area: 100m x 100m with potential 20m obstacles at edges
- Emergency landing probability: ≤1% per 100 flights (technical failure only, excluding pilot error)

**Ground Control Station (GCS) Requirements:**
- Display of UAV position, line-of-sight (LOS), and coordinates on moving map
- Operation in daylight and nighttime conditions with readable outdoor sunlight visibility
- Real-time emergency landing location selection capability
- "Camera guide mode" - automatic flight around target locations
- Drawing function for marking boundaries, areas of interest, event detections, suspicious areas
- Flexible hardware approach (PC, tablet, or ruggedized case) welcome

**Payload & Sensors:**
- Gimbal-preferred EO/IR sensor (fixed acceptable if justified)
- Continuous optical zoom in EO camera preferred (non-optical zoom acceptable if cost-justified and requirements met)
- Detection/recognition requirements in all light conditions (evaluation primarily in full daylight and moonlight conditions)
- Simple "training camera" for field training separate from primary mission payload
- Small fire detection capability (objects <1 meter diameter)
- Vehicle classification: distinguish family cars from pickup trucks from semi-trucks

**Data & Mission Requirements:**
- Mission data = flight parameters ("black box") stored in UAV and GCS (separate from video recording)
- Data elements: UAV path, coordinates, targets, altitude, indicated airspeed (IAS), temperature
- Post-mission SMART database integration via event flagging (location, time, event type/violation)
- Minimal acceptable solution: event export as Excel file or basic location/time/event data
- Video mosaic optional but evaluated

**Durability & Field Performance:**
- Rugged transport in vehicles over rough terrain
- High durability target: 98% of landings require only field-level (O) maintenance; only 2% require intermediate (I) level maintenance
- Protective coatings for sensitive electrical components
- Battery performance: can operate 3 flights/week at 2 hours per flight; acceptable to be <60 minutes in low temperatures if documented
- Data rate for storage: supplier to recommend

**Operational Constraints:**
- Detection capability with lights off
- Multiple systems in same area: two systems operating one UAV each within 50km x 50km area (two teams minimum, 2+ personnel each team)
- GCS operation in moving vehicles permitted (optional mode; UAV launched in static mode first)
- Modem reception antenna access in moving vehicles (not confined)
- Training location flexible (preferred on-site but open to alternatives)

## Use Cases & Applications

**Mission Context:** Wildlife crime detection and prevention at four protected sites over 3 years
- **Primary Location (2013):** Namibia
- **Secondary Location (pending):** Nepal  
- **Future Sites:** One additional Asia site, one additional Africa site
- **Site Coverage:** Highly variable (10,000 sq mi to <200 sq mi); system not expected to cover entire area but deployed in high-threat zones efficiently

**Operational Tempo:**
- Expected 3-4 days/week operations
- 1-2 missions per day
- 1-2 hour missions
- Theoretical lifetime: duration of 3-year project minimum

**Integration Requirements:**
- SMART database integration (post-mission event data export minimum; preferably real-time integration)
- Animal tracking device compatibility with multiple scenarios:
  - Passive RFID tags (≤1km detection range)
  - GSM-communicating tags (in areas with poor cellular reception)
  - Satellite-based tags (potentially independent of aerial system)
  - UHF-communicating tags
  - Other emerging solutions

## Contractual & Procurement Approach

**Acquisition Strategy:**
- Initial procurement: one system for first pilot site
- Second system purchase likely to follow if first system successful
- No budget ceiling disclosed for aerial systems component
- Open to multiple procurement models: purchase, lease, or service contracts
- Proposals may include multiple options (sale/lease/service) for selection flexibility
- Full-service solutions (hourly rate provision) acceptable alternative to asset provision

**System Deployment:**
- Systems will NOT be transferred between countries
- Target replication: selected system intended to serve as model for other organizations with similar missions
- Multiple awardees possible for evaluation phase; final contract with single provider preferred

**Contract Terms Expected:**
- Training
- On-the-job training (OJT)
- Long-term maintenance

## Notable Details

**Technical Flexibility:**
- RFP explicitly positioned as "conceptual document" - suppliers encouraged to propose alternative solutions outside stated parameters if justified by CONOPS requirements
- Not limited to fixed-wing UAVs despite RFP language
- SMART and RFID/GSM specifications incomplete; suppliers asked to respond based on current understanding and proposed integration approaches
- Supplier responsible for all export/trade control compliance and obtaining necessary licenses for deployment to Namibia, Nepal, and other international locations

**Evaluation Approach:**
- Emphasis on technical capability, flexibility of ideas, and system integration strength
- Field evaluation expected October 2013
- NIIRS rating acceptable for image quality assessment
- Durability, ruggedness, and field operability prioritized

**Operational Philosophy:**
- Emphasis on field-sustainable solutions (minimal maintenance in theater)
- Training approach flexible but preferably on-site with SMEs/trained operators potentially working with end users
- GCS hardware/interface approach flexible ("we welcome any idea you see as appropriate")# X20.3 SBIR CSO Topic AF203-CSO1 Phase II Proposal Instructions

## Document Metadata
- **Type:** Solicitation instructions / proposal preparation guidance
- **Client/Agency:** Department of the Air Force (DAF); AFWERX
- **Program/Solicitation:** AF203-CSO1 Phase II Commercial Solutions Opening (CSO)
- **Date:** Prepared 2021 (submission deadline June 3, 2021)
- **BST Products/Systems Referenced:** None mentioned
- **Key Personnel:** Captain Zoe Walters, AFRL/RGV (contracting officer contact)

## Executive Summary
This document provides comprehensive Phase II proposal preparation and submission instructions for the Air Force's SBIR Commercial Solutions Opening (AF203-CSO1). It details eligibility requirements, proposal structure, technical and cost volume specifications, and evaluation criteria for small businesses seeking to advance innovative solutions addressing Air Force needs through adaptation of non-defense commercial technologies.

## Document Type & Purpose
This is an official solicitation instruction document outlining mandatory requirements for Phase II SBIR proposals. It is not a proposal submission from Black Swift Technologies but rather the regulatory framework governing how proposals should be submitted and what they must contain.

## Key Administrative Details

### Submission Requirements
- **Deadline:** June 3, 2021, 12:00 p.m. Eastern Time (for Phase I awardees with deliverables due by June 2, 2021)
- **Portal:** Department of Defense SBIR/STTR Innovation Portal (DSIP)
- **Maximum Funding:** $750,000 per award
- **Performance Period:** 15 months maximum (12 months technical + 3 months reporting)
- **Award Type:** Firm-fixed-price contracts or Other Transactions for Prototype
- **Anticipated Awards:** ~60 awards
- **Review Timeline:** ~90 days from proposal submission

### Eligibility Requirements
- Must be a qualified small business concern (13 CFR §§ 701-705)
- Minimum 50% of Phase II R&D must be conducted by the offeror
- Principal Investigator must have primary employment with small business (>50% time)
- All R&D work must be performed in the United States
- Must meet SBA commercialization benchmarks
- No classified proposals accepted
- No majority ownership by venture capital, hedge funds, or private equity
- Must be registered in SAM.gov and DSIP

## Proposal Structure & Volume Requirements

### Volume 1: DoD Proposal Coversheet
- Technical abstract (max 200 words)
- Problem solved, advantage provided, end-user organization, commercialization potential
- Maximum 8 keywords
- Anticipated benefits/potential commercial applications
- Statement of prior/current/pending similar proposals

### Volume 2: Technical Volume (15 pages maximum)
Required sections:
- **Table of Contents** (not counted toward page limit)
- **Glossary of acronyms** (not counted)
- **Technical Summary:** Non-defense commercial solution description, problem scope, commercial history
- **Commercialization Potential:** Company info, customer/competition analysis, market analysis, IP protection, financing plans, assistance/mentoring
- **Non-Defense Commercial Customer Discovery:** Revenue history, potential projects
- **Proposed Adaptation of Non-Defense Commercial Solution:** Technical modifications, military applications, DoD customer identification
- **Phase I Feasibility Study Results:** R&D effort, DAF end-user/customer exploration methods, documented feasibility
- **Phase II Technical Objectives and Key Results:** 3-5 objectives with measurable key results; stakeholder interactions; compliance/regulatory activities
- **Phase II Work Plan:** Outcomes, deliverables, specifications, regulatory accommodation
- **Task Outline:** Work breakdown
- **Schedule of Milestones:** Max 15 milestones with delivery dates, deliverables, acceptance criteria
- **Deliverables:** Specific sample/prototype/hardware/software; data deliverables
- **Safety Requirements:** Preliminary hazard analysis (hardware); hazardous material reports
- **Required Reports:** Final report, quarterly status reports, technical interchange meetings, Phase II summary report
- **Key Personnel:** Names, education, experience, citizenship; PI resume required
- **Investors and Partners:** Identification and track record
- **Related Work:** Previous programs and state-of-the-art knowledge
- **Non-U.S. Citizens:** Complete identification and visa/work permit status
- **Supply Chain Integrity:** Joint ventures, suppliers, IP licensing, foreign customers/investors, FOCI mitigation, CFIUS compliance, Bayh-Dole compliance

### Volume 3: Cost Volume
- Direct labor costs (by person/category with rates)
- Direct material costs (itemized with quantities and prices)
- Other direct costs (specialized services, equipment leases, travel, subcontracts, consultants)
- Overhead and G&A
- Profit (minimum required; zero-profit proposals not acceptable)
- **Constraint:** Consultant fees + facility leases + subcontract costs ≤ 1/3 of total contract price
- Must be adequate for price analysis and cost reasonableness determination

### Volume 4: Company Commercialization Report
- Required for firms with prior SBIR/STTR awards
- New/startup companies can select "No"
- Must be completed in SBIR.gov database and uploaded

### Volume 5: Supporting Documents
- Signed Customer Memorandum (mandatory, using provided template) from DAF customer AND end-user
- Letters of support from end-users, partners, investors
- Lifecycle Certification (signed)
- Prior/current/pending support disclosure
- Foreign citizen table (if applicable)
- Supplemental cost information
- Key personnel resumes
- Compliance certifications
- Additional facilities/equipment information
- Additional subcontractor information

### Volume 6: Fraud, Waste, and Abuse Training
- Required documentation of completion

## Critical Mandatory Requirements

### Customer Memorandum
- **MANDATORY** for proposal consideration
- Must use provided template (Attachment 1)
- Must be signed by a DAF Customer AND End-User (if same person, sign twice)
- Required from at least one DAF/Joint organization
- If multiple DAF end-users, consolidate into single coherent memorandum signed by lead DAF Phase II PM
- Proposals without compliant Customer Memorandum will NOT be considered for award

### Commercialization Plan Requirements
Must address:
1. Company information (objectives, core competencies, previous funding, regulatory experience)
2. Customer and competition (key technology objectives, advantages vs. competitors, innovation hurdles)
3. Market analysis (milestones, target dates, market size, share estimates)
4. Intellectual property (patent status, protection plan, competitive advantage timeline)
5. Financing (plans for securing Phase III funding)
6. Assistance and mentoring (sources of technical/business support)
7. Specific questions answered:
   - What is the anticipated first product incorporating the technology?
   - Who are probable customers and what is estimated market size?
   - How much funding needed and how will it be raised?
   - Does firm have marketing expertise?
   - Who are probable competitors and what price/quality advantage?
   - Are there private sector/non-SBIR commitments demonstrated?
   - What past 12-month non-Defense commercial revenue?
   - What are Phase III transition plans?

### Phase I Feasibility Study Results Requirements
Must demonstrate:
- Specific problem/opportunity from Phase I
- Scientific/technical R&D effort (research questions, methods, results, literature)
- DAF end-user and customer exploration methods (both successful and unsuccessful)
- Documentation of at least one in-depth interview with DAF end-user
- Specific DAF end-users willing to support Phase II testing/trials (via Customer Memorandum)
- Specific AF customers assisting with Phase II transition/Phase III (via Customer Memorandum)
- Other US Government end-user commitments (via Customer Memorandum)

### Non-Defense Commercial Solution Requirements
Must address:
- Specific problem/opportunity addressed in Phase I
- Non-Defense commercial solution description (use by commercial customers, technical specifications, qualitative and quantitative value)
- Scope and importance of technical problem
- Whether item is "of a type" (similar to commercial items used by public/non-governmental entities)
- Whether item has been sold/leased/licensed or offered for sale
- Revenue, unit sales, user adoption, pre-sales, investments (where applicable)

### Adaptation to DAF Needs Requirements
Must describe:
- Scope and importance of technical problem
- Similarity of modified item to items sold to non-Defense customers
- Whether supplier performs similar modifications for non-Defense customers
- Whether DAF-unique modifications change product's essential use/purpose
- Differences in production/manufacturing/delivery processes vs. non-Defense customers
- Quantitative benefits expected for Air Force end-users

## Technical Objectives and Key Results Specifications

Phase II proposals must include 3-5 R&D objectives that are:
- Tied to specific Phase II tasks
- Qualitative but specific to participating DAF end-users
- Tied to specific time periods
- Tangible and unambiguous
- Describing end-state outcomes rather than processes
- Each accompanied by 3-5 specific, measurable "key results"
- Key results likely quantitative (e.g., "deliver X widgets to DAF end-user")
- Non-quantitative key results must be clearly measurable

## Work Plan and Milestone Specifications

- **Maximum 15 milestones/deliverables** including:
  - Refined Work Plan (due CA + 30 days)
  - Final technical report
  - Intervening milestones at offeror discretion
- Each milestone must include:
  - Expected delivery date (in months after contract award)
  - Deliverable of value
  - Clear acceptance criteria
- Status reports cannot count as milestones
- Fixed-price payments tied to negotiated milestones and deliverables

## Compliance and Regulatory Activities

Proposals must identify whether effort includes:
- Air flight (including taxi)
- Human subject research
- Animal research
- Directed energy devices or RF radiation
- Explosives, propellants, ammunition
- Hazardous materials
- Infectious agents, human-derived materials, or recombinant DNA

Special requirements if applicable:
- **Human subjects:** Must have IRB approval, Federal Assurance documentation, human subject protection training (1-3 months processing)
- **Animal subjects:** Must have IACUC approval plus DoD veterinarian approval (no funding until approvals granted)
- **Recombinant DNA:** Must have Institutional Biosafety Committee approval
- **UAS operations:** Must obtain UAS operational use exemption (up to 3 months processing)
- **Cyber security:** IT products must have RMF assessment and/or ATO; must meet NIST SP 800-171 and DFAR PGI 239.76 requirements

## Key Personnel Requirements

- Principal Investigator:
  - Primary employment with small business at award and throughout performance
  - Primary employment = >50% time with small business
  - Precludes full-time employment with another organization
  - Technical resume required including publications
- All key personnel must be identified with education, experience, citizenship
- Non-U.S. citizens must be identified with countries of origin, visa/work permit types, and anticipated involvement levels
- Non-U.S. citizens, if eligible, may be limited to work in public domain and non-key positions if subject to export control

## Supply Chain Integrity Requirements

Must disclose and verify:
- Joint ventures, partnerships, technology development agreements, teaming arrangements
- Main component, software, and other suppliers; licensed IP used
- Entities utilizing firm's IP
- Significant non-US customer or investment base (>5% of revenue)
- Foreign sovereign wealth funds or government instrumentalities as customers/investors
- Foreign interests with power to direct or control company management, IP, or operations (FOCI mitigation measures if applicable)
- Classified information needs and approving Federal agencies
- Owner, investor, and PI compliance with 13 CFR § 121.701-705
- Compliance with DFARS 252.225-7048 (Export-Controlled Items)
- CFIUS mandatory/voluntary reviews or eligibility (especially for emerging/foundational technologies: quantum information/computing, AI, machine learning, advanced sensors/networks)
- Compliance with Bayh-Dole Act (35 USC § 204) U.S. technology commercialization/manufacturing requirements

## Cost Volume Guidance

### Direct Labor
- Identify key personnel by name and/or labor category
- Hours, labor category, overhead/fringe benefits, hourly rates required
- Price analysis for reasonableness required
- May compare to prior efforts (identify basis)
- If price analysis inadequate, provide cost analysis IAW FAR 15.404-1(c)

### Travel
- Must# X224-OCSO1 Phase II RFP - Air Force SBIR Soil Moisture Mapping

## Document Metadata
- **Type:** Request for Proposal (RFP) / Solicitation Guidance
- **Client/Agency:** Department of the Air Force (DAF), AFWERX

- **Date:** April 5, 2023

- **BST Products/Systems Referenced:** None explicitly mentioned in this document

## Executive Summary
This is a Phase II SBIR RFP issued by the Air Force to companies that successfully completed Phase I awards under topic AFX224-OCSO1 (Phase I Open Call for Innovative Defense-Related Dual-Purpose Technologies/Solutions). Companies are invited to submit Phase II proposals for continued development of their technologies, with a maximum funding amount of $1,250,000 over 21 months, evaluated on commercialization potential, defense need relevance, and technical merit.

## Document Purpose & Scope
This is a comprehensive RFP guidance document outlining submission requirements, evaluation criteria, and administrative procedures for Phase II proposals. It is **not** a technical proposal but rather the solicitation framework and instructions for applicants.

## Key RFP Parameters

### Funding & Duration
- **Maximum SBIR Funding:** $1,250,000
- **Maximum Performance Period:** 21 months
- **Minimum Work Requirement:** At least 50% of research/analytical effort must be performed by awardee (measured by direct and indirect costs, excluding profit)

### Technical Requirements
- **Technical Volume Format:** White Paper (15-page limit, single PDF)
- **Page Limit:** Strictly 15 pages; pages in excess will not be reviewed
- **Evaluation Basis:** Peer review by engineers/scientists; each proposal judged on its own merits

## Evaluation Criteria (Equal Importance)

### Criteria A: Commercialization Potential
- Small business's record of commercializing SBIR or other research (pre-sales, pilots, sales, revenue, active users, subscriptions, downloads, traction/adoption)
- Phase II follow-on commitments and funding commitments from Government or private sources
- Sound transition strategy documented in Air Force Customer Memorandum

### Criteria B: Defense Need Appropriateness & Relevance
- Complete and compelling Air Force Customer Memorandum (signed by appropriate end-user/customer) required
- Adequacy of proposed effort relative to fulfilling identified Defense Need
- Evidence of previous investment (basic research grants, etc.) supporting the proposed effort

### Criteria C: Technical Soundness & Innovation
- Soundness, technical merit, and innovation of proposed approach
- Differentiation from current customer alternatives
- Incremental progress toward fulfilling identified Defense need
- Qualifications of proposed Principal Investigators/Project Managers, supporting staff, and consultants

**Note:** Technical and merit criteria combined are significantly more important than cost/price.

## Proposal Content Requirements

### Volume 1: Proposal Cover Sheet
- CAGE Code, EID, certification questions, business information
- **Technical Abstract:** Non-proprietary; may be publicly released by OSD
- **Anticipated Benefits/Anticipated Applications:** Must follow specific format: "We solved [DAF problem] by providing [advantage], to help [DAF end-user organization] accomplish [goal]. We will recognize profit by charging [non-Defense commercial customers] to get [non-Defense commercial benefit]."
- **Keywords:** Maximum 8 keywords/phrases describing project (used for categorization and Phase III transition partner identification)

### Volume 2: Technical Volume (15 pages maximum)
**Required Sections:**
1. **Table of Contents** (does not count against 15-page limit)
2. **Glossary of Acronyms/Abbreviations** (does not count against limit)
3. **Technical Summary** including:
   - Identification and significance of problem/opportunity
   - Air Force or Space Force Technology Strategic Capabilities alignment
   - Non-Defense commercial solution description and specifications
   - Proposed adaptation of commercial solution to meet Government end-user need
   - Compliance and regulatory activities (flight testing, hardware delivery, Government personnel/facilities use, weapons/munitions testing, explosives, hazardous materials, animal testing, human subject research, toxins, human data)

4. **Phase II Technical Objectives and Key Results** (3-5 objectives)
   - Tied to specific proposed Phase II trial tasks
   - Qualitative and specific to participating DAF end-user(s)
   - Time-bound, tangible, unambiguous regarding anticipated results
   - Each accompanied by 3-5 specific, measurable key results
   - List required stakeholders needed to accomplish Phase II

5. **Phase II Work Plan** (see Table 5 outline below)
6. **Commercialization Strategy** (see Table 6 outline below)
7. **Military Applications/DoD Customers:** Existing potential military requirement, DoD agency/organization likely to become customer, Phase III funding commitments
8. **Non-US Citizens:** Identification of all non-U.S. citizens/dual citizens with countries of origin, visa/work permit types, involvement level
9. **Key Personnel:** Qualifications for RDT&E and commercialization, education, experience, citizenship; technical resume for PI with publications
10. **Non-Defense Commercial Customers:** Past revenue from commercial customers; potential revenue-generating projects
11. **Investors and Partners:** Company investors, shareholders, strategic advisors; their experience/track record
12. **Related Work:** Significant related activities, previous programs, consultant involvement, state-of-the-art reviewer comments, related Government efforts

### Phase II Work Plan Outline (Non-Proprietary)
**Mandatory Features:**
- Work stated in terms of outcomes/results, not performance methods
- Measurable performance standards with assessment methods

**Work Plan Components:**
1. **Scope:** Major requirements and specifications
2. **Task Outline:** Work to be accomplished; clearly identify SBIR-funded vs. Government/private-funded tasks
3. **Milestone Schedule:** From signed Customer Memorandum; each milestone marks completion of required deliverable (prototype, test plan, final report, etc.)
4. **Deliverables:** Specific sample/prototype hardware/software to be delivered; data deliverables, schedules, quantities; Unique Item Identification (IAW DFARS 252.211-7003) may be required

**Required Reports (ALL Phase II awards):**
- **Final Report:** Draft due 30 days after technical effort completion; includes single-page project summary (may be published, no proprietary info), project objectives met, work completed, results obtained, technical feasibility estimates
- **Status Reports:** Quarterly minimum; concise (≤15 slides); describe progress toward selected DAF end-user needs; include quantitative measure (0-1 scale) of progress toward each objective/key result
- **Phase II Summary Report:** At technical effort completion; ≤700 words; description of technology and anticipated applications/benefits

**Safety-Related Deliverables:**
- Preliminary Hazard Analysis (if hardware developed; IAW MIL STD-882E requirements)
- Hazardous Material Report (if hazardous materials used): materials identification, purpose, alternatives/safeguards

**Additional Reporting:**
- Software documentation and user manuals
- Engineering drawings
- Operation and Maintenance documentation
- Updated commercialization results

### Commercialization Plan (Included in Volume 2)
**Required Components:**
1. **Company Information:** Focused objectives/core competencies, specialization area(s), products with significant sales, history of Federal/non-Federal funding, regulatory experience, commercialization results
2. **Customer and Competition:** Key technology objectives, current competition, advantages vs. competitors, hurdles to acceptance
3. **Market:** Milestones, target dates, market size analysis, estimated market share (Year 1 and Year 5), plan to obtain market share
4. **Intellectual Property:** Patent status, technology lead, trade secrets, plan for competitive advantage
5. **Financing:** Plans for securing further funding
6. **Assistance and Mentoring:** Plans for technical/business assistance (mentoring, partnering, State programs, Small Business Development Centers, FFRDCs, Manufacturing Extension Partnership, DAF Mentor-Protégé Program)

**Specific Questions to Address:**
- First product into which technology will be incorporated
- Customers and estimated market size
- Funding needed to bring to market and how it will be raised
- Marketing expertise possessed or to be obtained
- Competitor companies and firm's price/quality advantage
- Private sector/non-SBIR funding commitments (venture capital, angel investors, state/local programs, internal funding)
- Foreign investment sources and amounts
- Phase III (Government or commercial) follow-on commitments
- Other commercial potential indicators (pre-sales, pilots, sales, revenue, active users, subscriptions, downloads, traction, commercial signals)
- Last 12 months' total revenue from non-Defense commercial solution sales
- Phase II anticipated end results and plans to transition to Phase III with potential Government customer

### Volume 3: Cost Volume
- Submitted via online DSIP form
- **Direct Labor Costs:** Name of key personnel if possible or labor category; number of hours, labor overhead/fringe benefits, hourly rates
- **Direct Material Costs:** Itemized list (types, quantities, price, purpose); vendor quotes, historical costs as justification
- **Other Direct Costs:** Specialized services (machining, milling, testing, analysis), temporary equipment use
  - **Travel:** Must relate to project needs; break out by trip, travelers, airfare, per diem, lodging; recommend budgeting at least one trip to managing Air Force location
  - **Subcontracts:** Include subcontractor/consultant costs; proposed total of all consultant fees, facility leases, and subcontract/purchase agreements may not exceed one-half total contract price/cost (unless otherwise approved in writing by CO); support with copies of agreements
  - **Consultants:** Separate agreement letter for each; brief statement of services, hours required, hourly rate
  - **Special Tooling/Test Equipment/Material:** Carefully reviewed for need/appropriateness; title to Government-furnished property vests with AF unless title transfer deemed more cost-effective

**Measurable Milestones:** Fixed-price payments tied to measurable milestones agreed with Government

### Volume 4: Contractor Conflict of Interest Review (CCR)
- Completed through DSIP
- Not considered during proposal evaluations

### Volume 5: Supporting Documents
**Required at Proposal Submission:**
- Signed Customer Memorandum (Attachment 1) - **REQUIRED**
- DoD SBIR/STTR Lifecycle Certification (Attachment 2) - **REQUIRED**
- SBIR/STTR Environment, Safety, and Occupational Health (ESOH) Questionnaire (Attachment 3) - **REQUIRED**

- **Type:** Request for Information (RFI) / Competition Announcement

## Executive Summary

The U.S. Army xTechOverwatch competition seeks innovative concepts from eligible small businesses for advanced autonomous unmanned systems (UAVs, UGVs, and/or sensor networks) capable of conducting overwatch and terrain-shaping tasks using AI, robotics, secure networking, and real-time data processing. The three-round competition offers up to $1 million in cash prizes with the top 20 winners eligible to submit Direct to Phase II Army SBIR proposals worth up to $2 million each (total SBIR funding pool: $40 million).

---

## Technical Approach & Problem Statement

The Army seeks well-defined prototype technology solutions for autonomous unmanned platforms integrating:
- Multi-modal sensor fusion with AI-driven target recognition
- Secure communications and adaptive decision-making
- Systems capable of identifying and occupying advantageous overwatch positions with minimal human intervention

**Key Technical Areas of Interest (from Appendix A):**

1. **Autonomous Unmanned Systems (UAVs, UGVs, Stationary Sensors)**
   - UGVs with self-adjusting mobility, real-time terrain navigation, and automated repositioning
   - UAVs with adaptive flight control for ISR and dynamic mission execution
   - Stationary sensor networks with low-power, persistent surveillance capabilities integrated with mobile platforms

2. **Sensor Fusion, Data Integration, and AI-Driven Target Recognition & Classification**
   - AI-powered sensor fusion integrating EO/IR, LiDAR, acoustic, and RF sensors
   - Real-time threat detection, classification, and tracking
   - Robust performance in cluttered, low-visibility, or GPS-denied environments

3. **Secure Communications and Networking**
   - Encrypted, resilient, scalable communications using software-defined radios (SDRs), mesh networking, low-power long-range protocols
   - Network redundancy and self-healing architectures
   - Real-time data sharing across multiple autonomous systems without traditional infrastructure

4. **Human-Machine Interface (HMI) for Effective Decision-Making**
   - Advanced visualizations (augmented reality [AR])
   - AI-driven decision-support systems to reduce operator cognitive burden
   - Adaptive UIs tailored to mission context and operator workload

5. **Edge Computing for Onboard Processing**
   - High-performance, low-power embedded AI accelerators
   - Real-time onboard processing of sensor data and AI inference
   - Low-latency threat detection in disconnected/contested environments

6. **Resilient Robotics for Adaptive Terrain Navigation**
   - Mobility adaptation solutions (variable tire inflation, articulated suspensions, AI-driven path planning)
   - Biomimetic robotic adaptations
   - Terrain-aware decision-making for obstacles, mud, snow, unstable ground

7. **Automated Self-Recovery Mechanisms**
   - Self-righting mechanisms, robotic manipulator arms, cooperative recovery protocols
   - AI diagnostics for predictive maintenance
   - Autonomous fail-safe capabilities for rollovers, entrapment, hardware failures

8. **Collaborative/Mission-Focused Autonomy**
   - Decentralized AI-based mission execution using multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL)
   - Distributed decision-making and swarm robotics
   - Autonomous coordination with minimal human intervention

9. **UGV and UAS Payloads**
   - Modular ISR payloads for reconnaissance
   - Deployable terrain-shaping tools (automated barrier placement, excavation)
   - Electronic warfare (EW) payloads for disrupting adversary sensors/communications

10. **Modular & Open Architecture**
    - Plug-and-play hardware/software interfaces per Army Interoperability Profile (IOP), NATO STANAGs
    - Standardized data protocols and API-based integration
    - Future upgradability and cross-platform compatibility

## Competition Structure & Phases

**Part 1: Concept White Paper (Deadline: May 21, 2025, 5 p.m. ET)**
- Three-page white paper submission via template
- Evaluated by Army/DoD S&T, Warfighter, acquisition, and R&D subject matter experts
- **Scoring Criteria:**
  - Introduction (3%)
  - Army Benefits (15%)
  - Technical Approach (35%)
  - Programmatic Potential (20%)
  - Commercial Potential (25%)
  - Proposal Quality (2%)
- **Prize:** Up to 40 winners receive $15,000 each

**xTech Collider Event (August 2025, tentatively Austin, TX, Fed Supernova)**
- Optional networking event for Part 1 winners
- Designed to facilitate teaming and collaboration among finalists and industry partners
- No government role in team formation; collaboration optional and non-binding

**Part 2: Finals (October 27-29, 2025, tentatively Bush Combat Development Center, Bryan, TX)**
- In-person pitch and demonstration to Army/DoD expert panel
- Scheduled around Army Human-Machine Integration (HMI) Summit
- **Prize:** Up to 20 final winners receive $20,000 each

**Direct to Phase II (DP2) Army SBIR Proposals (Submission period: November 12-25, 2025)**
- Only Part 2 finalists eligible
- Up to $2 million per award, not to exceed 18 months
- Must demonstrate sufficient solution maturity and feasibility
- Total Army SBIR funding pool: $40 million (up to 20 awards possible)

## Eligibility Requirements

**Eligible Entities:**
- Small, for-profit, independent U.S. businesses
- Meet small business requirements in 13 C.F.R. § 121.702
- Majority (>50%) equity directly owned and controlled by:
  - U.S. citizens or permanent resident aliens, OR
  - Other for-profit SBCs (similarly owned), OR
  - Combination thereof
- Not more than 500 employees (including affiliates)
- Only one submission per eligible entity

**Submission Requirements:**
- Work must be substantially performed by the proposing firm
- Cannot be based on prior or ongoing federally funded Army SBIR/STTR work
- Disqualified if attestation cannot be made

The competition targets autonomous systems for:

- **GPS-denied and contested environments:** Autonomous navigation and decision-making without reliance on traditional infrastructure
- **Persistent surveillance:** Long-duration intelligence gathering via distributed sensor networks
- **Minimal human intervention missions:** Decentralized autonomous coordination and swarm operations

## Document Metadata
- **Type:** Concept White Paper (xTech Innovation submission)
- **Client/Agency:** U.S. Army
- **Program/Solicitation:** xTech Overwatch (Army innovation program)
- **Date:** 2025 (submission year; document created/modified May 21, 2025)
- **BST Products/Systems Referenced:** S2 UAS, S0 UAS, S0-VTOL (VTOL fixed-wing variant)
- **Key Personnel:** 
  - Dr. Maciej Stachura (CTO, Black Swift Technologies)
  - Dr. Jack Elston (CEO, Black Swift Technologies)
  - Dr. Gijs de Boer (Chair, Environmental Science & Technologies Dept., Brookhaven National Lab)
  - Dr. Arthur Sedlacek (Atmospheric Chemist, BNL)
  - Andrew McMahon (Electrical Engineer, BNL)

## Executive Summary
This innovation proposes an autonomous, distributed UAS swarm system that leverages Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) to achieve real-time 3D volumetric reconstruction of dynamic scenes, specifically for detecting, classifying, and tracking airborne plumes from explosions, chemical, or biological events. The system enables safe, rapid characterization of hazardous plumes using sparse, non-overlapping imagery from multiple small, fast-moving VTOL fixed-wing UAS operating autonomously as a coordinated team, with scalability to broader battlefield assessment applications.

## Technical Approach

### Core Technology
- **Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs):** High-fidelity 3D volumetric reconstruction of dynamic, semi-transparent scenes from sparse, non-overlapping imagery—unlike traditional photogrammetry
- **NeRF Extensions:** K-Planes and Dex-NeRF specifically designed to handle time-varying scenes and transparency characteristics of plumes
- **Platform Base:** Black Swift Technologies' hardened, fixed-wing VTOL UAS (S0-VTOL) engineered for stable, long-endurance flight in extreme conditions
- **Multi-UAS Coordination:** Autonomous mission execution with minimal human input, enabling one-to-many control and swarm operations

### Positioning and Sensing Requirements
- **GPS Accuracy:** Centimeter-level precision achievable via RTK GPS (already used on proposed UAS and commercial platforms)
- **Heading Accuracy:** S0 UAS uses dual GPS providing 0.2-degree heading accuracy
- **Gimbal Pointing Accuracy:** Commercial gimbals achieve 0.5-degree pointing accuracy
- **Goal:** Relax traditional NeRF requirements (sub-degree rotation, centimeter-level translation) to levels achievable by current government UAS systems

### Integration Approach
- Vertically integrated engineering: custom avionics, sensor development, and AI-driven flight control
- Modular, open-source software framework for adaptability and platform compatibility
- Machine-readable reconstructed scene data immediately shareable with other robotic systems for real-time navigation and hazard avoidance
- Hybrid and optimized processing strategies to handle computational intensity

### Partnership
- **Brookhaven National Laboratory (BNL):** Advanced machine vision development expertise; atmospheric science expertise (aerosol processes, particulate physics, emission plume evolution); AI/ML techniques for atmospheric measurement

### Technical Risks & Mitigation
**Risks:**
- NeRF fidelity issues in sparse or dynamic scenes
- Platform pointing accuracy and lighting condition challenges
- Real-time processing latency (NeRF methods computationally intensive, may hinder timely autonomous responses)
- Multi-sensor synchronization and calibration (EO/IR, GPS/IMU integration)

**Mitigation:**
- Controlled testing to define performance limits
- Leveraging BST's proven integration expertise
- Hybrid and optimized processing strategies
- Modular, open-source framework for adaptability

### TRL Level
TRL 1-2 (Basic Research)

## Executive Summary
Black Swift Technologies proposes an autonomous, distributed UAS swarm system leveraging Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) to achieve real-time 3D volumetric reconstruction of dynamic hazardous scenes (particularly airborne plumes from explosions, chemical, or biological events). Built on BST's hardened, fixed-wing VTOL platforms, the system enables autonomous detection, classification, and tracking with minimal human input, scalable to broader 3D battlefield assessment and situational awareness applications.

## Technical Approach

### Core Innovation
- **NeRF-based 3D Reconstruction**: Uses Neural Radiance Fields and extensions (K-Planes, Dex-NeRF) to enable high-fidelity volumetric reconstruction of dynamic, semi-transparent scenes (like plumes) from sparse, non-overlapping imagery
- **Key Advantage over Traditional Methods**: Unlike conventional photogrammetry, NeRF methods rapidly generate dense spatial-temporal data with minimal calibration; reconstructed scene data is machine-readable and immediately shareable with other robotic systems
- **Platform Integration**: Deployed on small, fast-moving VTOL fixed-wing UAS working as coordinated teams
- **Autonomous Coordination**: Enables multi-UAS platforms for enhanced data collection strategies and one-to-many control

### Technical Requirements & Solutions
**Positioning/Pointing Accuracy**:
- NeRF traditionally requires sub-degree rotation and centimeter-level translation
- BST mitigation strategy: S0 UAS uses dual GPS (0.2° heading accuracy), RTK GPS capability (centimeter-level precision already available on commercial UAS), and commercial gimbals (0.5° pointing accuracy) deemed sufficient for NeRF performance

**Real-Time Processing**:
- Challenge: NeRF methods are computationally intensive; latency could hinder timely autonomous UAS responses
- Mitigation: Exploration of hybrid and optimized processing strategies; modular, open-source software framework for adaptability

**Integration Challenges**:
- Multi-sensor synchronization (EO/IR, GPS/IMU) and calibration
- Mitigation: Controlled testing to define performance limits; leveraging BST's proven integration expertise

### Technical Team
- **Dr. Maciej Stachura** (CTO, Black Swift Technologies): 15 years' experience in UAS development for scientific remote sensing
- **Dr. Jack Elston** (CEO/PI, Black Swift Technologies): Extensive background in UAS development and atmospheric research for DoD, NOAA, NASA
- **Dr. Gijs de Boer** (Chair, Environmental Science and Technologies Dept., Brookhaven National Lab): Internationally recognized expert in lower atmospheric physics; decade of UAS development and deployment for atmospheric science
- **Dr. Arthur Sedlacek** (Atmospheric Chemist, BNL): Technical Manager, Aerosol Processes Team; expertise in atmospheric particulates and emission plume evolution
- **Andrew McMahon** (Electrical Engineer, BNL): Hardware and software design for environmental instruments and sensing systems

## Document Metadata
- Type: Grant Progress Report (Year 1)
- Client/Agency: Colorado Advanced Industries Accelerator Program
- Program/Solicitation: Early Stage Capital and Retention (ESCR) Grant
- Date: Report submitted August 29, 2016 (covering July 22, 2015 - May 1, 2017)
- Grant Award Amount: $240,000.00
- BST Products/Systems Referenced: SuperSwift airframe, SwiftCore Flight Management System, SwiftTrainer, soil moisture mapping sUAS
- Key Personnel: Bradley Cheetham (Point of Contact)
- Business Location: 2100 Central Ave Suite 102, Boulder, CO 80301

## Executive Summary
This year 1 report documents Black Swift Technologies' progress using Colorado Advanced Industries funding to commercialize soil moisture mapping small unmanned aircraft and enabling technologies. The grant funding accelerated commercialization efforts for the SuperSwift airframe and SwiftCore Flight Management System, resulting in follow-on NASA funding, commercial sales, and expansion of SwiftCore capabilities to support additional applications and partner companies.

## Grant Obligations & Progress

### Obligation 1: Commercialize Soil Moisture Mapping sUAS and Core Technologies
**Status:** Significant progress achieved

Key accomplishments:
- Secured follow-on NASA funding: $125,000 to support soil moisture system
- Secured deployment contract: $35,090
- Generated SuperSwift airframe sales revenues: $55,000
- Obtained formal export classification for key products, enabling overseas sales
- Funding accelerated commercialization timeline and enabled bootstrapping during FAA regulatory uncertainty

### Obligation 2: Expand SwiftCore Flight Management System Availability
**Status:** Two primary pathways executed

**Pathway 1 - Vertical Takeoff/Landing (VTOL) Support:**
- Customized SwiftCore capabilities for companies with aircraft requiring vertical takeoff/landing
- Expected to support at least three Colorado companies bringing systems to market
- Additional customers outside Colorado identified

**Pathway 2 - SwiftTrainer Development:**
- Created end-to-end entry-level mapping system based on SwiftCore FMS
- Targeted at surveyor market with majority of early customers in Colorado
- Generated revenues from both pathways: >$60,000 with additional sales pipeline

## Products & Capabilities Described

### SuperSwift Airframe
- sUAS platform for soil moisture mapping
- Commercial sales generated $55,000 in revenue during grant period
- Part of soil moisture system approved for NASA follow-on funding

### SwiftCore Flight Management System
- Core technology enabling multiple applications and partner companies
- Being customized for VTOL aircraft operations
- Foundation for SwiftTrainer product line
- Expanding to support broader UAV industry in Colorado

### SwiftTrainer
- Entry-level mapping system built on SwiftCore FMS features
- Targeted at surveyor market (primarily Colorado)
- Early customer traction demonstrated

### Soil Moisture Mapping System
- sUAS-based solution for agricultural applications
- Secured $125,000 NASA follow-on funding
- Customer deployment contract: $35,090
- Future work includes developing crop yield impact models using flight data

## Use Cases & Applications
- **Soil moisture mapping** for agriculture and crop management
- **Surveying operations** (SwiftTrainer targeted application)
- **VTOL aircraft operations** (customized SwiftCore implementations)
- Potential for reducing input costs and increasing crop yields through soil moisture data

## Technical Difficulties & Challenges
- **FAA Regulatory Delay:** Significant impediment to market entry; regulatory framework for commercial UAS operations undefined during most of grant period. Report notes FAA was "days away" from introducing reasonable regulations at time of reporting.
- **Commercialization Complexity:** Noted as inherent difficulty in bringing cutting-edge technologies to market
- **Mitigation:** Grant funding enabled company to bootstrap, focus on customer-driven development, and work through regulatory uncertainty

## Financial Results & Budget Performance

**Actual Spending vs. Budget:**
- Personnel Expenses: $184,079.02 / $170,000 budgeted (overage of $14,079.02)
- Materials and Supplies: $18,000 / $18,000 budgeted
- Legal and IP Services: $9,759.50 / $20,000 budgeted
- Other Consulting and Marketing: $6,658.48 / $14,000 budgeted
- Other Project Expenses: $4,737.71 / $18,000 budgeted
- **Remaining Budget:** $17,765.29
- **Total Grant Utilization:** $223,234.71 of $240,000

**Follow-on Funding & Revenue:**
- Follow-on capital secured: $160,000.00
  - NASA funding: $125,000
  - Deployment contract: $35,090
  - SuperSwift airframe sales: $55,000
- Commercial revenue from SwiftCore customization and SwiftTrainer: >$60,000
- Projected annual revenue increases: $300,000.00

## Job Creation & Retention
- Jobs created: 5.00 FTE
- Jobs retained: 3.25 FTE

## Intellectual Property
- Patents filed: 0 (during this period)
- Intellectual property developed: Primarily documentation and marketing materials (available online)
- Licenses issued: 0

## Commercial Progress & Partnerships
- Partnered with soil moisture experts and leaders in agricultural and insurance communities
- Supporting sales, distribution, and support through key partner relationships
- Three Colorado VTOL companies in pipeline to bring systems to market using customized SwiftCore
- Multiple external customers identified for SwiftCore integrations

## Notable Details
- Export classification achievement: Grant enabled formal export classification for key products, removing international sales barriers
- Customer-focused development: Close work with customers proved valuable during regulatory uncertainty period
- New business model: SwiftTrainer represents entry into surveyor market segment via accessible, integrated system
- Regulatory impact recognition: Report emphasizes that FAA regulatory clarification will "open up a broad segment of the market" previously precluded from using BST systems

## Executive Summary
Jun A. Zhang is a Scientist at the University of Miami specializing in tropical cyclone (hurricane) boundary layer physics, atmospheric dynamics, and in-situ aircraft observations. His extensive publication record and leadership roles in major hurricane research programs (NOAA, ONR, NASA) position him as a subject matter expert for Navy hazardous weather research involving unmanned aircraft systems and hurricane observations.

## Professional Background

**Current Position:**
- Scientist, University of Miami (2017-present)
- Prior progression: Associate Scientist (2012-2017), Assistant Scientist (2010-2012), NRC Postdoctoral Fellow at NOAA/AOML Hurricane Research Division (2008-2010)

**Educational Credentials:**
- Ph.D. Applied Marine Physics, University of Miami (2007)
- M.S. Applied Marine Physics, University of Miami (2005)
- B.E. Naval Architecture, Dalian University of Technology, China (2000)

## Research Expertise

**Primary Focus Areas:**
- Hurricane boundary layer structure and thermodynamics
- Tropical cyclone intensity change and forecasting
- Turbulent characteristics in hurricane low-level regions
- Enthalpy flux measurements in hurricane boundary layers
- Effects of environmental wind shear on hurricane asymmetry
- Planetary boundary layer (PBL) parameterization improvements
- Small unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) for hurricane observation

**Key Technical Contributions:**
- First direct measurements of enthalpy flux in hurricane boundary layer (CBLAST results, 2008)
- Turbulent characteristics analysis of Hurricanes Allen (1980) and Hugo (1989)
- Development of observation-based hybrid EDMF and EDMF-TKE PBL schemes
- Large-eddy simulation framework for tropical cyclone boundary layer
- Dropsonde composite analysis relating boundary layer structure to vertical wind shear

## Notable Publications (Relevant to Hazardous Weather)

**Hurricane Boundary Layer Physics:**
- Zhang et al. (2023): Mean kinematic structure of tropical cyclone boundary layer and relationship to intensity change
- Zhang et al. (2015): Effects of horizontal diffusion on tropical cyclone intensity change in 3D simulations
- Zhang et al. (2013): Asymmetric hurricane boundary layer structure from dropsonde composites

**Unmanned Systems & Observations:**
- Cione et al. (2020): Eye of the Storm - observing hurricanes with small UAS
- Zhang et al. (2023): Hurricane observations by uncrewed systems (co-author)
- Li et al. (2013): Tropical cyclone morphology from spaceborne synthetic aperture radar

**Model Parameterization:**
- Gopalakrishnan et al. (2021): Improving hurricane boundary layer parameterization based on observations
- Hazelton et al. (2022): Comparison of observation-based PBL schemes in 2020 tropical cyclone forecasts
- Zhang et al. (2015): Impact of boundary layer improvements on HWRF hurricane intensity/structure forecasts

## Leadership Roles & Current Activities

**Active Research Programs (2022-present):**
- Co-PI: ONR TCRI (Tropical Cyclone Rapid Intensification) and MAGPIE projects
- PI: Coordinated Hurricane Atmosphere-Ocean Sampling Experiment (2022-present)
- Co-I: ONR SASCWATCH Project (2024-present)

**Field Program Involvement:**
- Lead Project Scientist and Dropsonde/Radar Scientist for NOAA Aircraft Reconnaissance Missions (2008-present)
- Co-PI: Small unmanned aircraft system field experiments (2010-present)
- PI: NOAA's Ocean Survey Experiment and Gravity Wave Module for Hurricane Field Program (2010-present)

**Prior Major Programs:**
- NOAA Hurricane Forecast Improvement Project Physics Team (2011-present)
- NASA HS3 (Hurricane and Severe Storm Sentinel) Science Team (2012)
- ONR Rapid Intensification in Tropical Cyclones Science Team (2019)
- NOAA Sensing Hazards with Operational Unmanned Technology (SHOUT) Science Team (2014)

**Editorial & Advisory Roles:**
- Section Editor in Chief for Forecasting (2023-present)
- Associate Editor, Journal of the Atmospheric Sciences (2023-present)
- Co-Editor in Chief, Dynamics of Atmospheres and Oceans (2019-present)
- Editor, Tropical Cyclone Research and Review (2018-present)
- WMO Working Group on Tropical Meteorology Research (2020-present)

## Relevance to BST Navy STTR Hazardous Weather Work

Dr. Zhang's expertise is directly relevant to unmanned aircraft systems for hurricane/hazardous weather observation, boundary layer physics measurements, and integration of airborne observations with operational forecasting models.
